Part I

High Level

What storage is, the kinds that exist, how they compare, and how the pieces work together on the cluster. Every ▶ section has a step-through diagram (Next / Back, dots, arrow keys or swipe).

01

Definitions

§ 1.1INTERACTIVE

What Is a Volume?

Definition · Volume
  • What it isA piece of storage, exposed as a directory, that Kubernetes attaches to a Pod.
  • WhySo its containers can read and write files that do not live in the container's own filesystem.
  • DeclaredOnce on the Pod.
  • MountedEach container chooses the path where it appears.
  • TypeDecides where the files come from and how long they live.

A volume always has three parts

  1. Declaration — spec.volumes[] (Pod level)Gives the volume a name and a type (emptyDir, configMap, persistentVolumeClaim, …). It belongs to the Pod, not to any container.
  2. Mount — containers[].volumeMounts[] (container level)Each container that needs the volume refers to it by name and picks a mountPath. Containers that do not mount it cannot see it.
  3. Backing — what the type providesNode disk, node RAM, data from the Kubernetes API, a cloud disk, a network file share… The kubelet prepares it on the node before the containers start.
the-three-parts.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: order-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  volumes:                        # 1 DECLARATION (Pod level)
  - name: logs                    #   the name links declaration ↔ mount
    emptyDir: {}                  # 3 BACKING: the type (here: empty dir on node disk)
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: ghcr.io/jahez/order-service:2.14.0
    volumeMounts:                 # 2 MOUNT (container level)
    - name: logs
      mountPath: /var/log/order   #   where api sees it
  - name: fluent-bit
    image: fluent/fluent-bit:3.1
    volumeMounts:
    - name: logs
      mountPath: /logs            #   same volume, different path
      readOnly: true

Where the volume lives on the node

The kubelet keeps every volume in a folder named after the Pod UID (not the Pod name) and the volume name (not the container or the mountPath). The mountPath exists only inside the container.

node-path-anatomy.txt
/var/lib/kubelet/pods/7f3c9e2a-41b0-4c7e-9d1f-2b8a6e0c5d11/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/logs/
                      └─────────────── pod UID ───────────┘         └── volume type ──┘ └ volume name ┘

 pod UID      = metadata.uid — new for every Pod, even when the name is reused (orders-db-0)
 volume type  = empty-dir · configmap · secret · projected · csi …
 volume name  = spec.volumes[].name  ("logs")

 inside api        → /var/log/order      (mountPath — container view)
 inside fluent-bit → /logs               (mountPath — container view)
 both are bind mounts of the ONE node folder above

 find it:  kubectl get pod <name> -n jahez-prod -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}'
▶ Volume anatomy — what really happens on the node
1 / 6
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Without a volume
The api container writes /tmp/receipts/r-1001.pdf. Without a volume, that file lands in the container's writable layer, a directory on the node owned by the container runtime (…/overlayfs/snapshots/412/fs). No other container can see it.
Step 2 · Container restarts → file gone
The container is OOM-killed. Kubernetes starts a new container from the image, with a new, empty writable layer. The PDF is lost. This is the problem volumes solve.
Step 3 · Declare volumes
The Pod spec now declares logs (emptyDir) and receipts (a PVC). When the Pod is placed on the node, the kubelet creates the volume directory /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/logs/ — before any container starts.
Step 4 · Mount into containers
The container runtime bind-mounts that one directory into api at /var/log/order and into fluent-bit at /logs. Two paths, one directory: what api writes, fluent-bit reads immediately.
Step 5 · Container restarts → file kept
api crashes again. The Pod is still on the node, so the volume directory is untouched and is mounted into the new container. app.log is still there.
Step 6 · Pod deleted → depends on the type
The Pod is deleted. The emptyDir directory is deleted with it (ephemeral). The PVC data is on an EBS disk outside the node; it is only detached and can be mounted by the next Pod (persistent).
ℹ
Mental modelA volume is a drive plugged into the Pod. Every container in the Pod can plug into it at any path. Some drives are thrown away with the Pod (ephemeral); others are kept and plugged into the next Pod (persistent).
§ 1.2INTERACTIVE

Why We Need Volumes

Containers are designed to be disposable. That creates three problems; volumes are the answer to all three.

#Problem without volumesWhat the volume gives youVolume types
1Data is lost. A container's writable layer is thrown away on every restart, and the whole Pod can be replaced at any time.A place for data that survives container restarts — or survives the Pod itself.emptyDir (restarts) · PVC (Pod replacement, node loss)
2Containers cannot share files. Each container has its own filesystem, even inside one Pod.One directory mounted into several containers of the same Pod (or, with RWX, several Pods).emptyDir · RWX PVC (EFS)
3Apps need data from outside the image. Config, credentials and certificates must not be baked into images.Files injected at runtime from Kubernetes objects or external systems.configMap · secret · projected · CSI (Secrets Manager)
▶ The three problems on the Jahez cluster
1 / 6
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Problem 1: a database without a volume
orders-db-0 runs Postgres with nothing mounted at its data directory. Every row is in the container's writable layer on worker-a.
Step 2 · One crash wipes the data
Postgres is OOM-killed and restarted from the clean postgres:16 image: new writable layer, empty data directory. 1.58M rows are lost.
Step 3 · Fix: a persistent volume
A PVC backed by an EBS disk in me-central-1a is mounted at /var/lib/postgresql/data. The rows are written to the disk, not to the container.
Step 4 · Crashes no longer matter
Each restart mounts the same disk again. Nothing is lost.
Step 5 · Problem 2: sharing between containers
On worker-b, the API writes logs to an emptyDir; the fluent-bit sidecar in the same Pod reads the same files and ships them to Elasticsearch.
Step 6 · Problem 3: data from outside the image
On worker-c, catalog-service reads appsettings.json from a configMap volume. Changing the ConfigMap updates the file without rebuilding the image.
§ 1.3

The Two Families: Ephemeral vs Persistent

Every volume type falls into one of two families. The only question that decides the family is: does the data outlive the Pod?

Definition · Ephemeral volume
Created when the Pod starts on a node and deleted when the Pod is removed. Survives container restarts, not Pod replacement. Declared entirely inside the Pod spec.
Definition · Persistent volume
Storage that exists independently of any Pod. A Pod borrows it through a PersistentVolumeClaim; when the Pod goes away the data stays and the next Pod can mount it again.
EventContainer writable layerEphemeral volumePersistent volume
Container restarts✗ lost✓ kept✓ kept
Pod deleted / rescheduled✗ lost✗ lost (recreated empty / re-generated)✓ kept
Node lost✗ lost✗ lost✓ kept (network/cloud disk)
Who creates itcontainer runtimekubelet, from the Pod speca PersistentVolume, claimed by a PVC
Declared in— (implicit)the Pod spec onlyPod → PVC → PV (separate objects)
⚠
Two things that look like exceptionsconfigMap / secret volumes are ephemeral: the files are deleted with the Pod. The ConfigMap or Secret object stays in the API and the files are regenerated for the next Pod.
hostPath is neither: its files belong to one node, so they outlive the Pod but disappear from view as soon as the Pod lands on another node. It is a special case (§2.4).
ℹ
NamingIn this guide persistent volume (lower case) means the family. PersistentVolume / PV means the Kubernetes API object that represents one real disk or share (§2.3.2).
§ 1.4

Glossary — One Meaning per Term

Each term is defined once here and used with exactly this meaning in the rest of the guide.

TermMeaning
writable layerThe container's own filesystem on top of its image. Deleted with the container.
volumeA piece of storage, exposed as a directory, attached to a Pod and mounted into its containers (§1.1).
volume typeThe field under spec.volumes[] (emptyDir, configMap, persistentVolumeClaim…) that decides where the data comes from.
volumeMount / mountPathA container's reference to a volume by name, and the path where it appears inside that container.
ephemeral volumeA volume whose data lives as long as the Pod (§1.3).
persistent volumeA volume whose data outlives the Pod; always used through a PVC (§1.3).
PersistentVolume (PV)Cluster-scoped API object describing one real piece of storage (an EBS volume, an EFS access point).
PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)Namespaced API object: an app's request for storage (size, access mode, class). Bound to exactly one PV.
StorageClassCluster-scoped template that tells Kubernetes how to create PVs on demand (driver + parameters).
provisioningCreating a PV. Static: an admin creates it. Dynamic: a StorageClass creates it when a PVC asks.
bindingLinking one PVC to one PV, exclusively (§4.3).
CSI driverThe plugin that talks to the real storage system (AWS EBS, EFS, Secrets Manager). Runs as a controller Deployment + a node DaemonSet.
attach / mountAttach: connect a cloud disk to a node. Mount: make it appear as a directory, first on the node, then in the container.
access modeHow many nodes / Pods may mount a volume at once: RWO, ROX, RWX, RWOP (§2.3.8).
reclaim policyWhat happens to a PV's disk when its PVC is deleted: Retain or Delete (§4.6).
02

Types

§ 2.1INTERACTIVE

Volume Type Map

Two families, five groups, one special case. Tap a type to jump to its details.

Volume typessorted by one question: does the data outlive the Pod?

Ephemeral

Lifetime = the Pod. Declared only in the Pod spec.
A · Scratch spaceempty at start, filled by the containers
emptyDirdirectory on node diskemptyDir {medium: Memory}tmpfs in RAM
B · Projected from Kubernetesfiles generated from API objects, read-only
configMapconfig filessecretcredentials, on tmpfsdownwardAPIPod's own name, labels, limitsprojectedseveral of the above + SA token in one dir
C · Provided by a drivera CSI driver builds a per-Pod volume
csi (inline)e.g. secrets from AWS Secrets Managerephemeral (generic)a real PVC created & deleted with the Pod

Persistent

Lifetime = independent of the Pod. Used via persistentVolumeClaim → PVC → PV.
A · Block storagea disk attached to one node; the node formats it
EBS (gp3 / io2)cloud disk, one AZ, RWOlocal PVnode's own NVMe, pinned to that node
B · File storagea network filesystem many nodes mount at once
EFS / nfsshared, multi-AZ, RWX
How it is createdsame result, different origin
staticadmin creates the PVdynamicStorageClass creates the PV

Special case · node-bound: hostPath

A real directory of the node. Outlives the Pod, but only on that node — so it is neither ephemeral nor truly persistent. For system DaemonSets only (§2.4).

in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · The map
Three nodes, six Pods, every family in use. Colours stay the same through the guide: emptyDir, tmpfs, projected from Kubernetes, driver-provided, block, file, hostPath.
Step 2 · Ephemeral · scratch
order-service shares an emptyDir between api and fluent-bit on worker-a's disk; payment-service uses medium: Memory for /tmp on worker-c. Both are deleted with their Pod.
Step 3 · Ephemeral · projected from Kubernetes
A secret with DB credentials (tmpfs, worker-a), a configMap and a projected service-account token for AWS access (worker-b). Files are generated by the kubelet from API objects.
Step 4 · Ephemeral · driver-provided
payment-service mounts /mnt/secrets through the Secrets Store CSI driver: values are fetched from AWS Secrets Manager when the Pod starts.
Step 5 · Persistent · block
orders-db-0 uses a PVC bound to an EBS volume in me-central-1a, attached to worker-a as /dev/nvme1n1.
Step 6 · Persistent · file
menu-media replicas mount the same EFS file system over NFS; a file written on worker-c is visible on worker-a.
Step 7 · Special · hostPath
The fluent-bit DaemonSet mounts the real /var/log/pods of worker-b. Powerful, node-bound, security-sensitive.
§ 2.2INTERACTIVE

Ephemeral Volume Types

Ephemeral volumes are declared inside the Pod spec and live exactly as long as the Pod. They differ only in where the files come from.

GroupTypeFiles come fromStored on nodeWritable
A · ScratchemptyDirthe containersdisk (or RAM)✓
B · From KubernetesconfigMap · downwardAPIAPI objects / the Poddiskread-only
B · From Kubernetessecret · projectedAPI objects + tokensRAM (tmpfs)read-only
C · From a drivercsi (inline) · ephemeral (generic)a CSI driver / a provisioned diskdriver / cloud diskdriver / ✓
emptyDirEphemeral · scratch
An empty directory created on the node when the Pod starts, shared by all its containers.
Data comes from
the containers themselves (starts empty)
Lives as long as
the Pod on this node · survives container restarts
Stored on the node
disk: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/<name>/ · RAM with medium: Memory
Inside the container
not copied — a bind mount of the node folder at mountPath, read-write
Updates
live — every write is visible at once to all containers
Shared between
containers of the same Pod only
Use for
sidecar log hand-off · init → app hand-off · scratch · caches
Avoid for
anything needed after the Pod is gone
Must set / protect
sizeLimit + ephemeral-storage limits
▶ emptyDir on the cluster — share, isolate, evict, reschedule
1 / 6
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Created with the Pod
When order-service-…-k2p is placed on worker-a, the kubelet creates the empty directory before the containers start.
Step 2 · Shared inside the Pod
api mounts it at /var/log/order, fluent-bit at /logs (read-only). Same directory.
Step 3 · Not shared across Pods
The replica …-x9q on worker-b has its own, separate emptyDir.
Step 4 · medium: Memory
pricing-ml-0 keeps a 2.1Gi model in a RAM-backed emptyDir; those bytes count against its memory limit.
Step 5 · sizeLimit → eviction
invoice-pdf-job writes 2.4Gi into a 2Gi volume: the kubelet evicts the whole Pod.
Step 6 · Rescheduled = empty
worker-a is drained; the replacement Pod on worker-c starts with a new, empty emptyDir.

YAML sample

order-service-emptydir.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: order-service } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: order-service } }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: ghcr.io/jahez/order-service:2.14.0
        resources:
          requests: { ephemeral-storage: 1Gi }
          limits:   { ephemeral-storage: 3Gi }
        volumeMounts:
        - { name: logs, mountPath: /var/log/order }
        - { name: tmp,  mountPath: /tmp }
      - name: fluent-bit
        image: fluent/fluent-bit:3.1
        volumeMounts:
        - { name: logs, mountPath: /logs, readOnly: true }
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        emptyDir:
          sizeLimit: 1Gi          # disk; over the limit → Pod evicted
      - name: tmp
        emptyDir:
          medium: Memory          # tmpfs; counts toward api memory limit
          sizeLimit: 128Mi
configMapEphemeral · projected from Kubernetes
Each key of a ConfigMap becomes a read-only file in the volume.
Data comes from
a ConfigMap object in the same namespace (≤ 1 MiB)
Lives as long as
the Pod (the ConfigMap object stays in etcd)
Stored on the node
disk: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~configmap/<volume-name>/
Inside the container
not copied — a bind mount of the node folder at mountPath, read-only
Updates
automatic, ~1 min, atomic — not for subPath
Shared between
every Pod that mounts it gets its own copy on its node
Use for
appsettings.json, nginx.conf, feature flags
Avoid for
secrets · large or binary data
Must set / protect
immutable: true for config that must not change in place
QuestionAnswer
Where are the generated files?On the node, in the Pod's volume folder: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~configmap/<volume-name>/ (secret: kubernetes.io~secret/).
Disk or RAM?configMap: node disk. secret (and projected): a tmpfs mounted on that folder — RAM only.
Are they inside the container?No copy is made. The container sees the node folder through a read-only bind mount at its mountPath. Nothing goes into the image or the writable layer.
Who writes them?The kubelet of the node running the Pod — never the container, never other nodes.
How long do they live?From Pod start on that node until the Pod is removed. The ConfigMap/Secret object in etcd lives on independently.
▶ configMap — full lifecycle: object → node folder → container
1 / 10
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Create the object
kubectl apply stores ConfigMap catalog-config in etcd. It is only data in the API — no file exists anywhere yet.
Step 2 · Pod scheduled
catalog-service-…-b declares a configmap volume named config and lands on worker-b. Its containers stay in ContainerCreating until the volume is ready; if the ConfigMap does not exist the Pod waits with a FailedMount event (unless optional: true).
Step 3 · kubelet fetches it
The kubelet on worker-b gets catalog-config from the API server and watches it for changes, keeping it in its in-memory cache. Kubelets on other nodes cannot read it — the node authorizer only allows objects used by Pods on that node.
Step 4 · Files written on the NODE
The kubelet creates /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~configmap/config/ on the node's disk, and writes each key as a file inside a timestamped folder. ..data points to that folder, and appsettings.json is a symlink to ..data/appsettings.json.
Step 5 · Container sees it — by bind mount
The container runtime bind-mounts that node folder at /app/config, read-only. The file is not copied into the container: it is not in the image and not in the container's writable layer. The container only gets a view of the node folder.
Step 6 · App reads it
api opens /app/config/appsettings.json like any local file.
Step 7 · Update
After kubectl apply of v2, the kubelet's watch fires (typically within a minute). It writes a new timestamped folder, atomically swaps ..data, and deletes the old folder. The same mount now shows v2. A subPath mount would still show v1.
Step 8 · Container restart
If api crashes, the new container gets the same node folder mounted again. Nothing is re-downloaded.
Step 9 · Pod deleted
The mounts are removed and the node folder is deleted. The kubelet forgets the object. catalog-config itself remains in etcd; the next Pod gets fresh files.
Step 10 · Object deleted under a running Pod
Deleting catalog-config does not remove the files from running Pods — they keep the last content. New Pods that need it cannot start. Recreate it, or mark the volume optional: true if the app can live without it.

secretEphemeral · projected from Kubernetes
Each key of a Secret becomes a read-only file — kept in RAM, never on the node disk.
Data comes from
a Secret object in the same namespace (≤ 1 MiB, base64 — not encryption)
Lives as long as
the Pod (the Secret object stays in etcd)
Stored on the node
RAM: a tmpfs mounted on /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~secret/<volume-name>/ — only on nodes running a Pod that uses it
Inside the container
not copied — a bind mount of the node folder at mountPath, read-only
Updates
like configMap (not for subPath)
Shared between
every Pod that mounts it gets its own RAM copy on its node
Use for
DB passwords, TLS keys, API tokens
Avoid for
putting secrets in ConfigMaps or images
Must set / protect
KMS encryption at rest · tight RBAC · defaultMode: 0400/0440
QuestionAnswer
Where are the generated files?On the node, in the Pod's volume folder: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~configmap/<volume-name>/ (secret: kubernetes.io~secret/).
Disk or RAM?configMap: node disk. secret (and projected): a tmpfs mounted on that folder — RAM only.
Are they inside the container?No copy is made. The container sees the node folder through a read-only bind mount at its mountPath. Nothing goes into the image or the writable layer.
Who writes them?The kubelet of the node running the Pod — never the container, never other nodes.
How long do they live?From Pod start on that node until the Pod is removed. The ConfigMap/Secret object in etcd lives on independently.

Disk vs RAM — what exists where

secret-on-node.txt
/var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/                      ← DISK (node root filesystem)
├── etc-hosts                                         ← disk, unrelated to the secret
├── containers/api/<id>                               ← disk, termination log
└── volumes/kubernetes.io~secret/db/                  ← DISK: empty directory = mount point only
      ════ tmpfs mounted here ════                    ← from here down: RAM
      ├── ..2026_10_31_00_13_05.4417/password         ← file data + metadata in RAM
      ├── ..data -> ..2026_10_31_00_13_05.4417        ← symlink in RAM
      └── password -> ..data/password                 ← symlink in RAM

Pod deleted → tmpfs unmounted (RAM freed) → empty folder removed → nothing left on disk
▶ secret — full lifecycle: encrypted object → RAM folder on the node → container
1 / 10
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Create the object
kubectl apply stores Secret db-catalog in etcd (encrypted with KMS on EKS). It is only data in the API — no file exists anywhere yet.
Step 2 · Pod scheduled
catalog-service-…-b declares a secret volume named db and lands on worker-b. Its containers stay in ContainerCreating until the volume is ready; if the Secret does not exist the Pod waits with a FailedMount event (unless optional: true).
Step 3 · kubelet fetches it
The kubelet on worker-b gets db-catalog from the API server and watches it for changes, keeping it in its in-memory cache. Kubelets on other nodes cannot read it — the node authorizer only allows objects used by Pods on that node.
Step 4 · Files written on the NODE
The kubelet creates /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~secret/db/, mounts a tmpfs there (RAM), and writes each key as a file inside a timestamped folder. ..data points to that folder, and password is a symlink to ..data/password.
Step 5 · Container sees it — by bind mount
The container runtime bind-mounts that node folder at /var/run/secrets/db, read-only. The file is not copied into the container: it is not in the image and not in the container's writable layer. The container only gets a view of the node folder.
Step 6 · App reads it
api opens /var/run/secrets/db/password like any local file.
Step 7 · Update
After kubectl apply of v2, the kubelet's watch fires (typically within a minute). It writes a new timestamped folder, atomically swaps ..data, and deletes the old folder. The same mount now shows v2. A subPath mount would still show v1.
Step 8 · Container restart
If api crashes, the new container gets the same node folder mounted again. Nothing is re-downloaded.
Step 9 · Pod deleted
The mounts are removed and the node folder is deleted — the tmpfs is unmounted and the RAM freed. The kubelet forgets the object. db-catalog itself remains in etcd; the next Pod gets fresh files.
Step 10 · Object deleted under a running Pod
Deleting db-catalog does not remove the files from running Pods — they keep the last content. New Pods that need it cannot start. Recreate it, or mark the volume optional: true if the app can live without it.

YAML sample

db-catalog-secret.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-catalog
  namespace: jahez-prod
type: Opaque
stringData:
  password: change-me-via-external-secrets
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: catalog-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: catalog-service } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: catalog-service } }
    spec:
      securityContext: { runAsUser: 10001, fsGroup: 10001 }
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: ghcr.io/jahez/catalog-service:4.2.1
        volumeMounts:
        - name: db
          mountPath: /var/run/secrets/db
          readOnly: true
      volumes:
      - name: db
        secret:
          secretName: db-catalog
          defaultMode: 0440               # owner+group read (fsGroup 10001)
          items:
          - key: password
            path: password

Files that contain facts about the Pod itself: name, namespace, labels, annotations, requests and limits.

Inside the container
not copied — a bind mount of the node folder at mountPath, read-only

in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)

Step 1 · The source is the Pod
The Pod has labels app=catalog-service, version=2.14 and a CPU limit of 500m. A downwardAPI volume lists which of these fields become files.
Step 2 · No extra object
The kubelet on worker-b already holds this Pod's object; there is no ConfigMap or Secret to fetch.
Step 3 · Files on the node disk
The kubelet writes one file per item into …/kubernetes.io~downward-api/podinfo/, using the same timestamped folder + ..data symlink layout as configMaps.
Step 4 · Mounted into the container
The folder is bind-mounted read-only at /etc/podinfo: name, labels, cpu-limit.
Step 5 · App reads values
cpu-limit contains 500 (divisor 1m), so the app sizes its worker pool; name tags every log line.
Step 6 · Labels change
kubectl label pod … version=2.15 --overwrite → the kubelet rewrites the set and swaps ..data. The same value as an env var would stay at 2.14.
Step 7 · Pod deleted
The folder is removed. Nothing needs to be kept: the data was the Pod itself.

YAML sample

downward-api.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: catalog-service-probe
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels: { app: catalog-service, version: "2.14" }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: ghcr.io/jahez/catalog-service:4.2.1
    resources:
      limits: { cpu: 500m, memory: 1Gi }
    volumeMounts:
    - name: podinfo
      mountPath: /etc/podinfo
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: podinfo
    downwardAPI:
      items:
      - path: name
        fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.name }
      - path: labels                       # updates when labels change
        fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.labels }
      - path: cpu-limit
        resourceFieldRef: { containerName: api, resource: limits.cpu, divisor: 1m }   # "500"
      - path: mem-limit
        resourceFieldRef: { containerName: api, resource: limits.memory, divisor: 1Mi } # "1024"

One directory that combines several sources: secret, configMap, downwardAPI, serviceAccountToken, clusterTrustBundle.
Data comes from

Lives as long as
the Pod; tokens are rotated before they expire
Stored on the node
RAM: a tmpfs on /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~projected/<volume-name>/
Inside the container
not copied — a bind mount of the node folder at mountPath, read-only
Updates

Shared between

▶ projected — full lifecycle: four sources into one RAM folder
1 / 7
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Four sources
Secret db-catalog, ConfigMap catalog-config, a service-account token and the Pod name go into one volume.
Step 2 · kubelet gathers them
The kubelet on worker-b fetches the Secret and ConfigMap and calls the TokenRequest API for a token bound to this Pod, audience sts.amazonaws.com, valid 1 h.
Step 3 · Written into RAM
A tmpfs is mounted on the volume folder (the disk keeps only the empty mount point) and every source is written into one timestamped folder.
Step 4 · One directory in the container
Bind-mounted at /var/run/catalog: password, appsettings.json, token, pod-name.
Step 5 · AWS access without keys
The AWS SDK reads AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE and exchanges the token with STS for temporary credentials (IRSA).
Step 6 · Token rotation
Before the token expires the kubelet writes a new set with a fresh token and swaps ..data. The SDK re-reads the file.
Step 7 · Pod deleted
tmpfs unmounted, RAM freed. The Pod-bound token stops being valid.

YAML sample

catalog-projected.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: catalog-sa
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/catalog-service-s3
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: catalog-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: catalog-service } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: catalog-service } }
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: catalog-sa
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: ghcr.io/jahez/catalog-service:4.2.1
        env:
        - { name: AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE, value: /var/run/catalog/token }
        - { name: AWS_ROLE_ARN, value: "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/catalog-service-s3" }
        volumeMounts:
        - { name: catalog, mountPath: /var/run/catalog, readOnly: true }
      volumes:
      - name: catalog
        projected:
          defaultMode: 0440
          sources:
          - secret:
              name: db-catalog
              items: [{ key: password, path: password }]
          - configMap:
              name: catalog-config
              items: [{ key: appsettings.Production.json, path: appsettings.json }]
          - serviceAccountToken:
              path: token
              audience: sts.amazonaws.com
              expirationSeconds: 3600
          - downwardAPI:
              items:
              - path: pod-name
                fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.name }

Step 1 · Declared inline
The Pod declares csi: {driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io, …} pointing at SecretProviderClass payments-aws.
Step 2 · Node plugin
The driver + AWS provider DaemonSet on worker-c is called by the kubelet when the Pod starts.
Step 3 · Fetch with the Pod's identity
The provider uses the Pod's service account (IRSA) to read Secrets Manager.
Step 4 · Files appear
Values are written to a tmpfs and mounted at /mnt/secrets; rotation rewrites them.

Mirroring into a Kubernetes Secret (for env vars) stores the value in etcd again — use only if needed.

payment-secrets-csi.yaml
apiVersion: secrets-store.csi.x-k8s.io/v1
kind: SecretProviderClass
metadata:
  name: payments-aws
  namespace: jahez-prod

  provider: aws
  parameters:
    objects: |
      - objectName: "prod/payments/stc-pay-key"
        objectType: "secretsmanager"
        objectAlias: "stc-pay-key"
      - objectName: "prod/payments/psp-token"
        objectType: "secretsmanager"
        objectAlias: "psp-token"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payment-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: payment-service } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: payment-service } }
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: payment-sa        # IRSA role allowed to read the secrets
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: ghcr.io/jahez/payment-service:5.0.3
        volumeMounts:
        - { name: secrets, mountPath: /mnt/secrets, readOnly: true }
      volumes:
      - name: secrets
        csi:                                 # inline: no PVC, no PV
          driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io
          readOnly: true
          volumeAttributes:
            secretProviderClass: payments-aws

YAML sample

invoice-render-generic-ephemeral.yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: ebs-gp3-delete
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
reclaimPolicy: Delete                        # disk removed with the PVC
parameters: { type: gp3, encrypted: "true" }
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: invoice-render
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  parallelism: 3
  completions: 3
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: OnFailure
      containers:
      - name: render
        image: ghcr.io/jahez/invoice-render:1.4.0
        volumeMounts:
        - { name: scratch, mountPath: /scratch }
      volumes:
      - name: scratch
        ephemeral:
          volumeClaimTemplate:
            metadata:
              labels: { app: invoice-render }
            spec:
              accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
              storageClassName: ebs-gp3-delete
              resources:
                requests:
                  storage: 50Gi
§ 2.3.1

Persistent Volumes · The Problem & the Idea

Ephemeral volumes are simple: everything is written inside the Pod spec and dies with the Pod. A database disk cannot work that way.

The problem

#Why a disk cannot simply be written inside the Pod spec
1The disk must outlive the Pod. Pods are deleted and recreated all the time; the orders data must not be.
2Two different teams. The app team knows "Postgres needs 100Gi". The platform team knows "use EBS gp3, encrypted, in me-central-1". Neither should have to write the other's part.
3Portability. The same Deployment YAML must work on EKS, on a laptop cluster and in the exam — only the storage behind it differs.
4Control. Disks cost money; someone must decide sizes, classes and what happens when they are no longer needed.

The idea: split "what I need" from "what exists"

Definition · Persistent volume (the idea)
Storage is described by its own API objects, separate from the Pod. The app asks for storage (PVC), Kubernetes finds or creates real storage (PV), links the two, and the Pod only says which request it uses.

One analogy, used to the end of this group

KubernetesApartment rentalMeaning
PVan apartment that existsa real piece of storage (an EBS disk, an EFS share)
PVCyour rental request: "2 rooms, near the metro"what the app needs: size, access mode, class
StorageClassa builder who constructs a new apartment matching your requestcreates a new PV automatically when a PVC asks
Bindingthe lease — one tenant per apartmentone PVC ↔ one PV, exclusive
Podthe person living there — can move out and back in; the furniture staysmounts the PVC; can be deleted and recreated; the data stays
Reclaim policyafter the lease ends: keep the apartment or demolish itRetain keeps the disk, Delete destroys it
§ 2.3.2INTERACTIVE

The Objects: PVC, PV, StorageClass — and the Pod

Definition · PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)
A request for storage in a namespace: how much, how it will be mounted (access mode) and which StorageClass. Written by the app team.
Definition · PersistentVolume (PV)
The record of one real piece of storage (an EBS disk, an EFS share). Cluster-scoped. Created by a StorageClass or by an admin.
Definition · StorageClass
A recipe that tells Kubernetes how to create new PVs on demand: which CSI driver and which settings (gp3, encrypted…). Written by the platform team.
Definition · Pod (the user)
Mounts storage by naming a PVC in volumes[].persistentVolumeClaim.claimName. Never names a PV or a disk.
▶ Pod → PVC → PV → disk
1 / 5
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Pod
The Pod spec contains only claimName: orders-db-data.
Step 2 · PVC
The claim in jahez-prod asks for 100Gi, ReadWriteOnce, class ebs-gp3.
Step 3 · PV
A PV is bound to that claim. It holds the technical details: size, zone and the real disk ID.
Step 4 · The real disk
The EBS volume in AWS where the bytes are stored. Kubernetes reaches it through the EBS CSI driver.
Step 5 · Only the Pod is temporary
Deleting the Pod leaves the other three untouched. That is what "persistent" means.
ObjectScopeWritten byAnswers
Pod volumesnamespaceapp teamWhich claim do I mount, and where?
PersistentVolumeClaimnamespaceapp teamWhat storage do I need?
PersistentVolumeclusterStorageClass or adminWhat storage exists, and where is it?
StorageClassclusterplatform teamHow is new storage created?
▶ All the objects on the cluster — scopes and links

↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · StorageClasses
The platform team publishes classes such as ebs-gp3 (block) and efs-shared (file).
Step 2 · Static PV (optional)
For a disk that already exists, an admin writes a PV that points at it.
Step 3 · PVCs in the namespace
The app team writes claims in jahez-prod.
Step 4 · Binding — always 1:1
Each claim is bound to exactly one PV.
Step 5 · Pods use the claim
The Pod only names the claim.
Step 6 · Node-side records
VolumeAttachment records which node a PV is attached to.

PV, StorageClass and provisioning — in detail

Definition · PV — a reference to real storage
A Kubernetes object that is the cluster's record of one real piece of storage (an EBS disk, an EFS share, a local drive): its size, access modes, where it is, and what happens to it at the end. It is the record, not the disk: deleting the PV object does not always delete the disk — the reclaimPolicy decides.
Definition · StorageClass — a factory / template
Written once by the platform team. It tells the CSI driver what kind of disk to create, when, where, and its life rules. Each PVC chooses one. Every new PVC that asks a class gets a new, separate disk + PV with the same settings; the PVC decides the size and access mode.

How a PV comes to exist — provisioning

Static and dynamic are only about how the PV and its disk are created. Mounting comes later and is the same for both: the kubelet and the CSI driver attach and mount the disk when a Pod uses the claim.

Static (manual)Dynamic (StorageClass)
The diskalready exists (old EBS volume, NFS share, local disk)does not exist yet — it is created now
Who writes the PVan admin, by handthe CSI driver's provisioner, automatically
Triggerthe admin applies a PVa PVC that names the class (once per PVC)
Talks to AWSnobody — Kubernetes only learns about the diskthe CSI driver calls the AWS API (CreateVolume)
storageClassName"" or a name used only as a matching labelthe class that builds the disk
Typical useimport existing data, NFS, local NVMealmost every new workload

One class, many claims — what is the same and what differs

Same every time (from the StorageClass)Different every time (from the PVC)
disk type (gp3, io2, EFS…) and driverthe disk itself: new vol-… ID and new PV pvc-<uid>
IOPS, throughput, encryption, filesystemsize: resources.requests.storage
when and where it is created (volumeBindingMode)access mode and volumeMode
reclaimPolicy, allowVolumeExpansionname, namespace, starting data (dataSource)
ℹ
ExamplePVC menu-cache asks 20Gi → vol-0b2e…, gp3, 3000 IOPS, encrypted. PVC orders-data asks 100Gi → vol-0c3a…, gp3, 3000 IOPS, encrypted. Same recipe, two different disks. When their Pods restart or move, they get the same disks back — nothing new is created.
▶ Static — the disk already exists, the admin introduces it
1 / 5
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · The disk already exists
An EBS volume vol-0aa13… with years of finance reports sits in me-central-1a. It was created outside Kubernetes, so the cluster does not know about it.
Step 2 · The admin writes a PV
A person on the platform team applies a PV whose csi.volumeHandle is that disk ID. Kubernetes now has a reference to the disk. Nothing is created in AWS. Phase: Available.
Step 3 · The app team claims it
A PVC asks for 500Gi with storageClassName: "" and volumeName: legacy-reports. Kubernetes binds them 1:1.
Step 4 · A Pod uses it
The Pod names the claim. Because the PV's nodeAffinity says zone 1a, it is scheduled on a 1a node. The disk is attached there and mounted at /data: the old reports are visible at once.
Step 5 · Result
Static = Kubernetes learned about an existing disk. With Retain, deleting the PVC leaves the disk and data in AWS.
static-existing-disk.yaml
# The disk vol-0aa13c5e8f2b47d10 already exists in AWS (me-central-1a)
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: legacy-reports
spec:
  # ① What is the disk?
  capacity:
    storage: 500Gi
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  # ② Where is it really?
  csi:
    driver: ebs.csi.aws.com
    volumeHandle: vol-0aa13c5e8f2b47d10     # the EXISTING disk
    fsType: ext4
  # ③ Who may use it?
  nodeAffinity:
    required:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: topology.ebs.csi.aws.com/zone
          operator: In
          values: [me-central-1a]
  storageClassName: ""                      # no class: nothing will be created
  # ④ What happens at the end?
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: reports-archive
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What do I need?
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 500Gi
  # ② Where does it come from?
  storageClassName: ""
  volumeName: legacy-reports                # exactly this existing PV
▶ Dynamic — one StorageClass, claims from different Deployments
1 / 5
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · The factory
The platform team publishes StorageClass ebs-gp3 once. No disk exists yet — a class is a recipe, not storage.
Step 2 · menu-service asks
The menu team applies PVC menu-cache (20Gi). With WaitForFirstConsumer it stays Pending until a Pod needs it.
Step 3 · Disk #1 is built
The menu Pod is scheduled on worker-b (zone 1b). The EBS CSI driver calls AWS and creates vol-0b2e… (20Gi) in 1b, writes PV pvc-7a1f… and binds it. The disk is attached to worker-b.
Step 4 · orders-service asks the same class
PVC orders-data (100Gi) names the same class. Its Pod lands on worker-a (zone 1a), so a second, separate disk vol-0c3a… is created there with its own PV.
Step 5 · Same recipe, different disks
Both disks are gp3, 3000 IOPS, encrypted — from the class. Size, zone, ID and owner differ — from each PVC and its Pod. One class → many PVs; each PV ↔ exactly one PVC.
dynamic-one-class-two-claims.yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: ebs-gp3
# ① Who builds the disk?
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
# ② What kind of disk?  (SAME for every PVC)
parameters:
  type: gp3
  iops: "3000"
  encrypted: "true"
# ③ When and where?
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer     # disk is born in the Pod's zone
# ④ Life rules?
allowVolumeExpansion: true
reclaimPolicy: Delete
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: menu-cache
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What do I need?  (DIFFERENT per PVC)
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi
  # ② Where does it come from?
  storageClassName: ebs-gp3
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: orders-data
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What do I need?
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Gi
  # ② Where does it come from?
  storageClassName: ebs-gp3                 # same class → a second, separate disk

The idea in one paragraph

Definition · Why a crash or a new version keeps the same disk
When a PVC asks a StorageClass, the class creates a new disk in AWS, then creates a PV for it and binds it to the PVC. From then on the PVC and the PV are stored in etcd (the control plane) and hold the metadata of the disk that was already created. So when the Pod or the Deployment crashes, or a new version is deployed, the old PVC is not deleted — it is still there. The new Pod names the same claim, and Kubernetes only has to connect and mount the existing disk into the container. Nothing new is created.
DetailWhat it means
The PVC is its own objectThe Deployment only mentions the claim by name (claimName); it does not own it. A crash, a new version, a rollback, even kubectl delete deployment leaves the PVC untouched.
The disk details are in the PVThe PVC holds the link (volumeName: pvc-9d4c…); the PV holds the real disk ID (csi.volumeHandle: vol-0c3a…), size, zone and reclaim policy. Chain in etcd: PVC → PV → EBS disk.
CreateVolume runs onceThe disk is built only the first time the claim is bound. Every later Pod reuses it.
What happenedStorage work Kubernetes does
Container crash, restarted in the same PodNothing — the mount is still in place.
New Pod on the same node (new version, Pod deleted)The disk is still attached to the node; the kubelet only mounts it into the new Pod's folder.
New Pod on another node in the same zone (drain, node lost)Detach from the old node → attach to the new node (AWS AttachVolume) → mount into the Pod.
New Pod can only go to a node in another zoneCannot attach — EBS stays in its zone → Pod Pending.
The PVC is deleted or renamedThe only case that changes the disk: the old PV follows its reclaimPolicy; a new claim gets a new, empty disk.

In short: the Pod changes, the claim stays, and Kubernetes reconnects the same disk to whichever Pod uses that claim.

▶ Failure and new versions — new PV or the same one?
1 / 6
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Running
orders-service v2.14 runs on worker-a. Its Pod uses PVC orders-data → PV pvc-9d4c… → disk vol-0c3a… with 18 GB of data.
Step 2 · Container crash
The container is OOMKilled and restarted inside the same Pod. Same mount, same disk — storage is not involved at all.
Step 3 · Pod lost or node drained
The Deployment creates a new Pod (new name, new UID) on worker-c, which is in the same zone. The disk is detached from worker-a and attached to worker-c. Same PVC, same PV, same data.
Step 4 · New version v2.15
A new image creates a new ReplicaSet and a new Pod, but the Pod template still says claimName: orders-data. With strategy: Recreate the old Pod stops first, then v2.15 mounts the same disk. No new PV.
Step 5 · The rule
The disk follows the PVC — not the Pod, not the image, not the Deployment revision. Every version of the Deployment shares the one PV.
Step 6 · When you DO get a new disk
Only a new PVC (new name like orders-data-v2, or deleting and re-creating the claim) makes the class build a new, empty disk. The old disk is destroyed (Delete) or kept as Released (Retain).
orders-deployment-new-version.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 1                               # one RWO EBS disk → one Pod
  strategy:
    type: Recreate                          # stop old Pod first, so the disk can move
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: orders-service }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: orders-service }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: jahez/orders-service:2.15.0  # change the version freely…
        # ── Where does the container see the storage? ──
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /app/data
      # ── What storage does the Pod have? ──
      volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: orders-data            # …but keep this name: it IS the disk
⚠
RWO disk + RollingUpdateA rolling update starts the new Pod before stopping the old one. If the new Pod lands on another node, an EBS (RWO) disk cannot attach to two nodes → Multi-Attach error and the rollout hangs. For a single Deployment Pod with an EBS disk use strategy: Recreate, or use a StatefulSet (each replica keeps its own PVC: data-orders-db-0, -1…).
§ 2.3.3

The 6 Principles of Persistent Volumes

Six rules that are always true. Every later section is one of these rules in more detail.

  1. A Pod never touches a disk directly — it only names a PVC.Changing the storage (EBS → EFS, laptop → cloud) never changes the Pod spec. → §2.3.2
  2. A PVC is a request; a PV is the storage. One PVC binds to exactly one PV.Binding is exclusive. Sharing happens by many Pods using one PVC, never by many PVCs using one PV. → §4.3
  3. The PV and its data outlive Pods.Delete, restart or reschedule the Pod — the data waits for the next Pod. → §2.3.4
  4. A PV is either created for you or registered by an admin.Dynamic: a StorageClass creates it when a PVC asks. Static: an admin writes it for storage that already exists. → §2.3.5
  5. The storage kind decides how many Pods can use it and where they can run.Block (EBS): one node, one zone. File (EFS): many nodes, any zone. → §2.3.6, §2.3.8
  6. The reclaim policy decides what happens to the disk when the PVC is deleted.Retain: the disk is kept. Delete: the disk is destroyed. → §4.6
§ 2.3.4INTERACTIVE

The Full Lifecycle — From Claim to Reclaim

One claim from birth to deletion. Watch which objects change at each step — and which never do.

▶ Persistent volume — the full lifecycle on the cluster
1 / 7
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Create the claim
kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml. The PVC is Pending: with WaitForFirstConsumer the disk is created only once a Pod needs it, in that Pod's zone.
Step 2 · Pod scheduled → disk created → bound
The Deployment's Pod is scheduled to worker-b (zone 1b). The ebs-gp3 StorageClass creates EBS vol-07c… in 1b and a PV for it; the PVC and PV are Bound.
Step 3 · Attach, mount, write
The disk is attached to worker-b as /dev/nvme1n1 and mounted into the container at /var/lib/postgresql/data. All rows go to the disk.
Step 4 · Pod deleted — data stays
A rollout, crash or drain deletes the Pod. The disk is unmounted and detached, but the PVC, PV and EBS disk are unchanged.
Step 5 · New Pod — same data
The new Pod uses the same claimName, so the same disk is attached again (on any node in zone 1b). All 1.2M rows are there.
Step 6 · Delete the claim (reclaim: Delete)
Only when you delete the PVC does the storage end. With Delete (the default for dynamic PVs) the EBS disk is destroyed.
Step 7 · Delete the claim (reclaim: Retain)
With Retain the PV becomes Released and the disk is kept, so an admin can back it up or reuse it (§4.6).
orders-db-lifecycle.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: orders-db-data
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: ebs-gp3          # dynamic: no PV written by hand
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-db
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 1                        # one disk, one writer
  strategy:
    type: Recreate                   # old Pod releases the disk before the new one starts
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: orders-db }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: orders-db }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:16.4
        env:
        - { name: PGDATA, value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata }
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: db-orders, key: password } }
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
      volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: orders-db-data
watch-each-step.sh
kubectl get pvc orders-db-data -n jahez-prod            # step 1: Pending
kubectl apply -f orders-db-lifecycle.yaml
kubectl get pvc,pv -n jahez-prod                        # step 2: Bound
kubectl delete pod -n jahez-prod -l app=orders-db       # step 4: Pod gone, PVC still Bound
kubectl get pvc orders-db-data -n jahez-prod            #         → Bound
kubectl scale deploy orders-db -n jahez-prod --replicas=0
kubectl delete pvc orders-db-data -n jahez-prod         # step 6: storage ends here
kubectl get pv                                          # Delete → gone · Retain → Released
§ 2.3.5INTERACTIVE

Where PVs Come From: Dynamic vs Static

Definition · Dynamic provisioning
A PVC names a StorageClass; the class's driver creates the disk and the PV automatically. The builder constructs a new apartment for your request.
Definition · Static provisioning
An admin writes the PV first, pointing at storage that already exists; a PVC then binds to it. The apartment already exists and is listed.

Do I write a PV, or only a PVC?

Your situationYou writeWho creates the PV
A StorageClass exists (normal on EKS: ebs-gp3, efs-shared)PVC + Deployment/StatefulSet — no PVthe StorageClass driver, automatically (dynamic)
StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplatesStatefulSet only — no PV, no separate PVCcontroller creates PVCs → driver creates PVs
An existing disk / NFS share / hostPath / local disk, or the task says "create a PV"PV first, then PVC, then the Podyou (static)
ℹ
RuleIf there is a StorageClass that can create the storage, never write a PV yourself. You write a PV only when the storage already exists and Kubernetes must be told about it (§2.3.5). The Pod always references the PVC, never the PV.
▶ Static vs dynamic provisioning
1 / 10
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Existing disk
A 500Gi EBS volume holds reports migrated from the old platform.
Step 2 · Admin writes a PV
It points to vol-0aa… with Retain.
Step 3 · Developer claims it
storageClassName: "" + volumeName → only that PV can bind.
Step 4 · Bound
claimRef on the PV, volumeName on the PVC.
Step 5 · Mounted
Pods use the claim normally.
Step 6 · StorageClass exists
ebs-gp3 with WaitForFirstConsumer.
Step 7 · PVC waits
Pending until a Pod uses it — normal.
Step 8 · Pod scheduled
worker-b in me-central-1b is chosen.
Step 9 · Provisioned there
The driver creates the disk in 1b and a matching PV; they are bound.
Step 10 · Same end state
A bound PV/PVC pair. Only who creates the PV, and when, differs.
§ 2.3.6

Storage Kinds: Block vs File

For persistent volumes, "type" means storage kind: what the node actually receives. There are only two main kinds, plus a node-pinned variant.

Definition · Block storage
A raw disk attached to one machine. That machine's kernel formats it (ext4/xfs) and owns the filesystem — like an SSD plugged into one computer.
Definition · File storage
A filesystem that lives on a server. Machines access files over the network (NFS) — like a shared network drive many computers open at once.
Block (Amazon EBS)File (Amazon EFS)
What the node getsa device /dev/nvme1n1, formatted by the nodea network mount fs-…:/ (NFS)
Who owns the filesystemthe node's kernelthe storage server (AWS)
Machines at onceone (RWO / RWOP)many (RWX)
Scopeone Availability Zonewhole Region
Latencylowest — like a local diskhigher — every operation goes over the network
Best fordatabases: Postgres, Redis, Elasticsearch, Kafkashared files: uploads, images, exports
KindWhat it isExample productMoves with the Pod?
Block (network)a cloud disk attached to one nodeAmazon EBSyes — to another node in the same zone
Block (local)a disk physically inside one nodeinstance-store NVMe (local PV)no — Pod pinned to that node
Filea network file systemAmazon EFS, NFSyes — anywhere in the region
ℹ
What about object storage (Amazon S3)?S3 stores objects through an HTTP API, not as a disk or file system. Apps use it with an SDK; it is not a normal Kubernetes volume kind. (AWS uses it behind the scenes for EBS snapshots.)

The same comparison drawn on the cluster: §3.3.

▶ PVC → EBS on three zones (StatefulSet replicas)
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · One claim per replica
The StatefulSet creates data-orders-db-{0,1,2}; each Pod only names its claim.
Step 2 · Created in the Pod's zone
With WaitForFirstConsumer, each disk is created where its Pod was scheduled: 1a, 1b, 1c.
Step 3 · Attached and staged
The disk appears on the node as /dev/nvme1n1, is formatted on first use and mounted once per node.
Step 4 · Mounted into the Pod
A bind mount exposes it at /var/lib/postgresql/data. Every call is in §4.2.

YAML sample

orders-db-ebs.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: orders-db-hl, namespace: jahez-prod }
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector: { app: orders-db }
  ports: [{ port: 5432 }]
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: orders-db
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  serviceName: orders-db-hl
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: orders-db } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: orders-db } }
    spec:
      securityContext: { fsGroup: 999 }
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:16.4
        env:
        - { name: PGDATA, value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata }
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: db-orders, key: password } }
        volumeMounts:
        - { name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data }
  volumeClaimTemplates:                       # → data-orders-db-0/1/2, one EBS each
  - metadata: { name: data }
    spec:
      accessModes: [ReadWriteOncePod]
      storageClassName: ebs-gp3               # WaitForFirstConsumer (§8.0)
      resources: { requests: { storage: 100Gi } }

1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)

Step 1 · Regional file system
EFS has a mount target in each AZ.
Step 2 · Mounted per Pod
The EFS CSI node plugin mounts the access point over NFS (TLS) directly at each Pod's volume folder on the node.
Step 3 · Shared bytes
A file written on worker-a is served by replicas on worker-b and worker-c.
Step 4 · One claim, many Pods
Every replica uses the same PVC; the PVC is still bound to exactly one PV.

apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: menu-media
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]
  storageClassName: efs-shared                # efs-ap: one access point per PVC (§8.0)
  resources: { requests: { storage: 200Gi } } # required, not enforced by EFS
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-media
  namespace: jahez-prod

  replicas: 3

    spec:
      securityContext: { runAsUser: 10001, fsGroup: 10001 }

        - { name: media, mountPath: /media }
      volumes:
      - name: media
        persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: menu-media }

▶ local PV — fastest disk, pinned to one node
1 / 5
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · NVMe inside the node
worker-a is an i4i instance; its instance-store NVMe /dev/nvme1n1 is formatted and mounted at /mnt/nvme0 during node bootstrap.
Step 2 · Static PV with nodeAffinity
PV local-pv-worker-a points at /mnt/nvme0 and is pinned to kubernetes.io/hostname=worker-a.
Step 3 · Pod pinned to the node
kafka-0 binds it and can only run on worker-a. The kubelet bind-mounts /mnt/nvme0 into the Pod's volume folder and then into the container.
Step 4 · No moving
Restarts and rollouts return to worker-a. If worker-a is down, kafka-0 stays Pending.
Step 5 · Instance replaced = data lost
Instance-store disks are wiped when the instance stops. Kafka re-replicates from its peers after you delete the stale PV/PVC.

YAML sample

kafka-local-pv.yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: local-nvme
provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
reclaimPolicy: Retain
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: local-pv-worker-a
spec:
  capacity: { storage: 1700Gi }
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: local-nvme
  local:
    path: /mnt/nvme0                          # already formatted + mounted on the node
  nodeAffinity:
    required:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: kubernetes.io/hostname
          operator: In
          values: [worker-a]
---
# Kafka StatefulSet (excerpt of the storage part)
volumeClaimTemplates:
- metadata: { name: data }
  spec:
    accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
    storageClassName: local-nvme
    resources: { requests: { storage: 1700Gi } }
§ 2.3.8INTERACTIVE

Access Modes

Access modes follow directly from the storage kind: block storage can be written by one node (RWO) or one Pod (RWOP); file storage can be written by many nodes (RWX).

Definition · Access mode
A rule on a PV/PVC stating how many nodes or Pods may mount the volume at the same time, and whether they may write.
ModeAbbrWho can mountJahez backendsTypical use
ReadWriteOnceRWOread-write by Pods on one nodeEBSdatabases
ReadWriteOncePodRWOPread-write by one Pod in the clusterEBS (CSI)strict single writer
ReadWriteManyRWXread-write by many nodesEFSshared media
ReadOnlyManyROXread-only by many nodesEFS, restored snapshotsmodels, static assets
▶ Access modes on the cluster — node-scoped vs Pod-scoped
1 / 5
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · RWO is per node
orders-db-0 mounts an EBS-backed RWO claim on worker-a.
Step 2 · Same node: allowed
Another Pod on worker-a can mount the same RWO claim — RWO limits nodes, not Pods.
Step 3 · Other node: Multi-Attach
A Pod on worker-b would need the disk attached to worker-b too; EBS cannot, so the Pod waits with a Multi-Attach error.
Step 4 · RWX with EFS
Pods on all three nodes mount one RWX claim.
Step 5 · RWOP
With ReadWriteOncePod even a second Pod on the same node is refused.
⚠
Access mode ≠ bindingRWX does not let several PVCs bind one PV. Binding is always one PV ↔ one PVC. RWX lets many Pods mount that one PVC.
§ 2.3.9INTERACTIVE

Storage Sharing: Same Node vs Different Nodes

Two questions decide everything: does each Pod get its own claim? (StatefulSet = yes, Deployment = no) and what does the access mode allow? Each case below runs the same test: write a file in Pod 1, then try to read it from the other Pods.

Access modes in plain words

ModeFull namePlain meaningTypical storage
RWOReadWriteOnceThe volume can be mounted read-write on one node at a time. Several Pods on that same node may all use it; Pods on other nodes cannot.Amazon EBS
RWOPReadWriteOncePodRead-write by exactly one Pod in the whole cluster. A second Pod is refused even on the same node.Amazon EBS (CSI)
RWXReadWriteManyRead-write by many Pods on many nodes at the same time.Amazon EFS, NFS
ROXReadOnlyManyRead-only by many Pods on many nodes.EFS, restored snapshots
⚠
The two facts people mix up1) "Once" in RWO means one node, not one Pod. 2) The access mode controls who may mount the volume; it does not copy data. Whether Pods share data depends only on whether they mount the same claim.

Prerequisites (used by every case)

storage-cases-prereqs.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: storage-cases
---
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: ebs-gp3
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com                 # Amazon EBS — block storage
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer      # disk created in the zone of the first Pod
reclaimPolicy: Delete                        # lab: disks are removed with the PVC
allowVolumeExpansion: true
parameters:
  type: gp3
  encrypted: "true"
---
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: efs-shared
provisioner: efs.csi.aws.com                 # Amazon EFS — file storage
reclaimPolicy: Delete
parameters:
  provisioningMode: efs-ap                   # one access point (folder) per PVC
  fileSystemId: fs-0c1d2e3f4a5b6c7d8
  directoryPerms: "777"                      # lab: any uid may write
  basePath: /storage-cases
cleanup-between-cases.sh
kubectl delete deploy,sts,svc --all -n storage-cases
kubectl delete pvc --all -n storage-cases

Group 1 · all Pods on the same node (worker-a)

Pinned with nodeSelector: kubernetes.io/hostname: worker-a.

Case 1.1 · Deployment + one EBS claim (RWO) · 3 replicas on the same node

same node · worker-aRWO · EBS⚠ starts — all share one disk

What it means: a Deployment has one Pod template, so every replica gets the same claimName → the same disk. RWO only says "one node at a time"; because all three Pods are on worker-a, all three may mount it.

Why it is risky: three Pods write to one filesystem with nothing coordinating them. A database would corrupt its files. Fine only for read-mostly data written by one replica.

▶ Case 1.1 — write in Pod 1, read from the others
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · objects
One PVC and a Deployment with 3 replicas pinned to worker-a.
Step 2 · all mount one disk
The EBS disk is attached once to worker-a; all three Pods bind-mount the same folder.
Step 3 · write in Pod a
echo hello-from-pod-1 > /data/hello.txt
Step 4 · read from b and c
Both read the file — it is the same disk.
case-1-1-deploy-ebs-rwo-same-node.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: shared-ebs
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: ebs-gp3
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: case11
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: ' if strategy else 
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: case11 }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: case11 }
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        kubernetes.io/hostname: worker-a        # all Pods on ONE node (use: kubectl get nodes -L kubernetes.io/hostname)
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600000"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
      volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: shared-ebs           # every replica points at THIS one claim
prove-it.sh
kubectl get pods -n storage-cases -l app=case11 -o wide
P1=$(kubectl get pods -n storage-cases -l app=case11 -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl exec -n storage-cases $P1 -- sh -c 'echo hello-from-pod-1 > /data/hello.txt'     # WRITE in Pod 1
for P in $(kubectl get pods -n storage-cases -l app=case11 -o name); do               # READ in every Pod
  echo "$P → $(kubectl exec -n storage-cases $P -- cat /data/hello.txt 2>&1)"
done
expected-output.txt
case11-6c9…-a   1/1   Running   worker-a
case11-6c9…-b   1/1   Running   worker-a
case11-6c9…-c   1/1   Running   worker-a
pod/case11-6c9…-a → hello-from-pod-1
pod/case11-6c9…-b → hello-from-pod-1
pod/case11-6c9…-c → hello-from-pod-1

Case 1.2 · Deployment + one EBS claim (RWOP) · 3 replicas on the same node

same node · worker-aRWOP · EBS✗ only 1 Pod runs

What it means: ReadWriteOncePod is stricter than RWO: exactly one Pod in the cluster may use the claim. The scheduler enforces it, so extra replicas stay Pending instead of sharing the disk.

When to use it: any single-writer database. It turns the silent risk of case 1.1 into a clear, visible refusal.

▶ Case 1.2 — write in Pod 1, read from the others
1 / 4

↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · objects
Same as 1.1 with accessModes: [ReadWriteOncePod].
Step 2 · one Pod wins
Pod a mounts the disk. Pods b and c: node has pod using PersistentVolumeClaim with the same name and ReadWriteOncePod access mode.
Step 3 · write in Pod a
The file is on the disk.
Step 4 · read from b and c
Impossible — they are not running.

Case 1.3 · Deployment + one EFS claim (RWX) · 3 replicas on the same node

same node · worker-aRWX · EFS✓ shared by design

What it means: ReadWriteMany says many Pods on many nodes may read and write at once. EFS is a network file system, so the data lives in EFS, not on worker-a's disk.

Jahez use: menu images, uploaded documents — files every replica must see.

Case 1.4 · StatefulSet + EBS · 3 Pods on the same node

same node · worker-aRWO · EBS · claim per Pod✓ separate disks

What it means: a StatefulSet's volumeClaimTemplates creates a new claim for every Pod (data-case14-0, -1, -2), so each Pod gets its own disk. Being on the same node changes nothing: three different disks are attached to one machine.

Watch out: each EC2 instance can attach a limited number of EBS volumes; many StatefulSet Pods on one node can hit that limit.

▶ Case 1.4 — write in Pod 1, read from the others
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · objects
Headless Service + StatefulSet; the controller creates 3 claims.
Step 2 · three disks, one node
Each claim gets its own EBS volume, all attached to worker-a.
Step 3 · write in case14-0
The file lands on disk 0.
Step 4 · read from case14-1 and -2
No such file — their disks are empty.

Group 2 · every Pod on a different node

Spread with topologySpreadConstraints on kubernetes.io/hostname — one Pod per node, and here one node per zone.

Case 2.1 · Deployment + one EBS claim (RWO) · replicas on different nodes

different nodesRWO · EBS✗ only 1 Pod runs

What it means: all replicas reference one EBS disk, and an EBS disk can be attached to one node, in one zone. The Pods spread to other nodes cannot use it.

Exact error you see: in this cluster (one node per zone) the extra Pods stay Pending with volume node affinity conflict. If another node existed in the same zone, they would schedule there and hang in ContainerCreating with Multi-Attach error for volume ….

▶ Case 2.1 — write in Pod 1, read from the others
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · objects
One RWO claim; the Deployment spreads replicas one per node.
Step 2 · only one can attach
The disk is created in 1a with the first Pod. Nodes in 1b and 1c are not allowed to use it.
Step 3 · write in Pod a
Works on worker-a.
Step 4 · read from b and c
They are not running — nothing to read.

Case 2.2 · Deployment + one EBS claim · 1 replica · Recreate (the fix for 2.1)

one Pod · any node in the disk's zoneRWO · EBS✓ correct single-instance

What it means: with one disk you run one Pod. strategy: Recreate stops the old Pod before starting the new one, so the disk is free to attach again. (The default RollingUpdate starts the new Pod first — it would wait for a disk the old Pod still holds.)

"Other Pods" here: the next Pod after a restart. It reads what the previous Pod wrote.

▶ Case 2.2 — write in Pod 1, read from the others
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · objects
One claim, one replica, Recreate.
Step 2 · mounted
Disk created in 1b with the Pod on worker-b.
Step 3 · write in Pod a
The file is on the disk.
Step 4 · new Pod reads
kubectl rollout restart → Pod b mounts the same disk and reads the file.

Case 2.4 · StatefulSet + EBS · Pods on different nodes

different nodes · 3 zonesRWO · EBS · claim per Pod✓ separate, zone-pinned

What it means: the standard layout for databases. Each Pod has its own disk in its own zone; each Pod is tied to that zone (it can move only to another node in the same zone). Pods do not see each other's data — if they need the same data, the application replicates it (case 2.6).

metadata:
  name: case24
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  serviceName: case24-hl
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: case24 }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: case24 }
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:                # one Pod per node
      - maxSkew: 1
        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels: { app: case24 }
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600000"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumeClaimTemplates:                 # → data-case24-0, data-case24-1, data-case24-2
  - metadata:
      name: data
    spec:
      accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
      storageClassName: ebs-gp3
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 1Gi
prove-it.sh
kubectl get pods -n storage-cases -l app=case24 -o wide
P1=$(kubectl get pods -n storage-cases -l app=case24 -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl exec -n storage-cases $P1 -- sh -c 'echo hello-from-pod-1 > /data/hello.txt'     # WRITE in Pod 1
for P in $(kubectl get pods -n storage-cases -l app=case24 -o name); do               # READ in every Pod
  echo "$P → $(kubectl exec -n storage-cases $P -- cat /data/hello.txt 2>&1)"
done

case24-0   1/1   Running   worker-a
case24-1   1/1   Running   worker-b
case24-2   1/1   Running   worker-c
pod/case24-0 → hello-from-pod-1

pod/case24-2 → cat: can't open '/data/hello.txt': No such file or directory

Case 2.5 · StatefulSet + EFS · Pods on different nodes

different nodes · 3 zonesRWX class · claim per Pod✓ separate, not zone-pinned

What it means: EFS can be shared, but sharing needs the same claim. Here each Pod has its own claim, so each gets its own folder (access point). The difference from 2.4: the folders are regional, so a Pod can be rescheduled to any zone and still reach its data.

▶ Case 2.5 — write in Pod 1, read from the others

Step 3 · write in case25-0
Stored in folder data-case25-0.
Step 4 · read from case25-1 and -2
They look in their own folders — nothing there.

Case 2.6 · Replication · Redis StatefulSet (1 primary + 2 replicas) on different nodes

different nodes · 3 zonesRWO · EBS · claim per Pod✓ data copied by the APP

What it means: this is how Pods with separate disks end up with the same data. Kubernetes and AWS do not copy one Pod's disk to another Pod. The application does it over the network: the Redis primary sends every write to its replicas, and each replica stores it on its own disk.

Two kinds of copying, never confuse them: app replication (primary → replicas, different disks, different zones, visible to the app) vs AWS EBS redundancy (hidden copies of one disk inside one zone, for hardware failures only).

▶ Case 2.6 — write in Pod 1, read from the others
1 / 5
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · objects
redis-0 starts as primary; redis-1 and redis-2 start with --replicaof redis-0.redis-hl 6379.
Step 2 · own disks
Three claims, three EBS disks in three zones.
Step 3 · write on the primary
redis-cli SET order:1001 paid on redis-0.
Step 4 · replicas read it
Redis replication delivers the key to redis-1 and redis-2; writing on a replica returns READONLY.
Step 5 · AWS copies
Each EBS disk also has hidden copies inside its own AZ — a separate, lower-level mechanism.
case-2-6-redis-replication.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: redis-hl
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector: { app: redis }
  ports:
  - port: 6379
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: redis
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  serviceName: redis-hl
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: redis }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: redis }
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:                # one Pod per node
      - maxSkew: 1
        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels: { app: redis }
      containers:
      - name: redis
        image: redis:7.4
        ports:
        - containerPort: 6379
        command: ["sh", "-c"]
        args:
        - |
          if [ "$(hostname)" = "redis-0" ]; then
            exec redis-server --appendonly yes --dir /data
          else
            exec redis-server --appendonly yes --dir /data --replicaof redis-0.redis-hl 6379
          fi
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: data
    spec:
      accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
      storageClassName: ebs-gp3
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 1Gi
prove-it.sh
kubectl get pods -n storage-cases -l app=redis -o wide
kubectl exec -n storage-cases redis-0 -- redis-cli SET order:1001 paid          # WRITE on the primary
for P in redis-0 redis-1 redis-2; do                                       # READ everywhere
  echo "$P → $(kubectl exec -n storage-cases $P -- redis-cli GET order:1001)"
done
kubectl exec -n storage-cases redis-1 -- redis-cli SET x 1                      # write on a replica
kubectl exec -n storage-cases redis-1 -- redis-cli INFO replication | head -3

redis-0   1/1   Running   worker-a
redis-1   1/1   Running   worker-b
redis-2   1/1   Running   worker-c
OK
redis-0 → paid
redis-1 → paid
redis-2 → paid
(error) READONLY You can't write against a read only replica.
