master_host:redis-0.redis-hl

Summary — same node vs different nodes

SetupClaimsAll Pods on one nodePods on different nodesPod 1 writes → others see?
Deployment + EBS (RWO)one shared⚠ all run, share one disk (1.1)✗ only one runs (2.1)same node: yes · different: n/a
Deployment + EBS (RWOP)one shared✗ only one runs (1.2)✗ only one runsn/a
Deployment + EBS, 1 replica, Recreateonen/a✓ one Pod (2.2)the next Pod: yes
Deployment + EFS (RWX)one shared✓ shared (1.3)✓ shared (2.3)yes
StatefulSet + EBSone per Pod✓ separate disks (1.4)✓ separate disks (2.4)no
StatefulSet + EFSone per Pod✓ separate folders✓ separate folders (2.5)no
StatefulSet + app replicationone per Pod—✓ (2.6)yes, via the app
✓
One-line rulePods share data only when they mount the same claim (and the access mode allows it). Same node or different node only decides whether that is allowed — it never creates or copies data by itself.
§ 2.3.10INTERACTIVE

Manual vs Dynamic Provisioning — 11 Cases

Every persistent volume needs a PV. The only question is who creates it, and when: you (manual / static) or a StorageClass (dynamic). In every diagram below, objects marked ✍ are what you write and ⚙ are created automatically.

Manual (static)Dynamic
You writePV + PVC (+ Pod)PVC (+ Pod) only
Who creates the diskit already exists (or comes with the node)the StorageClass's CSI driver, on demand
storageClassName"" or a no-provisioner classa class with a provisioner (e.g. ebs-gp3)
Typical reclaim policyRetainDelete (class default)

Prerequisites: the storage-cases namespace and the ebs-gp3 / efs-shared classes from §2.3.9. Extra classes are included in the cases that need them.

Group 1 · Manual (static) — you write the PV

Case 1.1 · Import an existing EBS disk

manual (static)EBS · RWO · Retain✓ old data visible

What it means: the disk already exists with data on it. A StorageClass would create a new, empty disk, so here you register the existing one yourself: the PV is the "record" of that disk (volumeHandle = the EBS volume ID), and the PVC claims exactly that PV via volumeName.

Must include: nodeAffinity for the disk's zone (EBS cannot leave it), storageClassName: "" on both sides (so no provisioner creates a new disk), and Retain so deleting the claim never destroys the data.

▶ Case 1.1 — what you write vs what is created
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · The disk exists
EBS vol-0aa… in 1a already holds years of reports.
Step 2 · You write PV + PVC
The PV points at the disk; the PVC pins that PV with volumeName. They bind immediately.
Step 3 · Pod mounts it
The scheduler sends the Pod to a 1a node; the disk is attached and mounted at /reports.
Step 4 · Old data visible
The Pod lists the existing files.
case-m1-1-import-existing-ebs.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: legacy-reports
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 500Gi
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain      # never delete this disk
  storageClassName: ""                       # static: no StorageClass
  csi:
    driver: ebs.csi.aws.com
    volumeHandle: vol-0aa13c5e8f2b47d10       # the EXISTING EBS volume ID
    fsType: ext4
  nodeAffinity:                              # EBS lives in one zone
    required:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: topology.ebs.csi.aws.com/zone
          operator: In
          values: [me-central-1a]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: reports-archive
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: ""                       # do NOT dynamically provision
  volumeName: legacy-reports                 # bind to exactly this PV
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 500Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: reports-reader
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600000"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: reports
      mountPath: /reports
  volumes:
  - name: reports
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: reports-archive
prove-it.sh
kubectl get pv legacy-reports
kubectl get pvc reports-archive -n storage-cases
kubectl get pod reports-reader -n storage-cases -o wide
kubectl exec -n storage-cases reports-reader -- ls /reports
expected-output.txt
NAME             CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS   CLAIM                           STORAGECLASS
legacy-reports   500Gi      RWO            Retain           Bound    storage-cases/reports-archive
NAME              STATUS   VOLUME           CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS
reports-archive   Bound    legacy-reports   500Gi      RWO
reports-reader    1/1   Running   worker-a

2026-q1.csv

Case 1.2 · Several static PVs · PVC chooses by labels

manual (static)EBS · selector✓ smallest fitting PV

What it means: an admin keeps a small "pool" of ready PVs. A claim does not name one; it describes what it needs (size, mode, labels) and the PV controller chooses. Rule: among PVs that match, the smallest one that is big enough wins. A 30Gi request takes the 40Gi PV — the extra 10Gi cannot be claimed by anyone else (binding is 1:1).

▶ Case 1.2 — what you write vs what is created
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · A pool of PVs
Three static PVs: 20, 40 and 100Gi.
Step 2 · Binding by rules
20Gi is too small, 40Gi fits best, 100Gi stays free.
Step 3 · Mounted
The Pod gets arch-40's disk.
Step 4 · Result
kubectl get pv shows one Bound and two Available.

Case 1.3 · One existing EFS shared by two namespaces

manual (static)EFS · RWX · 2 PV/PVC pairs✓ cross-namespace sharing

What it means: a PVC lives in one namespace, and a PV can be bound to only one PVC. To let two namespaces use the same files, you create two PVs that point at the same EFS location, and one PVC in each namespace. Binding stays 1:1; the sharing happens in EFS.

▶ Case 1.3 — what you write vs what is created
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · EFS exists
File system fs-0c1… with access point fsap-reports.
Step 2 · Two PV/PVC pairs
Each namespace gets its own claim bound to its own PV; both PVs use the same volumeHandle.
Step 3 · Mounted in both
Each Pod mounts the EFS folder over NFS.
Step 4 · Shared files
A file written in jahez-prod is read in jahez-bi.

Case 1.4 · Local NVMe disk inside a node

manual (static)local · RWO · node-pinned✓ fastest · ⚠ pinned

What it means: there is no cloud API to "create" a local disk — it comes with the server — so a StorageClass cannot provision it. You write one PV per disk with local.path and nodeAffinity. The class still matters: WaitForFirstConsumer makes Kubernetes choose the node and the PV together.

Trade-off: the Pod can only ever run on that node, and the data disappears if the instance is replaced. Use it only for software that keeps its own copies (Elasticsearch replicas, Kafka).

▶ Case 1.4 — what you write vs what is created
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · You write class + PV
kubernetes.io/no-provisioner class and a PV for /mnt/nvme0 on worker-a.
Step 2 · Bound with the Pod
The scheduler can only place the Pod on worker-a.
Step 3 · Mounted
Local NVMe speed.
Step 4 · Pinned
Cordon worker-a and recreate the Pod → it stays Pending.
case-m1-4-local-nvme.yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: local-nvme
provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner     # cannot create disks
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
reclaimPolicy: Retain
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: local-worker-a
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 1700Gi
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: local-nvme
  local:
    path: /mnt/nvme0                         # mounted on the node at boot
  nodeAffinity:
    required:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: kubernetes.io/hostname
          operator: In
          values: [worker-a]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: search-scratch
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: local-nvme
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1500Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: search-indexer
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600000"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: index
      mountPath: /index
  volumes:
  - name: index
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: search-scratch
prove-it.sh
kubectl get pod search-indexer -n storage-cases -o wide
kubectl cordon worker-a && kubectl delete pod search-indexer -n storage-cases && kubectl apply -f case-m1-4-local-nvme.yaml
kubectl describe pod search-indexer -n storage-cases | tail -3
expected-output.txt
search-indexer   1/1   Running   worker-a
Warning  FailedScheduling  0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) were unschedulable,

Case 1.5 · Claim does not match the static PV

manual (static)size · mode · class✗ Pending until fixed

What it means: with static provisioning nothing is created for you — if no existing PV satisfies the claim (class, access mode, size ≥ request, selector), the claim waits forever. This is the most common static-provisioning problem in the CKAD exam (see Q8 in Part III).

▶ Case 1.5 — what you write vs what is created
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Mismatch
PV: 100Gi RWO. PVC: 200Gi RWX.
Step 2 · Pending
Claim and Pod both wait.
Step 3 · Diagnose
kubectl describe pvc big-claim → no persistent volumes available for this claim.
Step 4 · Fix
Recreate the claim with matching values; it binds at once.

A · The broken setup (claim stays Pending)

case-m1-5-broken.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: manual-100
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 100Gi
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: manual
  hostPath:                                  # lab only
    path: /mnt/manual-100
    type: DirectoryOrCreate
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: big-claim
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]               # ✗ the PV only offers ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: manual
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 200Gi                         # ✗ the PV is only 100Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: uses-big-claim
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600000"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: data
      mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: data
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: big-claim

B · The fix (claim binds, Pod runs)

case-m1-5-fixed-claim.yaml
# Step 4 — the FIX: recreate the claim so it fits the PV (PVC spec is immutable)
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: big-claim
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]               # ✓ was ReadWriteMany
  storageClassName: manual                   # ✓ same as the PV
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Gi                         # ✓ was 200Gi (must be ≤ PV size)
prove-it.sh
kubectl describe pvc big-claim -n storage-cases | tail -2             # with the WRONG claim
kubectl delete pod uses-big-claim -n storage-cases                   # release the claim first
kubectl replace --force -f case-m1-5-fixed-claim.yaml
kubectl apply -f case-m1-5-broken.yaml                      # re-creates the Pod (PV/claim unchanged)
kubectl get pvc big-claim -n storage-cases
expected-output.txt
Normal  FailedBinding  persistentvolume-controller  no persistent volumes available for this claim and no storage class is set
NAME        STATUS   VOLUME       CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS
big-claim   Bound    manual-100   100Gi      RWO            manual

Group 2 · Dynamic — a StorageClass writes the PV

Case 2.1 · EBS with WaitForFirstConsumer

dynamicEBS · ebs-gp3 · WFFC✓ disk in the Pod's zone

What it means: you write only the claim. Because the class says WaitForFirstConsumer, nothing is created until a Pod using the claim is scheduled; then the disk is created in that Pod's zone. This is the default to use for every zonal disk (EBS).

▶ Case 2.1 — what you write vs what is created
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Only a claim
PVC Pending, no PV.
Step 2 · Pod scheduled
worker-b (zone 1b).
Step 3 · Created for you
CreateVolume in 1b, PV created and bound.
Step 4 · Use it
The Pod writes to the new disk.
case-d2-1-ebs-wffc.yaml

kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: orders-data
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: ebs-gp3
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: orders-db
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600000"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: data
      mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: data
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: orders-data
prove-it.sh
kubectl get pvc orders-data -n storage-cases                         # before the Pod
kubectl get pvc orders-data -n storage-cases                         # after the Pod
kubectl get pv $(kubectl get pvc orders-data -n storage-cases -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumeName}') \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeAffinity.required.nodeSelectorTerms[0].matchExpressions[0].values}'; echo
expected-output.txt
orders-data   Pending                                    ebs-gp3
orders-data   Bound     pvc-91a…   20Gi   RWO            ebs-gp3
["me-central-1b"]

Case 2.2 · EBS with Immediate binding

dynamicEBS · Immediate⚠ Pod may be unschedulable

What it means: with volumeBindingMode: Immediate the disk is created the moment the claim exists — before Kubernetes knows which node the Pod needs (CPU, memory, taints, affinity). If the chosen zone has no suitable node, the Pod waits forever. Fine for regional storage (EFS); avoid for zonal storage (EBS).

▶ Case 2.2 — what you write vs what is created
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Created immediately
The claim alone creates a disk in 1c.
Step 2 · Pod needs memory
Only worker-a (1a) has 8Gi free.
Step 3 · Conflict
Disk in 1c, capacity in 1a → Pending.
Step 4 · Fix
Use a WaitForFirstConsumer class.
case-d2-2-ebs-immediate.yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: ebs-gp3-immediate
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
volumeBindingMode: Immediate                 # ← the problem
reclaimPolicy: Delete
parameters:
  type: gp3
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: cache-data
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: ebs-gp3-immediate        # fix: ebs-gp3 (WaitForFirstConsumer)
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: cache
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600000"]
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: 8Gi
    volumeMounts:
    - name: data
      mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: data
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: cache-data
prove-it.sh
kubectl get pvc cache-data -n storage-cases             # Bound before any Pod exists
kubectl describe pod cache -n storage-cases | tail -3
expected-output.txt
cache-data   Bound   pvc-0c3…   10Gi   RWO   ebs-gp3-immediate
Warning  FailedScheduling  0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had volume node affinity conflict,
         2 node(s) Insufficient memory.

Case 2.3 · Default StorageClass (class omitted)

dynamicEBS · default class✓ works · class chosen silently

What it means: omitting storageClassName is not "no class" — Kubernetes fills in the class marked as default. Convenient, but the same YAML can get a different storage type on another cluster. In production manifests write the class explicitly. (storageClassName: "" is different — case 2.5.)

The claim has no storageClassName.

Case 2.4 · EFS dynamic provisioning (access point per claim)

dynamicEFS · efs-ap · RWX✓ new folder per claim

What it means: "dynamic" on EFS does not create a new EFS file system — the file system is created once by the platform team (Terraform). For each claim the driver creates an access point: a dedicated folder with its own owner, isolated from other claims. Pods sharing the claim share that folder.

▶ Case 2.4 — what you write vs what is created
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Claim
PVC on efs-shared.
Step 2 · Folder created
A new access point and a PV.
Step 3 · Mounted
Both replicas mount the folder.
Step 4 · Shared
A write in one replica is read in the other.
case-d2-4-efs-dynamic.yaml
# StorageClass efs-shared (provisioningMode: efs-ap) from the prerequisites
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: media
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]
  storageClassName: efs-shared
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi                           # required, not enforced by EFS
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: media
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: media }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: media }
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
      - maxSkew: 1
        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels: { app: media }
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600000"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: media
          mountPath: /media
      volumes:
      - name: media
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: media
prove-it.sh
kubectl get pv $(kubectl get pvc media -n storage-cases -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumeName}') -o jsonpath='{.spec.csi.volumeHandle}'; echo
P=($(kubectl get pods -n storage-cases -l app=media -o name))
kubectl exec -n storage-cases ${P[0]} -- sh -c 'echo img > /media/1043.webp'
kubectl exec -n storage-cases ${P[1]} -- ls /media
expected-output.txt
fs-0c1d2e3f4a5b6c7d8::fsap-0f9e8d7c6b5a4f321

Case 2.5 · storageClassName: "" and no static PV

neitherclass ""✗ Pending forever

What it means: three different things look alike: omitting the class = use the default (2.3); a class name = dynamic with that class (2.1); an empty string "" = static only, never dynamic. With "" and no matching static PV, nothing will ever bind.

Group 3 · What happens at the end

Case 3.1 · Delete the claim — manual (Retain) vs dynamic (Delete)

bothRetain vs DeleteRetain keeps · Delete destroys

What it means: the reclaim policy acts only when the claim is deleted (never when a Pod is deleted). Dynamic PVs inherit the class's policy — Delete by default — so deleting the claim destroys the disk. Static PVs are usually Retain: the PV becomes Released and the disk stays until an admin decides.

Production tip: set reclaimPolicy: Retain on database classes, or patch a dynamic PV to Retain before risky changes.

▶ Case 3.1 — what you write vs what is created
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Two claims in use
Static (Retain) on worker-a, dynamic (Delete) on worker-b.
Step 2 · Delete Pods + claims
Same command for both.
Step 3 · Different outcomes
Retain: disk kept, PV Released. Delete: disk destroyed.
Step 4 · Reuse
Clear claimRef; a new claim with volumeName gets the old data.
case-r3-1-delete-retain-vs-delete.yaml
# 1) protect a dynamic PV before risky work (optional)
#    kubectl patch pv <pv-name> -p '{"spec":{"persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy":"Retain"}}'
# 2) after deleting the old claim, make the retained PV reusable:
#    kubectl patch pv legacy-reports --type json -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/claimRef"}]'
# 3) new claim + Pod that reuse the retained disk
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: reports-archive-v2
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: ""
  volumeName: legacy-reports
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 500Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: reports-reader-v2
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600000"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: reports
      mountPath: /reports
  volumes:
  - name: reports
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: reports-archive-v2
prove-it.sh
kubectl delete pod reports-reader orders-db -n storage-cases
kubectl delete pvc reports-archive orders-data -n storage-cases
kubectl get pv
kubectl patch pv legacy-reports --type json -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/claimRef"}]'
kubectl apply -f case-r3-1-delete-retain-vs-delete.yaml
kubectl exec -n storage-cases reports-reader-v2 -- ls /reports
expected-output.txt
NAME             CAPACITY   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS     CLAIM
legacy-reports   500Gi      Retain           Released   storage-cases/reports-archive

§ 2.3.11INTERACTIVE

Linking Pod → PVC → PV — Every Way

A Pod reaches its disk through two links: Link A Pod → PVC, and Link B PVC → PV. Each link can be made in several ways. They look different in YAML but always end in the same place.

▶ The two links and every way to make them
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Link A · Pod → PVC
The Pod only ever knows a claim name. You write it yourself (A1), or a controller writes it for you (A2 StatefulSet, A3 ephemeral).
Step 2 · Link B · static
The PV already exists. Exact first: the claim names the PV (B1) or the PV reserves the claim (B2). Then pools: Kubernetes picks by rules (B3) or by labels (B4).
Step 3 · Link B · dynamic
No PV exists. A StorageClass creates one for the claim: default class (C1), named class (C2), or pre-filled from a snapshot or another claim (C3).
Step 4 · Same result
After binding, the PVC has spec.volumeName and the PV has spec.claimRef. That pair is the link.

All the ways — grouped, simple → complex

Inside each group the ways go from simplest (●) to most complex (●●●●). Rows marked ↳ are variants of the way above them; they use the same diagram.

#WayField you writeWho completes the linkUse it when
A · Link A — Pod → PVC
A1
●●●●		Pod names the claimvolumes[].persistentVolumeClaim.claimNameyousingle Pod or Deployment with one claim
↳Many Pods, one claimsame claimName in a Deployment (RWX, e.g. EFS)youshared files across replicas — see §2.3.9
A2
●●●●		StatefulSet claim templatespec.volumeClaimTemplatesStatefulSet controller creates <tpl>-<sts>-<n> and writes claimNamedatabases, one disk per Pod
↳Pre-created claims adoptedcreate PVC data-redis-0 yourself firstcontroller finds the name and reuses itmove existing disks under a StatefulSet
A3
●●●●		Ephemeral claim templatevolumes[].ephemeral.volumeClaimTemplateephemeral controller (PVC owned by the Pod)big per-Pod scratch, deleted with the Pod
B · Link B static, exact — you name ONE PV
B1
●●●●		Claim names the PVpvc.spec.volumeNamePV controller tries that PV onlyimporting one known disk
B2
●●●●		PV reserves the claimpv.spec.claimRefPV controller accepts that claim onlystop any other claim taking the disk
↳Both sides (strongest)volumeName + claimRefbinds at once, nothing else can raceevery import at Jahez
B · Link B static, pool — Kubernetes picks from many PVs
B3
●●●●		Automatic matchingclass + accessModes + size onlyPV controller picks the smallest PV that fitsa simple pool of equal PVs
↳Classless poolstorageClassName: "" on PVC and PVsno default class, no provisioning, pool onlystatic-only clusters / labs
B4
●●●●		Label selectorpvc.spec.selector (matchLabels / matchExpressions)PV controller keeps labelled PVs, then as B3pools per team / tier / zone
C · Link B dynamic — a StorageClass creates the PV
C1
●●●●		Default StorageClassclass omittedadmission fills the default class, then as C2quick tests
C2
●●●●		Named StorageClasspvc.spec.storageClassName: ebs-gp3CSI provisioner creates disk + PValmost everything new
C3
●●●●		Pre-filled volumepvc.spec.dataSource → VolumeSnapshotprovisioner restores the snapshot into a new diskrestores
↳Clone a claimdataSource → PersistentVolumeClaim (same namespace + class)provisioner copies the source diskstaging copies, test data (only if the CSI driver supports cloning — the AWS EBS driver does not; use a snapshot there)
↳Volume populatordataSourceRef → custom resourcea populator controller fills the diskadvanced: data from a custom source

Full chains — Link A + Link B together

A real workload always uses one way from Link A and one from Link B.

CombinationChainTypical use
A1 + C2Deployment / Pod → PVC → new EBSthe normal app disk
A2 + C2StatefulSet → one PVC per Pod → one new EBS per PodRedis / PostgreSQL / MongoDB
A1 + B1 + B2Pod → PVC → existing PV (both sides)bring an old disk back
A2 (adopted) + B1 + B2StatefulSet → pre-created PVCs → existing PVsmove a database onto old disks
A1 + C3Pod → PVC restored from a snapshotrecovery drill, staging copy
A3 + C2Pod → its own temporary PVC → new EBSlarge scratch space
A1 + B3 / B4Pod → PVC → PV picked from a poolpre-made pools (rare on AWS)
ℹ
How to read the casesEvery case uses the same lab: namespace storage-cases, classes ebs-gp3 / efs-shared from §2.3.9. Diagrams mark ✍ what you write and ⚙ what Kubernetes writes. The last step of each diagram shows the link fields you can check with kubectl.

Group A · Link A — Pod → PVC

Way A1 · Pod names the claim — claimName

Link APod → PVCyou write the link

What it means: the most common way. You create the PVC yourself and the Pod (or Deployment template) refers to it by name in volumes[].persistentVolumeClaim.claimName. The claim must be in the same namespace as the Pod. Every replica of a Deployment uses this same claim (see §2.3.9).

▶ Way A1 — how the link is made
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · You write both
PVC orders-data and a Deployment whose volume says claimName: orders-data.
Step 2 · Chain followed
Pod → claim → PV → EBS disk.
Step 3 · Mounted
The disk appears at /data.
Step 4 · Proof
The claim name is visible in the Pod spec.
link-a1-claimname.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: orders-data
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: ebs-gp3
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  replicas: 1
  strategy:
    type: Recreate
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: orders-api }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: orders-api }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600000"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
      volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: orders-data             # ← Link A, written by you
prove-it.sh
kubectl get pod -n storage-cases -l app=orders-api -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.volumes[0].persistentVolumeClaim.claimName}'; echo
kubectl get pvc orders-data -n storage-cases -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumeName}'; echo
expected-output.txt
orders-data
pvc-91a…

Way A2 · StatefulSet writes the link — volumeClaimTemplates

Link APod → PVC (one per Pod)controller writes the link

What it means: you write a claim template, not a claim. For each Pod the StatefulSet controller creates a PVC named <template>-<statefulset>-<ordinal> and inserts a volume with that claimName into the Pod. The template's name must match the container's volumeMounts.name; do not add a volumes: entry for it yourself.

▶ Way A2 — how the link is made
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Template only
A StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates named data.
Step 2 · Claims created
data-web-0, data-web-1 — each provisioned by ebs-gp3.
Step 3 · Link injected
Each Pod gets claimName: data-web-N.
Step 4 · Proof
Read the claimName from each Pod.
link-a2-volumeclaimtemplates.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-hl
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector: { app: web }
  ports:
  - port: 80
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  serviceName: web-hl
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: web }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: web }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600000"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data                         # matches the template name
          mountPath: /data
      # no volumes: entry for "data" — the controller adds it
  volumeClaimTemplates:                      # ← Link A, written by the controller
  - metadata:
      name: data
    spec:
      accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
      storageClassName: ebs-gp3
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 5Gi
prove-it.sh
for P in web-0 web-1; do
  echo "$P → $(kubectl get pod $P -n storage-cases -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumes[?(@.name=="data")].persistentVolumeClaim.claimName}')"
done
kubectl get pvc -n storage-cases -l app=web 2>/dev/null || kubectl get pvc -n storage-cases
expected-output.txt
web-0 → data-web-0
web-1 → data-web-1
NAME         STATUS   VOLUME     CAPACITY   STORAGECLASS
data-web-0   Bound    pvc-a…     5Gi        ebs-gp3
data-web-1   Bound    pvc-b…     5Gi        ebs-gp3

Way A3 · Ephemeral claim template — claim lives and dies with the Pod

Link APod → PVC (owned by the Pod)controller writes · deleted with Pod

What it means: the same PVC/PV machinery, but the claim is created for one Pod and owned by it (ownerReferences). The claim is named <pod>-<volume>. Use it when a Pod needs more or faster scratch space than the node disk, not for data you must keep.

Under volumes[].ephemeral.volumeClaimTemplate.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod

  name: render-job
  namespace: storage-cases
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600000"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: scratch
      mountPath: /scratch
  volumes:
  - name: scratch
    ephemeral:                               # ← Link A, PVC created FOR this Pod
      volumeClaimTemplate:
        spec:
          accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
          storageClassName: ebs-gp3
          resources:
            requests:
              storage: 50Gi

Link B · staticpvc.spec.volumeNameclaim chooses one PV

Way B2 · PV reserves the claim — claimRef

Link B · staticpv.spec.claimRefPV accepts one claim

What it means: the opposite direction of B1: the PV says which claim may bind to it (namespace + name). No other claim can take it, even one that matches perfectly. For importing a disk, set both sides — claimRef on the PV and volumeName on the PVC — so the pair can only ever bind to each other.

Group B · Link B static, pool — Kubernetes picks a PV

Way B3 · Automatic matching (no names, no labels)

Link B · staticclass + mode + sizecontroller picks

What it means: the claim describes what it needs; the PV controller looks at every Available PV and keeps those with the same storageClassName, all requested access modes, and capacity ≥ request. The smallest one wins. You cannot predict the PV if several are equal — use B4–B2 when it matters.

Which way to use at JahezLink A: A1 for single-instance apps, A2 for every database. Link B: C2 with an explicit class for everything new; B1 + B2 together when importing an existing disk; C3 for restores and staging copies.
§ 2.3.12INTERACTIVE

StatefulSet: Before and After Failure

What happens to a StatefulSet Pod and its disk when something breaks? Two examples with the same database: first the failure stays on the same node, then node 1 dies and the Pod moves to node 2.

FailureWhat diesDiskWhere the Pod comes backTypical time
Container crash / OOMKillthe containerstays attached and mountedsame Pod, same nodeseconds
Pod deleted / evictedthe Pod objectunmounted, usually re-mounted on the same nodesame name, any node in the disk's zonetens of seconds
Node lostthe node and its Podsstuck "attached" to the dead node until detachedanother node in the SAME zoneminutes (faster with out-of-service taint)
Zone has no healthy node—cannot leave its zonenowhere until a node exists in that zoneuntil capacity returns

Example 1 · Before and after failure — on the same node

same node · worker-aStatefulSet · EBS · RWOP✓ data intact

What it means: most failures kill only the container. The Pod object, its node and its mounted disk stay exactly where they are; the kubelet starts a new container and mounts the same folder. Even when the whole Pod is deleted, the StatefulSet recreates it with the same name, so it uses the same claim data-orders-db-0 and the same disk.

▶ Example 1 — orders-db-0 before and after failure (same node)
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Before
orders-db-0 runs on worker-a. EBS vol-07c… is attached as /dev/nvme1n1 and mounted into the container; 1.2M rows are on the disk.
Step 2 · Failure
Postgres is OOM-killed (exit 137). Only the container stops — the Pod object, node and disk are untouched.
Step 3 · After
The kubelet starts a new container (RESTARTS 1) with the same mount. Postgres replays its write-ahead log and every row is there.
Step 4 · Pod deleted
kubectl delete pod orders-db-0: the StatefulSet creates a new Pod with the same name and a new UID. It mounts the same claim, so the same disk and the same rows.
example-1-orders-db-statefulset.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-db-hl
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector: { app: orders-db }
  ports:
  - port: 5432
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: orders-db
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  serviceName: orders-db-hl
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: orders-db }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: orders-db }
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120      # time to checkpoint on a normal stop
      securityContext:
        fsGroup: 999
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:16.4
        env:
        - name: PGDATA
          value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef: { name: db-orders, key: password }
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: "1", memory: 2Gi }
          limits:   { memory: 2Gi }
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
        startupProbe:                           # allow time for attach + WAL replay
          exec: { command: ["pg_isready", "-U", "postgres"] }
          periodSeconds: 5
          failureThreshold: 60
        readinessProbe:
          exec: { command: ["pg_isready", "-U", "postgres"] }
          periodSeconds: 10
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: data                               # → data-orders-db-0
    spec:
      accessModes: [ReadWriteOncePod]
      storageClassName: ebs-gp3                # WaitForFirstConsumer
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 100Gi
example-1-break-it.sh
# BEFORE
kubectl exec -n jahez-prod orders-db-0 -- psql -U postgres -c "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS orders(id int); INSERT INTO orders SELECT generate_series(1,1200000);"
kubectl get pod orders-db-0 -n jahez-prod -o wide

# FAILURE A — kill the container only (simulates a crash / OOMKill)
kubectl exec -n jahez-prod orders-db-0 -- pkill -9 postgres
kubectl get pod orders-db-0 -n jahez-prod -w                     # RESTARTS 0 → 1, same node

# FAILURE B — delete the whole Pod
kubectl delete pod orders-db-0 -n jahez-prod
kubectl get pod orders-db-0 -n jahez-prod -o wide                # recreated, same name

# AFTER
kubectl exec -n jahez-prod orders-db-0 -- psql -U postgres -tc "SELECT count(*) FROM orders;"
expected-output.txt
orders-db-0   1/1   Running   0   …   worker-a
orders-db-0   1/1   Running   1   …   worker-a        # after FAILURE A: same Pod, RESTARTS 1
orders-db-0   1/1   Running   0   …   worker-a        # after FAILURE B: new Pod (new UID), same name
 1200000

Example 2 · Node 1 fails — the Pod moves to node 2

node 1 → node 2 (same zone)StatefulSet · EBS · RWOP✓ data intact · ⚠ zone-bound

What it means: the data is not on the node — it is on an EBS disk — so it can follow the Pod to another node. Two rules decide how fast and where:

  • At most one copy. A StatefulSet never runs two orders-db-0 at once. While the dead node might still be running the old Pod, Kubernetes waits. You confirm the node is gone with the node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service taint (or Kubernetes force-detaches the disk after about 6 minutes).
  • Same zone only. An EBS disk can attach only to nodes in its own Availability Zone, so node 2 must be in zone 1a. If no 1a node exists, the Pod waits until one is added (Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter), or you restore a snapshot in another zone, or fail over to a database replica.
▶ Example 2 — node 1 fails, orders-db-0 moves to node 2
1 / 5
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Before
orders-db-0 runs on worker-a1 (zone 1a). worker-a2 is a second node in 1a; worker-b is in 1b. The VolumeAttachment says the disk is attached to worker-a1.
Step 2 · Node 1 fails
worker-a1 stops responding and becomes NotReady. The Pod shows Terminating/Unknown, and AWS still lists the disk as attached to the dead instance. No replacement is created yet — Kubernetes cannot be sure the old Pod has stopped writing.
Step 3 · Confirm it is gone
kubectl taint node worker-a1 node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service=nodeshutdown:NoExecute → the old Pod is force-deleted and the disk is force-detached immediately.
Step 4 · Pod moves to node 2
The StatefulSet recreates orders-db-0. The PV's nodeAffinity allows only zone 1a, so the scheduler picks worker-a2. The disk is attached there, mounted, and Postgres finds all 1.2M rows.
Step 5 · If node 2 is in another zone
With no healthy node in 1a, the Pod stays Pending (volume node affinity conflict). Fix: add a node in 1a, restore a snapshot into a new disk in 1b, or promote a replica that already runs in 1b (case 2.6 in §2.3.9).
example-2-orders-db-statefulset.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-db-hl
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector: { app: orders-db }
  ports:
  - port: 5432
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: orders-db
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  serviceName: orders-db-hl
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: orders-db }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: orders-db }
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120      # time to checkpoint on a normal stop
      securityContext:
        fsGroup: 999
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:16.4
        env:
        - name: PGDATA
          value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef: { name: db-orders, key: password }
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: "1", memory: 2Gi }
          limits:   { memory: 2Gi }
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
        startupProbe:                           # allow time for attach + WAL replay
          exec: { command: ["pg_isready", "-U", "postgres"] }
          periodSeconds: 5
          failureThreshold: 60
        readinessProbe:
          exec: { command: ["pg_isready", "-U", "postgres"] }
          periodSeconds: 10
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: data                               # → data-orders-db-0
    spec:
      accessModes: [ReadWriteOncePod]
      storageClassName: ebs-gp3                # WaitForFirstConsumer
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 100Gi
example-2-break-a-node.sh
# BEFORE — where is the Pod, and which node holds the disk?
kubectl get pod orders-db-0 -n jahez-prod -o wide
kubectl get volumeattachment | grep pvc-4e1c
kubectl get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone

# FAILURE — stop the EC2 instance behind worker-a1 (lab only!)
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60718
kubectl get nodes -w                                   # worker-a1 → NotReady
kubectl get pod orders-db-0 -n jahez-prod              # Terminating / Unknown — no replacement yet

# RECOVER — tell Kubernetes the node is really gone (non-graceful node shutdown)
kubectl taint node worker-a1 node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service=nodeshutdown:NoExecute

# AFTER
kubectl get pod orders-db-0 -n jahez-prod -o wide -w   # recreated on worker-a2
kubectl get volumeattachment | grep pvc-4e1c           # now attached to worker-a2
kubectl exec -n jahez-prod orders-db-0 -- psql -U postgres -tc "SELECT count(*) FROM orders;"

# when worker-a1 is repaired, remove the taint
kubectl taint node worker-a1 node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service-
expected-output.txt

Design for this at JahezKeep at least two nodes per zone for stateful workloads, set startupProbe generously (attach + WAL replay), use ReadWriteOncePod, and run replicas in other zones (§2.3.9 case 2.6) so losing a whole zone is a failover, not an outage.
§ 2.3.13INTERACTIVE

Where It Lives in AWS

EBS and EFS are Amazon Web Services products. This is where each piece physically lives.

NameFull nameTypeWhere it livesRedundancy (done by AWS)
EBSAmazon Elastic Block Storeblockone Availability Zoneautomatically replicated inside its AZ
EFSAmazon Elastic File Systemfile (NFS)the Region (mount target per AZ)Standard: stored across multiple AZs · One Zone: one AZ
S3Amazon Simple Storage Serviceobjectthe Regionholds EBS snapshots; not mounted as a normal volume

Kubernetes does not talk to these services directly: the EBS CSI driver and EFS CSI driver (EKS add-ons) call the AWS APIs. On another cloud the same idea uses that cloud's services (e.g. Google Persistent Disk / Filestore, Azure Disk / Azure Files).

▶ Where EBS, EFS and snapshots live in AWS
1 / 5
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Region, AZs, nodes
The EKS worker nodes are EC2 instances in three Availability Zones (separate data centres) of Region me-central-1.
Step 2 · EBS is zonal
Each EBS volume exists in one AZ and is attached to one EC2 instance there. AWS keeps redundant copies of its blocks inside that AZ — automatic and invisible to you.
Step 3 · No cross-AZ attach
A volume in 1a cannot attach to a node in 1b. That is why a Pod using it can only run in 1a.
Step 4 · EFS is regional
One file system for the whole Region, with a mount target (network endpoint) in each AZ. Every node mounts the same files; AWS stores them across AZs.
Step 5 · Snapshots in S3
EBS snapshots are stored by AWS in S3 (regional). Restoring creates a new volume in any AZ — the way to move or back up EBS data.
§ 2.4INTERACTIVE

Special Case: hostPath

hostPathSpecial · node-bound
Mounts a real file or directory of the node into the container — no copy, no isolation.
Data comes from
the node's filesystem
Lives as long as
the node — a Pod on another node sees a different directory
Stored on the node
the path itself, e.g. /var/log/pods (no kubelet volume folder in between)
Inside the container
a bind mount of that node path at mountPath
Updates
live — whatever the node writes
Shared between
every Pod on that node that mounts it
Use for
system DaemonSets: log collectors, node monitoring, CSI plugins
Avoid for
application data — ever
Must set / protect
narrowest path · type check · readOnly: true · Pod Security blocks it in app namespaces
▶ hostPath — the right way and the two wrong ways
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Real node path
fluent-bit mounts the node's /var/log/pods: the same directory the kubelet writes container logs to.
Step 2 · DaemonSet: one per node
Each node's fluent-bit Pod reads only its own node's logs. This is the correct use.
Step 3 · Wrong: app data
uploads-api stores photos in /data/uploads on worker-a. Rescheduled to worker-b, it sees an empty directory. Use a PVC.
Step 4 · Wrong: broad paths
Mounting / or the container runtime socket gives the Pod control of the node.

YAML sample

fluent-bit-hostpath.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: fluent-bit
  namespace: logging                          # system namespace, not jahez-prod
spec:
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: fluent-bit } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: fluent-bit } }
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: fluent-bit
      containers:
      - name: fluent-bit
        image: fluent/fluent-bit:3.1
        volumeMounts:
        - { name: podlogs, mountPath: /host/var/log/pods, readOnly: true }
        - { name: state,   mountPath: /fluent-bit/state }
      volumes:
      - name: podlogs
        hostPath:
          path: /var/log/pods
          type: Directory                     # must exist
      - name: state
        hostPath:
          path: /var/lib/fluent-bit           # read offsets survive restarts
          type: DirectoryOrCreate

TypeContainer restartPod deletedNode lostMulti-node writeBest for
emptyDir✓✗ deleted✗Nosidecar sharing, scratch

§ 3.2INTERACTIVE

emptyDir vs hostPath vs PVC — When a Node Dies

The most practical comparison: what is left after a node disappears? worker-a runs one Pod of each kind. Walk through the failure.

▶ emptyDir vs hostPath vs PVC — when worker-a dies
1 / 5
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Before the failure
worker-a runs order-service (emptyDir logs not yet shipped), uploads-api (hostPath /data/uploads, 3,200 files) and orders-db-0 (PVC → EBS in 1a).
Step 2 · Node goes NotReady
The node controller marks worker-a NotReady and adds node.kubernetes.io/unreachable. Pods tolerate it for 300 s by default, then are evicted.
Step 3 · Replacements: two kinds of loss
The new order-service on worker-b gets a fresh empty emptyDir: the unshipped logs are gone. The new uploads-api on worker-c sees worker-c's /data/uploads — empty. orders-db-0 cannot start on b or c: its PV has nodeAffinity for zone 1a.
Step 4 · The stale attachment
The VolumeAttachment still says "attached to worker-a". The attach-detach controller waits up to 6 min (maxWaitForUnmountDuration) before force-detaching; with the node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service taint (non-graceful node shutdown, GA 1.28) it detaches immediately.
Step 5 · PVC data intact
Karpenter/ASG brings up worker-d in 1a. The StatefulSet recreates orders-db-0, EBS is attached there, and Postgres replays its WAL. Only the PVC kept its data.
✓
TakeawayemptyDir = data you can afford to lose with the Pod. hostPath = data tied to one machine. PVC = data that must survive anything short of deleting the volume. For EBS, also keep at least one node per AZ that hosts stateful Pods.
§ 3.3INTERACTIVE

Block (EBS) vs File (EFS)

▶ Block (EBS) vs File (EFS) on the same cluster
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Block storage
Each database replica has its own EBS volume, attached to its node as a block device. ext4 runs in the node's kernel: local-disk semantics, fsync, low latency.
Step 2 · Zone-locked
EBS volumes exist in one AZ. A Pod whose volume is in 1a can only run on 1a nodes. Plan node groups per zone.
Step 3 · File storage
Every report-exporter replica mounts the same EFS file system through its AZ's mount target. The filesystem logic runs on AWS's side.
Step 4 · Choosing
See the table below.
EBS (block)EFS (file)
Access modesRWO, RWOPRWX, ROX, RWO
Scopeone AZ, one node at a timeregional, any node, many at once
Latencysub-millisecondlow single-digit ms, higher for metadata-heavy work
Throughput / IOPSgp3: 3,000 IOPS / 125 MiB/s baseline, provisionableelastic; scales with usage
Good forPostgres, Redis AOF, Elasticsearch, Kafkashared uploads, media, exports, CI caches
Bad forsharing between Pods on different nodesdatabases (locking + latency)
Cost modelpay for provisioned GiB (+IOPS/throughput)pay for stored GiB (+throughput mode)
§ 3.4INTERACTIVE

Deployment + PVC vs StatefulSet

▶ Deployment + PVC vs StatefulSet + volumeClaimTemplates
1 / 5
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Deployment with one PVC
Fine for a single replica: one Pod, one RWO claim. Use strategy: Recreate.
Step 2 · Scaling breaks it
All replicas reference the same claim. A second Pod on the same node mounts the same directory (two Postgres instances on one data dir); a Pod on another node hits Multi-Attach.
Step 3 · RollingUpdate deadlock
The new Pod is created before the old one is deleted. If it lands on another node it waits forever for the volume. Recreate avoids it, at the cost of a short outage.
Step 4 · StatefulSet
Each ordinal gets its own claim data-orders-db-N, a stable name and DNS identity. With WaitForFirstConsumer + topology spread, volumes land in three zones.
Step 5 · Stable identity
Delete orders-db-0 and it is recreated with the same name, so it mounts the same claim and the same EBS volume.
Deployment + PVCStatefulSet
PVCsone, shared by all replicasone per replica (volumeClaimTemplates)
Replicas with RWOmax 1 (realistically)many
Pod identityrandom namesstable: name-0, name-1 …
RolloutRecreate (downtime)ordered, one Pod at a time, same PVC
PVC cleanupmanualretained by default; persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy can delete
Jahez usesingle-instance tools (e.g. a small admin DB)Postgres, Redis, Elasticsearch, Kafka
04

Architecture & Workflow

§ 4.1INTERACTIVE

Cluster Storage Architecture

Definition · Storage control path
Four layers cooperate through API objects: API objects describe what is wanted, controllers decide what must happen, the CSI driver does the cloud work, and the kubelet makes the result appear inside the container.
LayerComponentsJob
API objectsPVC · PV · StorageClass · VolumeAttachment · CSINodethe single source of truth, stored in etcd
Controllerskube-scheduler (VolumeBinding) · PV controller · attach-detach controllerchoose the node, bind claims, decide attachments
CSI controllercsi-provisioner · csi-attacher · csi-resizer · csi-snapshotter + drivercreate, attach, resize, snapshot disks via AWS APIs
Nodekubelet VolumeManager · CSI node plugin (DaemonSet) · containerdformat, mount on the node, bind-mount into containers
▶ Cluster storage architecture — every component and every link
1 / 7
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · The layers
Control plane on top, CSI controller beside it, three worker nodes each running kubelet + CSI node plugins, AWS at the bottom.
Step 2 · API objects
PVC, PV, StorageClass, VolumeAttachment, CSINode and CSIDriver are all stored in etcd. Every component coordinates only through these objects.
Step 3 · Scheduling & binding
The scheduler's VolumeBinding plugin checks that a node can satisfy a Pod's claims (zone, capacity). The PV controller in kube-controller-manager binds claims and triggers provisioning.
Step 4 · CSI controller → AWS
csi-provisioner sees a PVC needing a volume and calls CreateVolume on the ebs-plugin, which calls the EC2 API. csi-resizer/csi-snapshotter work the same way.
Step 5 · Attach
The attach-detach controller creates a VolumeAttachment (PV × node). csi-attacher calls ControllerPublishVolume → EC2 AttachVolume. The disk appears on the node as an NVMe device.
Step 6 · Node plugin
On the node, the kubelet's VolumeManager reconciles desired vs actual mounts and calls the ebs-csi-node plugin through /var/lib/kubelet/plugins/ebs.csi.aws.com/csi.sock: NodeStageVolume (format + global mount), NodePublishVolume (Pod mount).
Step 7 · Into the container
containerd bind-mounts the Pod volume directory into the container's mount namespace at mountPath.
§ 4.2INTERACTIVE

How a Mount Happens — Step by Step

Every PVC-backed mount follows the same chain. Knowing it tells you exactly where a Pod stuck in Pending or ContainerCreating is waiting.

StepDone byResult
1 DeclareyouPod + PVC objects exist
2 Schedulekube-schedulernode chosen (zone-aware)
3 Provisioncsi-provisioner → EC2disk + PV created, bound
4 Attachcsi-attacher → EC2disk visible on the node
5 Stagekubelet → node pluginformatted, mounted once per node
6 Publishkubelet → node pluginbind-mounted into the Pod's directory
7 Container mountcontainerd / runcvisible at mountPath
8 Teardownreverse orderunmounted, detached
▶ How a mount happens — 8 steps with real paths and calls
1 / 8
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Declare
You apply a StatefulSet; it creates Pod orders-db-0 and PVC data-orders-db-0. They are only rows in etcd.
Step 2 · Schedule
The scheduler picks worker-b in me-central-1b. With WaitForFirstConsumer it writes volume.kubernetes.io/selected-node: worker-b on the PVC.
Step 3 · Provision
csi-provisioner calls CreateVolume with accessibility requirement topology.ebs.csi.aws.com/zone=me-central-1b. EC2 creates vol-0b2…; a PV is created and bound.
Step 4 · Attach
The attach-detach controller creates a VolumeAttachment; csi-attacher calls ControllerPublishVolume → EC2 AttachVolume. The disk shows up as /dev/nvme1n1. This cloud call is the slow part.
Step 5 · Stage
kubelet → NodeStageVolume: on first use the plugin runs mkfs.ext4, then mounts the device at the node-global staging path …/globalmount.
Step 6 · Publish
kubelet → NodePublishVolume: bind-mount the staging path into /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/pvc-…/mount.
Step 7 · Into the container
containerd/runc bind-mounts that directory into the container's mount namespace at /var/lib/postgresql/data. The Pod moves from ContainerCreating to Running.
Step 8 · Teardown
On Pod deletion: containers stop → NodeUnpublishVolume → NodeUnstageVolume (when no other Pod on the node uses it) → ControllerUnpublishVolume (detach). The reclaim policy decides the disk's fate only when the PVC is deleted.
⚡
Why Pods with new PVCs start slowlyProvisioning (~5–10 s) and attaching (~10–40 s) are cloud API calls, plus a format on first use. Budget 30–90 s on first start; give probes a startupProbe rather than a huge initialDelaySeconds.
§ 4.3INTERACTIVE

PV ↔ PVC Binding

Definition · Binding
The PV controller links one PVC to one PV that satisfies it — same class, compatible access modes, enough capacity, matching selector — and records the link on both objects. The link is exclusive.
▶ PV ↔ PVC binding — criteria, choice, and the 1:1 rule
1 / 5
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · The claim
A claim asks for class manual, RWO, 30Gi, and label tier=archive.
Step 2 · Filter
Candidates must match class, support the access modes, have capacity ≥ request, match the selector, and not be bound to someone else.
Step 3 · Choose the smallest fit
Of the PVs that pass, the controller picks the smallest one — 40Gi rather than 100Gi — to waste the least capacity.
Step 4 · Bind both ways
The PV gets claimRef; the PVC gets volumeName. The binding is exclusive: no other claim can use this PV, even if it is RWX and has spare space.
Step 5 · Pin when it matters
For static volumes you can pin with spec.volumeName on the PVC, or reserve a PV for a claim by pre-filling its claimRef.
⚠
Correction from v2Earlier versions said several PVCs can bind one RWX PV. They cannot. PV ↔ PVC is always 1:1. To share storage, create one RWX PVC and mount it from many Pods. (Cross-namespace sharing needs one static PV per namespace pointing to the same backend, e.g. the same EFS access point.)
§ 4.4INTERACTIVE

Dynamic Provisioning — WaitForFirstConsumer vs Immediate

▶ Dynamic provisioning — WaitForFirstConsumer vs Immediate
1 / 6
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · PVC Pending
search-idx-data references class ebs-gp3 (WaitForFirstConsumer). kubectl describe pvc shows waiting for first consumer to be created before binding. Normal.
Step 2 · Pod appears
es-search-0 requests 8Gi memory and mounts the claim.
Step 3 · Scheduler decides
worker-a lacks memory, worker-c has a taint; worker-b fits. The scheduler records the choice on the PVC (volume.kubernetes.io/selected-node).
Step 4 · Provision in that zone
csi-provisioner calls CreateVolume with the node's topology; the PV is created with nodeAffinity on topology.ebs.csi.aws.com/zone=me-central-1b.
Step 5 · Mount and run
Binding, attach, stage, publish (§4.2). Pod Running.
Step 6 · The Immediate trap
With volumeBindingMode: Immediate the disk is created as soon as the PVC exists, in whatever zone the driver picks. The Pod is then forced into that zone — where there may be no capacity. Use WaitForFirstConsumer for every zonal class.
§ 4.5INTERACTIVE

Pod Rescheduled to Another Node

▶ Graceful drain — moving a stateful Pod to another node
1 / 5
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Drain
kubectl drain worker-a --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data cordons the node and evicts Pods through the Eviction API, honouring PDBs. Note the flag name: emptyDir data will be deleted.
Step 2 · Graceful shutdown
Redis receives SIGTERM and writes its RDB/AOF to the PVC within terminationGracePeriodSeconds.
Step 3 · Detach
Kubelet unpublishes and unstages; the attach-detach controller removes the VolumeAttachment and csi-attacher detaches the EBS volume.
Step 4 · Zone filter
The recreated Pod can only go where the PV's nodeAffinity allows: zone 1a. worker-b (1b) is filtered out.
Step 5 · Reattached
worker-a2 gets the volume. Redis loads its data. Typical total: 30–90 s — why you run replicas and PDBs for stateful services.
§ 4.6INTERACTIVE

PV Lifecycle & Reclaim

Definition · Reclaim policy
Decides what happens to a PV's real disk after its PVC is deleted: Retain keeps the disk and data for an admin to handle; Delete destroys the disk. Dynamic PVs inherit it from their StorageClass (default Delete).
PhaseMeaning
Pendingbeing created
Availablefree, not bound to a claim
Boundbound to exactly one PVC
Releasedits PVC was deleted; still holds the old claimRef
Failedautomatic reclaim failed
▶ PV lifecycle — phases, protection and reclaim
1 / 7
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Pending → Available
A static PV is Available right after creation. (Dynamic PVs are created already bound.)
Step 2 · Bound
The PV is bound to exactly one PVC.
Step 3 · Protected while in use
kubectl delete pvc while a Pod uses it leaves the PVC Terminating until the Pod is gone — thanks to the pvc-protection finalizer. Don't strip finalizers to "unstick" it unless you know why.
Step 4 · Released
Once the PVC is really deleted, the PV becomes Released: it still has the old claimRef and cannot be bound by a new claim.
Step 5 · Retain
Disk and data remain. Back them up, then clear claimRef to make the PV Available — or create a fresh static PV for the same volume ID.
Step 6 · Delete
The provisioner calls DeleteVolume: the EBS volume is gone. Default for dynamic PVs.
Step 7 · Failed
If automatic reclamation fails (e.g. AWS returns an error), the PV is Failed and needs manual cleanup.
§ 4.7INTERACTIVE

Snapshots, Cloning & Resize

▶ Snapshot before a migration, restore to staging, then resize
1 / 6
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Request a snapshot
Before running a schema migration on orders-db, apply a VolumeSnapshot referencing data-orders-db-0 and class ebs-snapclass.
Step 2 · Driver snapshots EBS
csi-snapshotter calls CreateSnapshot; EBS stores an incremental, regional snapshot. readyToUse: true when done.
Step 3 · Restore to staging
A new PVC with dataSource: {kind: VolumeSnapshot, name: orders-db-pre-migration} creates a fresh volume — here in 1b — for the staging copy.
Step 4 · Clone
PVC → PVC cloning uses dataSource.kind: PersistentVolumeClaim. It requires driver support (CLONE_VOLUME); on EBS the common route is snapshot → restore.
Step 5 · Resize
Raise resources.requests.storage from 100Gi to 200Gi. csi-resizer calls ControllerExpandVolume → EC2 ModifyVolume. (EBS allows one modification per volume every 6 hours.)
Step 6 · Online filesystem growth
The kubelet calls NodeExpandVolume, which runs resize2fs while Postgres keeps running. Volumes can grow, never shrink.
Part II

Low Level Details

YAML by object: Pod → PVC → PV → StorageClass → StatefulSet. Every section has the same four steps: ① the logic (what it is and how its fields group), ② full apply-ready YAML, ③ every property in a collapsible tree (tap ▸ to open), ④ a deep dive with value tabs where useful.

05

Pod

§ 5.0INTERACTIVE

Pod Storage — The Logic, the Structure, the Full YAML

◆ The logic — read this first
A Pod's storage is two lists joined by a name. spec.volumes[] (Pod level) says what storage exists and where its data comes from. containers[].volumeMounts[] (container level) says where each container sees it. One volume can be mounted by many containers, at different paths, read-write or read-only.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
What storage does the Pod have?
spec.volumes[] — name + one type
the shelf of disks, owned by the Pod
Where does a container see it?
containers[].volumeMounts[]
plugging a disk into a folder
Raw device instead of a folder?
containers[].volumeDevices[]
plugging a disk in as /dev/xvdb
Who owns the files?
securityContext.fsGroup
chown once, so a non-root app can write
Where does the data come from, how long does it live?
the type key inside each volume
the family: ephemeral · persistent · special

The volume types at a glance

TypeFamilyWhere the data comes fromLives as long as§
Ephemeral — dies with the Pod
