Structure tree

🌳 Pod — where storage lives in the spec
▸specobjectEverything about storage sits under the Pod spec, at two levels.
▸volumes[]list · Pod levelWHAT storage the Pod has. Each item = a name + exactly one type key.

Declared once for the whole Pod. A volume does nothing until at least one container mounts it.

•namestringrequiredThe id that mounts refer to. Unique inside the Pod.
▸<one type key>objectExactly one of the types below decides where the data comes from and how long it lives.

emptyDir · configMap · secret · downwardAPI · projected · ephemeral · csi · persistentVolumeClaim · hostPath · nfs · image

▸containers[]list · container levelWHERE each container sees the storage.
▸volumeMounts[]listPlug a volume into a folder of this container (most volumes).
Deep dive: §5.1 volumeMounts
▸volumeDevices[]listPlug a raw block device (PVC with volumeMode: Block) into /dev/….
Deep dive: §5.2 volumeDevices
•initContainers[]listSame volumeMounts / volumeDevices. Typical: an init container fills an emptyDir before the app starts.
▸securityContextobjectPod-wide ownership of volume files.
▸fsGroupintGroup id that owns the volume files, so a non-root app can write them.

The kubelet sets the group of every file in supported volumes (emptyDir, PVC, configMap, secret…) to this gid and adds it to every container process.

Default: unset (no change)
▸fsGroupChangePolicystringWhen to re-apply fsGroup ownership.

For big disks a full recursive change at every mount slows Pod start by minutes.

Values
Alwayswalk and change every file at every mount (slow on big volumes)
OnRootMismatchonly if the volume root does not match already — use this for databases
Default: Always

Full YAML — one Pod using every type

One Deployment that uses every Pod-level volume source, numbered in volumeMounts. The supporting ConfigMap, Secret, PVC and SecretProviderClass are included so it applies as-is. Each type is then explained alone in §5.3 – §5.12.

order-service-all-volumes.yaml
# order-service — every Pod-level volume type in one apply-ready manifest
# Prereqs: namespace jahez-prod, StorageClass efs-shared (§8.0),
#          Secrets Store CSI driver + AWS provider, IRSA role for order-service-sa
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: order-service-config
  namespace: jahez-prod
data:
  appsettings.Production.json: |
    {
      "Kafka": { "BootstrapServers": "kafka-0.kafka-hl:9092" },
      "Cache": { "TtlSeconds": 300 },
      "Logging": { "File": "/var/log/order/app.json" }
    }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-orders
  namespace: jahez-prod
type: Opaque
stringData:                          # stringData = plain text in, stored base64
  username: order_svc
  password: change-me-via-external-secrets
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: order-receipts
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What does it need?
  accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]       # shared by every replica on every node
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50Gi                  # EFS is elastic; value is required but not enforced
  # ② Where does it come from?
  storageClassName: efs-shared
---
apiVersion: secrets-store.csi.x-k8s.io/v1
kind: SecretProviderClass
metadata:
  name: order-service-aws
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  provider: aws
  parameters:
    objects: |
      - objectName: "prod/orders/psp-api-key"
        objectType: "secretsmanager"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels: { app: order-service }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: order-service }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: order-service }
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: order-service-sa
      # ── Who owns the files? ──
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 10001
        fsGroup: 10001                         # group-owns mounted volumes (EFS/EBS) for this user
        fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch    # skip recursive chown when already correct
      # ── Where does each container see the storage? (volumeMounts per container) ──
      initContainers:
      - name: warm-templates
        image: ghcr.io/jahez/order-templates:1.8
        command: ["sh", "-c", "cp -r /templates/* /work/templates/"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: scratch
          mountPath: /work                     # init → main hand-off through emptyDir
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: ghcr.io/jahez/order-service:2.14.0
        ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512Mi, ephemeral-storage: 1Gi }
          limits:   { memory: 1Gi, ephemeral-storage: 3Gi }
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs                           # 1 emptyDir (disk) shared with fluent-bit
          mountPath: /var/log/order
        - name: scratch                        # 2 emptyDir written by the init container
          mountPath: /app/templates
          subPath: templates                   #   mount only one sub-directory
          readOnly: true
        - name: tmp                            # 3 emptyDir in RAM
          mountPath: /tmp
        - name: config                         # 4 configMap (hot-reload: whole dir, no subPath)
          mountPath: /app/config
          readOnly: true
        - name: db                             # 5 secret on tmpfs
          mountPath: /var/run/secrets/db
          readOnly: true
        - name: identity                       # 6 projected: token + pod info
          mountPath: /var/run/identity
          readOnly: true
        - name: receipts                       # 7 PVC → EFS (RWX)
          mountPath: /data/receipts
        - name: psp                            # 8 CSI inline → AWS Secrets Manager
          mountPath: /mnt/psp
          readOnly: true
      - name: fluent-bit
        image: fluent/fluent-bit:3.1
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi }
          limits:   { memory: 128Mi }
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
          readOnly: true
      # ── What storage does the Pod have? (name + ONE type key each) ──
      volumes:
      # ephemeral · scratch
      - name: logs
        emptyDir:
          sizeLimit: 1Gi
      - name: scratch
        emptyDir:
          sizeLimit: 200Mi
      - name: tmp
        emptyDir:
          medium: Memory
          sizeLimit: 128Mi                     # counts toward the api memory limit
      # ephemeral · config
      - name: config
        configMap:
          name: order-service-config
          defaultMode: 0444
          items:
          - key: appsettings.Production.json
            path: appsettings.Production.json
      - name: db
        secret:
          secretName: db-orders
          defaultMode: 0400
      - name: identity
        projected:
          defaultMode: 0440
          sources:
          - serviceAccountToken:
              path: token
              audience: sts.amazonaws.com
              expirationSeconds: 3600
          - downwardAPI:
              items:
              - path: pod-name
                fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.name }
              - path: mem-limit
                resourceFieldRef: { containerName: api, resource: limits.memory }
      # persistent
      - name: receipts
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: order-receipts
      # ephemeral · external
      - name: psp
        csi:
          driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io
          readOnly: true
          volumeAttributes:
            secretProviderClass: order-service-aws

See it happen — step through

▶ One Pod, three volumes — WHAT vs WHERE
1 / 5
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Declare WHAT
The Pod spec lists three volumes. On the node the kubelet creates one folder per volume under the Pod's own folder /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<uid>/volumes/.
Step 2 · Mount WHERE (container 1)
Container api plugs each volume into a path of its own filesystem. Paths are only in the container; the files live in the host folders.
Step 3 · Same volume, second container
log-shipper mounts logs at /logs, read-only. Both containers see the same files — that is how sidecars share data.
Step 4 · The type decides the source
config is filled by the kubelet from the ConfigMap in the API. receipts is an EFS file system from AWS mounted over NFS. logs starts empty.
Step 5 · The rule
Pod level declares; container level mounts; the name joins them.
§ 5.1INTERACTIVE

containers[].volumeMounts

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
Each volumeMounts item is one plug: it takes one volume and attaches it to one folder of this container. Its fields answer four questions in order: which volume → where → which part → how.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
Which volume?
name
the cable
Where in the container?
mountPath
the socket on the wall
All of it or one piece?
subPath · subPathExpr
a splitter
With what rights / visibility?
readOnly · recursiveReadOnly · mountPropagation
the switch

2 · Full YAML

pod-volumemounts.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: order-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: jahez/order-service:2.14.0
    env:
    - name: POD_NAME
      valueFrom:
        fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.name }
    volumeMounts:
    - # ① Which volume?
      name: logs                       # matches spec.volumes[].name
      # ② Where in the container?
      mountPath: /var/log/order
      # ④ With what rights?
      readOnly: false                  # read-write (default)
    - # ① Which volume?
      name: config
      # ② Where in the container?
      mountPath: /app/appsettings.Production.json
      # ③ All of it or one piece?
      subPath: appsettings.Production.json   # one file, not the whole volume
      # ④ With what rights?
      readOnly: true
    - # ① Which volume?
      name: dumps
      # ② Where in the container?
      mountPath: /dumps
      # ③ All of it or one piece?
      subPathExpr: $(POD_NAME)         # a folder named after this Pod
  - name: log-shipper
    image: fluent/fluent-bit:3.1
    volumeMounts:
    - # ① Which volume?
      name: logs                       # same volume, second container
      # ② Where in the container?
      mountPath: /logs
      # ④ With what rights / visibility?
      readOnly: true                   # reader only
      recursiveReadOnly: IfPossible    # also make sub-mounts read-only when the runtime supports it
      mountPropagation: None           # default; no mount events cross between host and container
  # What storage does the Pod have?
  volumes:
  - name: logs
    emptyDir: {}
  - name: config
    configMap:
      name: order-service-config
  - name: dumps
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: order-dumps

See it happen — step through

▶ volumeMounts — which volume, where, which part, how
1 / 5
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · name + mountPath
name: logs picks the volume; mountPath: /var/log/order is where it appears inside api. Read-write by default.
Step 2 · readOnly
The sidecar mounts the same folder with readOnly: true. Writes from that container fail; api can still write.
Step 3 · subPath
Only appsettings.Production.json from the config volume is placed at one path. The image's other files in /app/ stay visible — a whole-volume mount would hide them.
Step 4 · subPathExpr
Each replica gets its own sub-folder on a shared PVC, named from $(POD_NAME). The Pod sees only its folder.
Step 5 · Trap
When the ConfigMap changes, the volume folder updates, but a subPath mount is a fixed copy of the old file and never updates.

3 · Every property

🌳 containers[].volumeMounts[] — one item per plug
▸namestringrequiredWHICH volume: must equal a spec.volumes[].name.

The only link between the two lists. A typo gives the Pod error volumeMounts[0].name: Not found at creation.

▸mountPathstringrequiredWHERE: the absolute path inside this container.

The mount hides whatever the image had at that path. Mount into an empty or dedicated folder. Must not contain :. Two mounts cannot share a path.

Deep dive: mountPath tabs below
▸readOnlyboolHOW: block writes from this container only.
Values
falseread-write
truewrites fail with EROFS — use for secrets, config, log shippers
Default: false
▸recursiveReadOnlystringHOW: also make mounts nested inside the volume read-only.

Plain readOnly covers only the top mount; a sub-mount under it could still be writable. Needs readOnly: true and mountPropagation: None.

Values
Disabledold behaviour
IfPossiblerecursive when the runtime + kernel support it
Enabledrecursive or the Pod fails to start
Default: Disabled
▸subPathstringWHICH PART: mount one file or sub-folder of the volume, not the whole thing.

Lets you drop one file into a folder without hiding the rest of the image's folder. Trap: configMap / secret files mounted with subPath are never updated when the object changes.

Default: "" (whole volume)
▸subPathExprstringWHICH PART: like subPath but built from env vars, e.g. $(POD_NAME).

Gives each replica its own folder on a shared volume. Only $(VAR) syntax. Cannot be used together with subPath.

▸mountPropagationstringHOW: whether mounts made later on the host or in the container are seen by the other side.
Values
Noneisolated (default) — almost every app
HostToContainercontainer sees mounts the host makes later (e.g. node agents)
Bidirectionalboth ways — privileged containers only (CSI node plugins)
Default: None

4 · Deep dive — values compared

What

volumeMounts[].mountPath is the path inside the container where a volume appears; readOnly makes that mount read-only for this container only.

Why

The same volume may need different paths and permissions per container: the app writes logs, the shipper only reads them.

◆ Goals & Principles
Goals
  • Let each container see a volume where its software expects it
  • Grant the minimum write access per container
  • Keep image contents and mounted data clearly separated
Principles
  1. A mount hides whatever the image had at that path — mount into an empty or dedicated directory.
  2. readOnly: true is per mount; the volume itself can still be written by other containers.
  3. Secrets, configMaps and sidecar readers should always be read-only.
  4. Never mount two volumes on the same path; volumes cannot be nested inside other volumes.
How

The kubelet prepares the volume directory on the node; the runtime bind-mounts it at mountPath with ro or rw flags. recursiveReadOnly: Enabled (recent releases, needs runtime support) also makes sub-mounts read-only.

readOnly: false (default)

The container can create, modify and delete files. Use for the writer — e.g. api writing /var/log/order.

snippet.yaml
volumeMounts:
- name: logs
  mountPath: /var/log/order
  readOnly: false
readOnly: true

Writes fail with EROFS. fluent-bit cannot accidentally truncate the app's logs; a compromised sidecar cannot alter config.

snippet.yaml
volumeMounts:
- name: logs
  mountPath: /logs
  readOnly: true
mountPath: /app (dangerous)

Mounting at /app hides the application binaries baked into the image — the container then fails to start. Mount at a sub-directory such as /app/data or use subPath (§5.1).

SettingContainer can writeTypical use
readOnly: false✓app data, logs writer, DB data
readOnly: true✗secrets, config, log shippers
recursiveReadOnly: Enabled✗ incl. sub-mountshardened read-only trees

subPath & subPathExpr

What

subPath mounts a single file or sub-directory of a volume instead of its root. subPathExpr does the same with $(VAR) expansion from env vars.

Why

Sometimes you must drop one file into a directory the image already populates (/etc/nginx/nginx.conf), or give each Pod its own folder on a shared volume.

◆ Goals & Principles
Goals
  • Insert one file without hiding the rest of the image directory
  • Partition one shared volume into per-Pod folders
  • Reuse one volume for several mount points
Principles
  1. subPath mounts of configMap/secret/projected never receive updates — roll the Pod after changes.
  2. Prefer mounting a whole directory and pointing the app at it when hot-reload matters.
  3. subPathExpr: $(POD_NAME) gives each replica its own folder on an RWX volume.
  4. subPath is resolved at container start; the path must not escape the volume (symlinks are checked).
How

The kubelet bind-mounts the resolved sub-path into /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<uid>/volume-subpaths/ and the runtime mounts that. Because it binds the file itself (not the ..data symlink), atomic updates never reach it.

▶ subPath vs directory mount after a ConfigMap update
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Directory mount
Mounting the whole volume at /etc/nginx/conf.d exposes the kubelet's symlink tree.
Step 2 · subPath mount
Mounting key nginx.conf with subPath places one file at /etc/nginx/nginx.conf and keeps the rest of the image's /etc/nginx.
Step 3 · Update arrives
After kubectl apply, the directory mount follows the swapped ..data symlink to v2.
Step 4 · subPath is frozen
The subPath bind still points at the original file. Fix: kubectl rollout restart deploy/nginx-gw, or a checksum annotation on the Pod template so every config change triggers a rollout.
subPath: nginx.conf

One key from a configMap at an exact file path.

snippet.yaml
volumeMounts:
- name: conf
  mountPath: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
  subPath: nginx.conf
subPathExpr: $(POD_NAME)

Per-replica folders on one shared RWX claim: /exports/report-exporter-7d…-abc/.

snippet.yaml
env:
- name: POD_NAME
  valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.name } }
volumeMounts:
- name: exports
  mountPath: /exports
  subPathExpr: $(POD_NAME)
Mount styleHides image dirReceives configMap updatesUse
whole volume✓✓config dirs, data dirs
subPath✗✗single file into image dir
subPathExpr✗n/a (data volumes)per-Pod folders on RWX
§ 5.2INTERACTIVE

containers[].volumeDevices (raw block)

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
volumeDevices is the twin of volumeMounts for raw block storage. Instead of a folder, the container gets a device file. It only works with a PVC whose volumeMode is Block (§6.3).
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
Which volume?
name
same as volumeMounts
Where?
devicePath
a /dev entry, not a folder
When?
claim has volumeMode: Block
databases with their own disk format

2 · Full YAML

pod-volumedevices.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: ledger-raw
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What does it need?
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Gi
  volumeMode: Block                 # raw device, no filesystem
  # ② Where does it come from?
  storageClassName: ebs-gp3
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: ledger-engine
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: engine
    image: jahez/ledger-engine:1.4.2
    volumeDevices:                  # NOT volumeMounts
    - # ① Which volume?
      name: raw
      # ② Where? (a device file, not a folder)
      devicePath: /dev/xvdb
  volumes:
  - name: raw
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: ledger-raw

See it happen — step through

▶ volumeDevices — a raw disk, not a folder
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · A Block claim
The PVC asks for volumeMode: Block. The EBS disk is created but never formatted.
Step 2 · Attached to the node
AWS attaches the disk to worker-a, where it appears as /dev/nvme1n1. The kubelet maps it for the Pod.
Step 3 · devicePath
Inside the container the disk is the device file /dev/xvdb — there is nothing to ls.
Step 4 · Block vs Filesystem
The engine writes raw blocks itself. With the default Filesystem mode, the node would format the disk and mount a folder instead.

3 · Every property

🌳 containers[].volumeDevices[]
•namestringrequiredWHICH volume: a PVC volume whose claim has volumeMode: Block.
▸devicePathstringrequiredWHERE: the device file path inside the container, e.g. /dev/xvdb.

The app opens it like a disk and writes bytes directly — no filesystem, no files. Only databases or engines that manage their own on-disk format want this.

§ 5.3INTERACTIVE

volumes[].emptyDir

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
An emptyDir is a blank folder created when the Pod lands on a node. All containers of the Pod can share it. It survives container restarts but is deleted when the Pod leaves the node. It has only two settings: where the folder is and how big it may get.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
Where is the folder?
medium
disk or RAM
How big may it get?
sizeLimit
eviction line
Family
ephemeral · scratch
Starts
empty
Survives
container restart ✓ · Pod delete ✗
Shared by
all containers of the Pod

2 · Full YAML

pod-emptydir.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: report-builder
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  initContainers:
  - name: fetch
    image: amazon/aws-cli:2.17.0
    command: ["sh", "-c", "aws s3 cp s3://jahez-reports/templates/ /work/templates/ --recursive"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: work
      mountPath: /work
  containers:
  - name: builder
    image: jahez/report-builder:3.2.0
    resources:
      limits:
        memory: 1Gi                 # a Memory emptyDir counts against this
    volumeMounts:
    - name: work
      mountPath: /work
    - name: fast-cache
      mountPath: /cache
  volumes:
  - name: work
    emptyDir:
      # ① Where is the folder?  (medium omitted = node disk)
      # ② How big may it get?
      sizeLimit: 5Gi                # Pod is evicted if it writes more than 5Gi here
  - name: fast-cache
    emptyDir:
      # ① Where is the folder?
      medium: Memory                # tmpfs in RAM
      # ② How big may it get?
      sizeLimit: 256Mi

See it happen — step through

▶ emptyDir — born empty with the Pod, gone with the Pod
1 / 5
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Created empty
When the Pod lands on worker-a, the kubelet creates work/ on the node disk and fast-cache/ as a tmpfs in RAM. Both are empty.
Step 2 · Init container fills it
The init container copies templates from S3 into /work. The bytes land in the node folder.
Step 3 · App sees the same files
The builder mounts the same work volume and finds the templates. It writes temporary data to /cache, which is RAM.
Step 4 · Container restart
A crash restarts the container inside the same Pod. emptyDir content survives.
Step 5 · Pod removed
Deleting or evicting the Pod deletes both folders. Writing past sizeLimit also evicts the Pod.

3 · Every property

🌳 volumes[].emptyDir
▸mediumstringWHERE the empty folder is created on the node.
Values
"" (empty)node disk: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/<name>
Memorytmpfs in RAM: very fast, cleared on node reboot, counts toward the container memory limit
Default: ""
▸sizeLimitquantityHOW BIG it may grow before the kubelet evicts the Pod.

Disk medium: counted as ephemeral storage, the Pod is evicted when exceeded. Memory medium: also caps the tmpfs size (otherwise it can grow to the node's memory).

Default: unset (no limit)

4 · Deep dive — values compared

What

emptyDir.medium chooses the backing store ("" = node disk, Memory = tmpfs). sizeLimit caps how much the volume may hold.

Why

Scratch data has very different needs: logs want cheap disk, model files want RAM speed, and nothing should be able to fill the node's disk.

◆ Goals & Principles
Goals
  • Protect the node from a runaway writer
  • Pick speed vs cost per volume
  • Make eviction behaviour predictable
Principles
  1. Always set sizeLimit on disk-backed emptyDir — and ephemeral-storage requests/limits on the container.
  2. Memory-backed bytes count against the container's memory limit (and the node's RAM).
  3. Exceeding sizeLimit evicts the whole Pod; it is not a quota that returns ENOSPC.
  4. For tmpfs, sizeLimit also caps the tmpfs mount size, so a runaway writer hits a full filesystem before it can eat all the RAM of the node.
How

The kubelet's eviction manager periodically measures emptyDir usage (du or project quotas) and evicts the Pod with reason Evicted: Usage of EmptyDir volume "x" exceeds the limit.

medium: "" (default)

Node root disk (EKS: the instance root volume, often 20–80Gi shared by images, logs and all emptyDirs).

snippet.yaml
volumes:
- name: logs
  emptyDir:
    sizeLimit: 1Gi
medium: Memory

tmpfs in RAM. Survives container restarts, not node reboots. A 2Gi model in tmpfs + 1.5Gi heap needs a ≥ 4Gi memory limit.

snippet.yaml
volumes:
- name: models
  emptyDir:
    medium: Memory
    sizeLimit: 2Gi
sizeLimit: 2Gi

Exceed it and the kubelet evicts the Pod. Pair with container-level limits:

snippet.yaml
resources:
  requests: { ephemeral-storage: 1Gi }
  limits:   { ephemeral-storage: 3Gi }   # writable layer + logs + emptyDir

§ 5.4INTERACTIVE

volumes[].configMap

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
A configMap volume turns each key of a ConfigMap into a file. The kubelet writes the files into a folder on the node and keeps them in sync: when the ConfigMap changes, the files change too (within about a minute), using an atomic ..data symlink swap. The fields answer: which object → which keys as which files → with what permissions → what if it is missing.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
Which object?
name
the source
Which keys, which file names?
items[] (key → path)
a picking list
Which permissions?
defaultMode · items[].mode
chmod
Missing object?
optional
wait or continue
Family
ephemeral · config
On node
disk, under the Pod folder
Live update
✓ (not with subPath)
Max size
1 MiB per ConfigMap

2 · Full YAML

pod-configmap-volume.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: order-service-config
  namespace: jahez-prod
data:
  appsettings.Production.json: |
    { "Cache": { "TtlSeconds": 300 } }
  feature-flags.json: |
    { "splitPayments": true }
  log-level: Information
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: order-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: jahez/order-service:2.14.0
    volumeMounts:
    - name: config
      mountPath: /app/config
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: config
    configMap:
      # ① Which object?
      name: order-service-config    # same namespace
      # ② Which keys, which file names?
      items:                        # without items every key becomes a file
      - key: appsettings.Production.json
        path: appsettings.Production.json
      - key: feature-flags.json
        path: flags/feature-flags.json   # sub-folders allowed
        mode: 0400                       # ③ per-file permission, overrides defaultMode
      # ③ Which permissions?
      defaultMode: 0444             # every file (octal)
      # ④ Missing object?
      optional: false               # Pod waits if the ConfigMap is missing

See it happen — step through

▶ configMap — keys become files, updated atomically
1 / 5
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Source object
The ConfigMap lives in the API (stored in etcd). It has three keys.
Step 2 · kubelet writes files
On the node the kubelet writes the two keys listed in items into a timestamped folder and points the ..data symlink at it. Each visible file is a symlink through ..data.
Step 3 · Container view
The container sees plain files at /app/config, read-only. Permissions come from defaultMode / items[].mode.
Step 4 · Live update
After the ConfigMap changes, a new timestamped folder is written and ..data is swapped atomically. The app sees the new files without a restart.
Step 5 · Missing object
With optional: false (default) the Pod waits in ContainerCreating until the ConfigMap exists.

3 · Every property

🌳 volumes[].configMap
•namestringrequiredWHICH ConfigMap, in the Pod's namespace.
▸items[]listPICK which keys become files and what they are called. Without it, every key becomes a file named after the key.

If you list a key that does not exist, the volume fails to set up (unless optional: true).

•keystringrequiredThe key in the ConfigMap.
•pathstringrequiredThe relative file path inside the mount (may include sub-folders, no ..).
•modeint (octal)Permission for this one file; overrides defaultMode.
▸defaultModeint (octal)Permission bits for every file. Write 0444 in YAML (JSON needs decimal 292).
Default: 0644
▸optionalboolWhat if the ConfigMap or a listed key is missing.
Values
falsethe Pod stays in ContainerCreating until it exists
truethe Pod starts with an empty folder
Default: false

volumes[].secret

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
A secret volume works exactly like a configMap volume — each key becomes a file, updated live — with one difference: the folder is a tmpfs (RAM) on the node, so secret values are never written to the node's disk.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
Which object?
secretName
the source
Which keys, which file names?
items[]
a picking list
Which permissions?
defaultMode · items[].mode
chmod — keep it tight
Missing object?
optional
wait or continue
Family
ephemeral · config
On node
tmpfs (RAM)
Live update
✓ (not with subPath)
Max size
1 MiB per Secret

2 · Full YAML

pod-secret-volume.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: order-db-credentials
  namespace: jahez-prod
type: Opaque
stringData:
  username: order_app
  password: change-me
  ca.crt: |
    -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
    MIIB...
    -----END CERTIFICATE-----
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: order-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  securityContext:
    fsGroup: 2000                   # files group-owned by 2000 so the non-root app can read 0440
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: jahez/order-service:2.14.0
    securityContext:
      runAsUser: 1000
    volumeMounts:
    - name: db-creds
      mountPath: /etc/secrets/db
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: db-creds
    secret:
      # ① Which object?
      secretName: order-db-credentials   # NOTE: secretName, not name
      # ② Which keys, which file names?
      items:
      - key: password
        path: password
      - key: ca.crt
        path: tls/ca.crt
      # ③ Which permissions?
      defaultMode: 0440
      # ④ Missing object?
      optional: false

See it happen — step through

▶ secret — like configMap, but in RAM
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Source object
The Secret lives in the API. Values are base64-encoded there and encrypted at rest on EKS.
Step 2 · tmpfs on the node
The disk only holds an empty mount point. The kubelet decodes the keys and writes them into a tmpfs (RAM), with the same ..data swap as configMap.
Step 3 · Container view
The app reads /etc/secrets/db/password. Mode 0440 plus fsGroup: 2000 lets the non-root user read it.
Step 4 · Gone without a trace
When the Pod leaves, the tmpfs is unmounted. No secret value ever touched the node disk.

🌳 volumes[].secret
•secretNamestringrequiredWHICH Secret, in the Pod's namespace. (Field is secretName, unlike configMap's name.)
▸items[]listPICK which keys become files and what they are called. Without it, every key becomes a file named after the key.

If you list a key that does not exist, the volume fails to set up (unless optional: true).

•keystringrequiredThe key in the Secret.
•pathstringrequiredThe relative file path inside the mount (may include sub-folders, no ..).
•modeint (octal)Permission for this one file; overrides defaultMode.
▸defaultModeint (octal)Permission bits for every file. Use 0400 / 0440 for credentials.
Default: 0644
▸optionalboolWhat if the Secret or a listed key is missing.
Values

trueempty folder

volumes[].downwardAPI

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
A downwardAPI volume lets the app read facts about its own Pod as files: its name, namespace, labels, annotations, and its CPU / memory numbers. No API call, no permissions needed. Each item is one file with one source: a Pod field or a container resource.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
Which file?
items[].path
the file name
A fact about the Pod?
items[].fieldRef.fieldPath
identity & labels
A CPU / memory number?
items[].resourceFieldRef
sizing info, with a unit
Permissions?
defaultMode · items[].mode
chmod
Family
ephemeral · config
Live update
labels / annotations ✓
vs env vars
env is set once at start
Typical
log tags, auto-tuning heap

2 · Full YAML

pod-downwardapi-volume.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: order-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: order-service
    version: "2.14.0"
  annotations:
    jahez.io/team: orders
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: jahez/order-service:2.14.0
    resources:
      requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }
      limits:   { cpu: "1",  memory: 512Mi }
    volumeMounts:
    - name: podinfo
      mountPath: /etc/podinfo
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: podinfo
    downwardAPI:
      items:
      # ── A fact about the Pod? (fieldRef) ──
      - path: name                  # ① which file: /etc/podinfo/name
        fieldRef:
          fieldPath: metadata.name
      - path: namespace
        fieldRef:
          fieldPath: metadata.namespace
      - path: uid
        fieldRef:
          fieldPath: metadata.uid
      - path: labels                # all labels, one per line: key="value"
        fieldRef:
          fieldPath: metadata.labels
      - path: annotations
        fieldRef:
          fieldPath: metadata.annotations
      - path: team                  # one annotation
        fieldRef:
          fieldPath: metadata.annotations['jahez.io/team']
      # ── A CPU / memory number? (resourceFieldRef) ──
      - path: mem_limit_mi
        resourceFieldRef:
          containerName: api        # required in a volume
          resource: limits.memory
          divisor: 1Mi              # file contains 512
      - path: cpu_request_m
        resourceFieldRef:
          containerName: api
          resource: requests.cpu
          divisor: 1m               # file contains 250
      # ── Permissions? ──
      defaultMode: 0444

See it happen — step through

▶ downwardAPI — the Pod reads facts about itself
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · The facts
The Pod object in the API holds its name, labels and resource numbers.
Step 2 · Written as files
The kubelet writes one file per item. Resource values are divided by divisor (512Mi / 1Mi = 512).
Step 3 · App reads them
The app reads /etc/podinfo/* with no API call and no RBAC.
Step 4 · Live labels
Changing a label rewrites the labels file. Environment variables are fixed at start and would not change.

3 · Every property

🌳 volumes[].downwardAPI
▸items[]listOne item = one file. Each item has a path and exactly ONE source: fieldRef or resourceFieldRef.
•pathstringrequiredFile name (relative) inside the mount.
▸fieldRefobjectSOURCE 1: a field of the Pod itself.
▸fieldPathstringrequiredWhich field.

spec.nodeName, status.podIP, spec.serviceAccountName are env-only; they are not allowed in a volume.

Values

metadata.namespacenamespace
metadata.uidPod UID
metadata.labelsall labels — updated live
metadata.annotationsall annotations — updated live
metadata.labels['k']one label
metadata.annotations['k']one annotation
▸apiVersionstringSchema version of fieldPath.
Default: v1
▸resourceFieldRefobjectSOURCE 2: a container's CPU / memory / storage request or limit.
•containerNamestringrequiredWhich container. Required in volumes (env can default to its own container).
▸resourcestringrequiredWhich value.
Values
requests.cpu / limits.cpuCPU
requests.memory / limits.memorymemory
requests.ephemeral-storage / limits.ephemeral-storagescratch disk
▸divisorquantityUnit of the number written to the file (1m, 1, 1Mi, 1Gi…).
Default: 1
•modeint (octal)Permission for this file.
▸defaultModeint (octal)Permission for every file.
Default: 0644

volumes[].projected

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
A projected volume merges several sources into one folder: configMap, secret, downwardAPI and service-account tokens. Use it when an app expects all its config in one directory. The only new field is sources[]; each source keeps the same sub-fields it has as a standalone volume.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
Which sources?
sources[] (one key per item)
a list of the volumes you already know
A token for an API / AWS?
sources[].serviceAccountToken
a rotating badge
Permissions?
defaultMode
one chmod for all
Family
ephemeral · config
On node
tmpfs (RAM)
Live update
✓
Built-in use

2 · Full YAML

pod-projected-volume.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: order-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: order-service
spec:
  serviceAccountName: order-service-sa
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: jahez/order-service:2.14.0
    volumeMounts:
    - name: all-in-one
      mountPath: /etc/order
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: all-in-one
    projected:
      # ── Which sources? (several → ONE folder) ──
      sources:
      - configMap:
          name: order-service-config
          items:
          - key: appsettings.Production.json
            path: appsettings.json
      - secret:
          name: order-db-credentials     # NOTE: name here (not secretName)
          items:
          - key: password
            path: db/password
      - downwardAPI:
          items:
          - path: labels
            fieldRef:
              fieldPath: metadata.labels
      # ── A token for an API / AWS? ──
      - serviceAccountToken:
          path: tokens/payments-token
          audience: payments.jahez.internal   # who the token is for
          expirationSeconds: 3600              # rotated by the kubelet before expiry
      # ── Permissions? ──
      defaultMode: 0440

See it happen — step through

▶ projected — four sources, one folder
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Four sources
A ConfigMap, a Secret, the Pod's labels, and a ServiceAccount token requested from the API server.
Step 2 · Merged on the node
The kubelet writes all of them into one tmpfs folder. File paths must not clash.
Step 3 · One folder in the app
The app reads everything under /etc/order.
Step 4 · Rotating token
The token file is replaced before it expires, so the app always reads a valid token.

🌳 volumes[].projected
▸sources[]listEach item is ONE source; all of them are written into the same folder. File paths must not collide.
▸configMapobjectSame fields as the configMap volume: name, items[], optional.
Deep dive: §5.4
▸secretobjectSame as the secret volume, but the field is name (not secretName): name, items[], optional.

▸audiencestringWho the token is for; the receiver rejects tokens for other audiences.
Default: the API server
▸expirationSecondsintToken lifetime. Minimum 600. The kubelet refreshes the file at 80% of the lifetime or 24h.
Default: 3600
▸clusterTrustBundleobjectCA certificates from ClusterTrustBundle objects (newer feature; needs it enabled).
•pathstringrequiredFile name for the PEM bundle.
•name / signerName + labelSelectorstringPick one bundle by name, or all bundles of a signer.

volumes[].ephemeral (generic ephemeral volume)

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
A generic ephemeral volume is a real disk that lives only as long as the Pod. It is an emptyDir that comes from a StorageClass: the Pod gets a fresh PVC (and EBS volume), and when the Pod is deleted the PVC is garbage-collected. Use it when scratch space is too big for the node's disk.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
What disk?
volumeClaimTemplate.spec
a PVC written inline
Extra labels?
volumeClaimTemplate.metadata
tags for the PVC
Family
ephemeral · scratch
Backed by
a PVC → PV → EBS
PVC name
<pod>-<volume>
Deleted
with the Pod (ownerReference)

2 · Full YAML

pod-ephemeral-volume.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: image-resizer
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: resizer
    image: jahez/image-resizer:1.9.0
    volumeMounts:
    - name: scratch
      mountPath: /scratch
  volumes:
  - name: scratch
    ephemeral:
      volumeClaimTemplate:            # Kubernetes creates PVC "image-resizer-scratch"
        # ── Extra labels for the PVC? ──
        metadata:
          labels:
            app: image-resizer
          annotations:
            jahez.io/purpose: scratch
        # ── What disk? (a normal PVC spec, §6) ──
        spec:
          # ① What does it need?
          accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
          resources:
            requests:
              storage: 200Gi
          volumeMode: Filesystem
          # ② Where does it come from?
          storageClassName: ebs-gp3

See it happen — step through

▶ ephemeral — a real disk that dies with the Pod
1 / 5
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Pod created
The Pod has an inline claim template. The ephemeral controller creates PVC image-resizer-scratch, owned by the Pod.
Step 2 · Disk created
The StorageClass builds a 200Gi EBS disk and a PV, just like any dynamic claim.
Step 3 · Mounted
The disk is attached to the Pod's node and mounted at /scratch.
Step 4 · Working
The job uses far more space than the node disk could give an emptyDir.
Step 5 · Pod deleted
Because the Pod owns the PVC, the PVC is garbage-collected; the PV (reclaim Delete) and the EBS disk go with it.

3 · Every property

🌳 volumes[].ephemeral
▸volumeClaimTemplateobjectrequiredThe PVC to create for this Pod. Named <pod-name>-<volume-name>, owned by the Pod, deleted with it.
•metadataobjectOnly labels and annotations are allowed (the name is generated).
▸specPVC specrequiredAny PersistentVolumeClaim spec: accessModes, storageClassName, resources, volumeMode, dataSource…
Deep dive: §6 PVC

volumes[].csi (inline CSI volume)

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
An inline csi volume asks a CSI driver to build a folder just for this Pod — no PVC, no PV. The driver decides what goes in it. At Jahez the common case is the Secrets Store CSI driver pulling values from AWS Secrets Manager.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
Which driver?
driver
the plug-in
Driver settings?

Credentials for the driver?
nodePublishSecretRef

Needs
driver installed + Ephemeral mode
vs PVC + CSI
no PV object, no lifecycle
Typical
Secrets Manager, cert-manager csi

2 · Full YAML

pod-csi-inline-volume.yaml
apiVersion: secrets-store.csi.x-k8s.io/v1
kind: SecretProviderClass
metadata:
  name: order-service-aws-secrets
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  provider: aws
  parameters:
    objects: |
      - objectName: "prod/order-service/stripe"
        objectType: "secretsmanager"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: order-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  serviceAccountName: order-service-sa       # IRSA role allowed to read the secret
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: jahez/order-service:2.14.0
    volumeMounts:
    - name: aws-secrets
      mountPath: /mnt/secrets
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: aws-secrets
    csi:
      # ① Which driver?
      driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io      # must support Ephemeral mode
      # ② Driver settings?
      volumeAttributes:
        secretProviderClass: order-service-aws-secrets
      readOnly: true
      # fsType: ext4                         # only for drivers that create a filesystem
      # ③ Credentials for the driver?
      # nodePublishSecretRef:                # only if the driver needs them
      #   name: driver-creds

See it happen — step through

▶ csi inline — a driver builds the folder for this Pod
1 / 5
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · kubelet calls the driver
For an inline csi volume the kubelet asks the node's CSI driver to publish a volume for this Pod. The driver reads the SecretProviderClass.
Step 2 · Driver calls AWS
Using the Pod's IAM role (IRSA), the driver reads the secret from AWS Secrets Manager.
Step 3 · Writes to tmpfs
The value is written into a tmpfs folder for this Pod only.
Step 4 · App reads a file
The app reads /mnt/secrets/prod_order-service_stripe.
Step 5 · No storage objects
There is no PVC or PV. When the Pod goes, the driver unmounts the folder.

3 · Every property

🌳 volumes[].csi
•driverstringrequiredWHICH CSI driver serves the volume. It must be installed and declare the Ephemeral lifecycle mode in its CSIDriver object.
•volumeAttributesmapDriver-specific settings, passed as-is (e.g. secretProviderClass).
▸readOnlyboolAsk the driver for a read-only volume.
Default: false
▸fsTypestringFilesystem to create, for drivers that format a disk.
Default: driver decides
▸nodePublishSecretRefobjectA Secret (same namespace) with credentials the driver needs on the node.
•namestringSecret name.

volumes[].persistentVolumeClaim

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
A persistentVolumeClaim volume is just a pointer to a claim. All the real decisions — size, access mode, class, where the disk is — live in the PVC (§6) and the PV (§7). That is the point: the Pod spec stays the same in every cluster.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
Which claim?
claimName
a ticket number
Read-only here?
readOnly
a lock on this Pod only
Family
persistent
Data lives
on the PV's disk (EBS / EFS)
Survives
Pod delete ✓ · node loss ✓
Details
§6 PVC · §7 PV

2 · Full YAML

pod-pvc-volume.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: order-uploads
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What does it need?
  accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50Gi
  # ② Where does it come from?
  storageClassName: efs-shared
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: order-service }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: order-service }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: jahez/order-service:2.14.0
        volumeMounts:
        - name: uploads
          mountPath: /app/uploads
      volumes:
      - name: uploads
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          # ① Which claim?
          claimName: order-uploads    # same namespace
          # ② Read-only here?
          readOnly: false             # true = force read-only for this Pod

See it happen — step through

▶ persistentVolumeClaim — the Pod just names a claim
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · The claim chain
PVC order-uploads is bound to a PV that points at an EFS access point.
Step 2 · Three replicas, three nodes
Every replica has the same claimName. Each node mounts EFS over NFS — no attach step, so RWX works across nodes and zones.
Step 3 · Shared files
A file written by the replica on worker-b is visible to the others at once.
Step 4 · Persistent
Pods come and go; the claim and the files stay.

3 · Every property

🌳 volumes[].persistentVolumeClaim
▸claimNamestringrequiredWHICH PVC, in the Pod's namespace. This is Link A (Pod → PVC).

If the claim is missing the Pod stays Pending. If it is not yet bound, the Pod waits; with WaitForFirstConsumer the Pod's scheduling is what triggers the disk creation.

Deep dive: §2.3.11 ways to link
▸readOnlyboolMount the claim read-only in this Pod, whatever the access mode.
Default: false
§ 5.11INTERACTIVE

volumes[].hostPath

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
A hostPath volume mounts a path of the node itself into the container. The data is the node's, not the Pod's: it stays after the Pod is gone, but a Pod on another node sees different data. Reserved for node agents (DaemonSets) — a security risk for apps.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
Which path on the node?
path
a hole in the wall to the host
What must be there?
type
a pre-flight check
Family
special · node
Survives
Pod ✓ · node loss ✗
Moves with Pod
✗
Use for
DaemonSets only

2 · Full YAML

daemonset-hostpath.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: node-log-agent
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: node-log-agent }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: node-log-agent }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: agent
        image: fluent/fluent-bit:3.1
        volumeMounts:
        - name: varlog
          mountPath: /var/log
          readOnly: true
        - name: state
          mountPath: /var/fluent-bit/state
      volumes:
      - name: varlog
        hostPath:
          # ① Which path on the node?
          path: /var/log
          # ② What must be there?
          type: Directory             # must already exist as a folder
      - name: state
        hostPath:
          # ① Which path on the node?
          path: /var/lib/fluent-bit
          # ② What must be there?
          type: DirectoryOrCreate     # create it (0755, root) if missing

See it happen — step through

▶ hostPath — a window into the node itself
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · The node's own folders
/var/log belongs to the node: it holds the logs of every Pod on worker-a. It is not under the Pod's kubelet folder.
Step 2 · Mounted directly
The DaemonSet's agent mounts the node path straight into the container, read-only. type: Directory checks it exists first.
Step 3 · DirectoryOrCreate
The state folder is created on the node if missing and survives Pod restarts — on this node only.
Step 4 · Why apps must not use it
Each node has different content. Move the Pod and the data is not there. Use it only for per-node agents.

3 · Every property

🌳 volumes[].hostPath
•pathstringrequiredWHICH path on the node's own filesystem. Mounted directly — no copy, no Pod folder.
▸typestringA CHECK the kubelet runs before mounting.
Values
"" (empty)no check (default)
DirectoryOrCreatecreate the folder if missing
Directorymust exist and be a folder
FileOrCreatecreate an empty file if missing (parent must exist)
Filemust exist and be a file
Socketmust be a UNIX socket
CharDevice / BlockDevicemust be a device
Default: ""

4 · Deep dive — values compared

What

hostPath.path names a path on the node; hostPath.type validates what must be there before the Pod starts.

Why

A DaemonSet that expects /var/log or a socket should fail fast if the node does not have it — instead of silently mounting an empty directory.

◆ Goals & Principles
Goals
  • Fail early when node layout differs
  • Avoid accidental directory creation on the node
  • Document the exact host dependency
Principles
  1. Use the most specific type (Directory, Socket, File).
  2. Avoid DirectoryOrCreate except for agent state directories you own.
  3. Always pair with readOnly: true unless writing is the point.
  4. Only in system namespaces; enforce PSA baseline/restricted everywhere else.
How

The kubelet checks the path type before mounting; on mismatch the Pod stays in ContainerCreating with a FailedMount event such as hostPath type check failed: /var/log is not a directory.

type: Directory

Must already exist as a directory.

snippet.yaml
volumes:
- name: varlog
  hostPath:
    path: /var/log/pods
    type: Directory
type: DirectoryOrCreate

Creates it (0755, owned by kubelet user) if missing — e.g. an agent's state dir /var/lib/fluent-bit for read offsets.

type: Socket

Must be a Unix socket — e.g. a CSI plugin registration socket. Mounting the container runtime socket is equivalent to root on the node.

typeMust existCreates
"" (default)no check—
Directory / File✓✗
DirectoryOrCreate / FileOrCreate✗✓
Socket / CharDevice / BlockDevice✓✗
§ 5.12INTERACTIVE

volumes[].nfs and volumes[].image

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
Two less common sources. nfs mounts a network share directly — the data is persistent but the Pod knows the server address. image ships read-only data (an ML model, static assets) as an OCI image and mounts its files.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
Network share without a PVC?
nfs.server · nfs.path
a hard-coded share
Read-only data from a registry?
image.reference · pullPolicy
a data package

2 · Full YAML

pod-nfs-and-image.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: catalog-importer
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: importer
    image: jahez/catalog-importer:5.0.1
    volumeMounts:
    - name: legacy-share
      mountPath: /mnt/legacy
    - name: ml-model
      mountPath: /models
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: legacy-share
    nfs:                                # an NFS export, mounted directly (no PVC)
      # ① Which share?
      server: fs-0a1b2c3d.efs.me-central-1.amazonaws.com
      path: /catalog
      # ② Read-only?
      readOnly: false
  - name: ml-model
    image:                              # files of an OCI image, read-only
      # ① Which image?
      reference: registry.jahez.net/ml/eta-model:2026.10
      # ② When to pull?
      pullPolicy: IfNotPresent

See it happen — step through

▶ nfs and image — two direct sources
1 / 3
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · nfs
The kubelet mounts the NFS export into the Pod folder; the app reads and writes /mnt/legacy. Data stays on the server.
Step 2 · image
The kubelet pulls an OCI image that holds only data and mounts its files read-only at /models.
Step 3 · When to use which
Prefer a PVC over a hard-coded NFS server. Use an image volume to ship versioned read-only data.

3 · Every property

🌳 volumes[].nfs · volumes[].image
▸nfsobjectAn NFS export mounted straight into the Pod. Works, but a PVC is preferred so the Pod does not hard-code a server.
•serverstringrequiredNFS server host name or IP.
•pathstringrequiredExported path on the server.
▸readOnlyboolMount read-only.
Default: false
▸imageobjectMounts the files of an OCI image (read-only). Newer feature (beta from v1.33); needs a container runtime that supports it.
•referencestringrequiredThe image, like a container image reference.
▸pullPolicystringWhen to pull.
Values
Alwaysevery Pod start
IfNotPresentonly if not on the node
Nevermust be on the node
Default: Always if tag is :latest, else IfNotPresent
06

PersistentVolumeClaim

§ 6.0INTERACTIVE

PVC — The Logic, the Structure, the Full YAML

◆ The logic — read this first
A PVC is a request for storage, written by the app team. It says what the app needs, not how it is built. Read every PVC as three questions: what do I need (size, sharing, shape), where does it come from (a class that creates it, or an existing PV), and what does it start with (empty or a copy). Kubernetes answers by binding the PVC to exactly one PV.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
① What do I need?
accessModes · resources.requests.storage · volumeMode
the order: size + how it is shared
② Where does it come from?
storageClassName · volumeName · selector
the shop: new disk or an existing one
③ What does it start with?
dataSource · dataSourceRef
empty box or a copy
What did I get?
status (read-only)
the receipt
Scope
namespaced
Written by
app team
Binds to
exactly one PV
Used by
Pods via claimName

Structure tree

🌳 PersistentVolumeClaim
▸metadataobjectIdentity of the claim.
•namestringrequiredClaim name — what Pods put in claimName.
•namespacestringPVCs are namespaced: only Pods in the same namespace can use them.
•labels / annotationsmapYour tags. Kubernetes adds annotations such as volume.kubernetes.io/selected-node and pv.kubernetes.io/bind-completed.
•finalizerslistkubernetes.io/pvc-protection: the claim is not removed while a Pod still uses it.
▸specobjectYour request, in three groups.
▸① what it needsgroupsize, sharing, shape
▸accessModeslistrequiredHOW MANY nodes / Pods may use the disk, and how.

A request, matched against what the PV / driver supports. EBS = RWO / RWOP only; EFS = all.

Values
ReadWriteOnce (RWO)read-write by Pods on ONE node at a time
ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP)read-write by ONE Pod in the whole cluster
ReadOnlyMany (ROX)read-only by many nodes
ReadWriteMany (RWX)read-write by many nodes (file storage: EFS)
Deep dive: §6.1
▸resourcesobjectrequiredHOW BIG.
▸requests.storagequantityrequiredThe minimum size you need, e.g. 100Gi. Raise it later to grow the disk (if the class allows).
Deep dive: §6.2
•limits.storagequantityRarely used; most drivers ignore it.
▸volumeModestringWHAT SHAPE the container gets.
Values
Filesystema formatted folder (volumeMounts)
Blocka raw device (volumeDevices)
Default: Filesystem
Deep dive: §6.3
▸② where it comes fromgroupclass, or a specific / labelled PV
▸storageClassNamestringWHERE FROM: which StorageClass creates or matches the PV.
Values

omittedthe default class is filled in
"" (empty)no class: bind only to existing PVs with no class

▸volumeNamestringWHERE FROM: pin to one existing PV by name (static). Also written by Kubernetes after binding.
Deep dive: §6.5

Deep dive: §6.5
•matchLabelsmapLabels that must all be equal.
•matchExpressions[]listkey + operator (In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist) + values.
▸③ what it starts withgroupempty, or a copy
▸dataSourceobjectSTARTS WITH: create the new disk pre-filled from a snapshot or another PVC.
Deep dive: §6.6
•apiGroupstringsnapshot.storage.k8s.io for a snapshot; empty for a PVC.
•kindstringrequiredVolumeSnapshot or PersistentVolumeClaim.
•namestringrequiredObject name, same namespace.
▸dataSourceRefobjectSTARTS WITH: the newer, general form: any populator kind, optional namespace (cross-namespace needs a ReferenceGrant).
Deep dive: §6.6
▸④ performance tiergroupoptional, newer
•volumeAttributesClassNamestringChange IOPS / throughput of a live disk by switching class (newer feature; driver must support it).
▸statusobjectWritten by Kubernetes. Read it, never write it.

Full YAML — every PVC field

pvc-every-field.yaml
# PVC — every field
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: reports-archive
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels: { app: reports }
  annotations:
    # set by the scheduler with WaitForFirstConsumer — do not write it yourself
    # volume.kubernetes.io/selected-node: worker-a
spec:
  # ① What do I need?
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]             # RWO | ROX | RWX | RWOP
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 300Gi                       # minimum size; raise later to expand
  volumeMode: Filesystem                   # Filesystem (default) | Block
  # ② Where does it come from?
  storageClassName: manual                 # omit = default class · "" = no dynamic provisioning
  volumeName: legacy-reports               # pin to one PV (overrides matching)
  selector:                                # or: any PV with these labels
    matchLabels:
      tier: archive
  # ③ What does it start with?
  # dataSource:                            # pre-populate from a snapshot or PVC
  #   apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io
  #   kind: VolumeSnapshot
  #   name: reports-2026-10-01

See it happen — step through

▶ A PVC from request to use
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · The request
The claim states ① what it needs, ② where the PV comes from, ③ what the disk starts with. Status: Pending.
Step 2 · The answer is built
Group ② names ebs-gp3, so the class creates an EBS disk and a PV for it.
Step 3 · Bound
The PVC and PV point at each other. Status shows Bound and the real capacity.
Step 4 · Used
A Pod names the claim; the disk is attached to its node and mounted.
§ 6.1INTERACTIVE

PVC accessModes

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
Access modes say how many nodes or Pods may use the disk at once. They are a promise you ask for, and the storage must be able to keep it: a block disk (EBS) attaches to one node, a file share (EFS) to many.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
One node read-write?
RWO
one machine
One Pod only?
RWOP
one process — databases
Many nodes?
RWX / ROX
needs file storage

2 · Full YAML

pvc-access-modes.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: orders-db-data
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What do I need?
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOncePod]   # one Pod only (EBS)
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Gi
  # ② Where does it come from?
  storageClassName: ebs-gp3
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: order-uploads
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What do I need?
  accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]      # many nodes (EFS)
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50Gi
  # ② Where does it come from?
  storageClassName: efs-shared

See it happen — step through

▶ Access modes on real nodes
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · RWO
An EBS disk attached to worker-a. Two Pods on that same node can both mount it.
Step 2 · RWO across nodes
A third replica scheduled on worker-c fails: an EBS disk cannot attach to two nodes (Multi-Attach error).
Step 3 · RWOP
ReadWriteOncePod allows exactly one Pod, even on the same node. Ideal for databases.
Step 4 · RWX
EFS is a network file system: Pods on every node, in every zone, can read and write.

3 · Every property

🌳 accessModes
▸accessModeslistrequiredHOW MANY nodes / Pods may use the disk, and how.

A request, matched against what the PV / driver supports. EBS = RWO / RWOP only; EFS = all.

Values
ReadWriteOnce (RWO)read-write by Pods on ONE node at a time
ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP)read-write by ONE Pod in the whole cluster
ReadOnlyMany (ROX)read-only by many nodes
ReadWriteMany (RWX)read-write by many nodes (file storage: EFS)
Deep dive: §6.1

4 · Deep dive — values compared

What

spec.accessModes on a PVC states how the volume will be mounted: RWO, ROX, RWX or RWOP.

Why

The scheduler, attach-detach controller and driver all enforce it; it is how Kubernetes prevents two nodes writing to a block device at once.

◆ Goals & Principles
Goals
  • Prevent concurrent writers corrupting a filesystem
  • Express sharing needs independently of the backend
  • Let the binder pick a compatible PV
Principles
  1. Request exactly what the app needs — usually one mode.
  2. RWO is per node; use RWOP for a single Pod.
  3. RWX needs a file backend (EFS/NFS); EBS cannot do it.
  4. Access modes are not file permissions — combine with fsGroup / readOnly.
How

Binding requires the PV to list every requested mode. At runtime, RWO/RWOP are enforced by attach (one node) and, for RWOP, by the scheduler (one Pod). See the diagram in §2.3.8.

accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]

EBS default. Multiple Pods may mount it only if they are on the same node.

accessModes: [ReadWriteOncePod]

One Pod cluster-wide; a second Pod is unschedulable. Ideal for orders-db.

accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]

EFS. Any number of Pods on any nodes.

accessModes: [ReadOnlyMany]

Many readers. Combine with readOnly: true in the Pod — the mode alone does not force read-only mounts on every driver.

ModeNodesPodsBackend
RWO1many on that nodeEBS, EFS
RWOP11CSI only
RWXmanymanyEFS / NFS
ROXmanymany (read)EFS, NFS

PVC resources.requests.storage & expansion

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
resources.requests.storage is the minimum size. You can raise it later and the disk grows online, if the class has allowVolumeExpansion: true. You can never shrink it.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
How big?
requests.storage
a minimum
Grow later?
edit the number up
needs allowVolumeExpansion
Shrink?
not possible
copy to a smaller PVC

2 · Full YAML

pvc-size.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: reports-data
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What do I need?
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 200Gi                 # was 100Gi — edit + apply to grow
  # ② Where does it come from?
  storageClassName: ebs-gp3        # class must have allowVolumeExpansion: true

See it happen — step through

▶ Growing a claim while the Pod runs
1 / 5
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Before
100Gi claim, 100Gi PV, 100Gi EBS disk, mounted on worker-a.
Step 2 · Edit the claim
Raise requests.storage to 200Gi. The class allows expansion, so the claim shows Resizing.
Step 3 · The disk grows
The CSI resizer calls AWS ModifyVolume; the EBS disk becomes 200Gi online and the PV is updated.
Step 4 · The filesystem grows
The kubelet on worker-a grows the ext4 filesystem. df shows 200G inside the running Pod — no restart.
Step 5 · Shrinking
Lowering the size is rejected by the API. To shrink, copy the data to a new, smaller claim.

3 · Every property

🌳 resources
▸resourcesobjectrequiredHOW BIG.
▸requests.storagequantityrequiredThe minimum size you need, e.g. 100Gi. Raise it later to grow the disk (if the class allows).
Deep dive: §6.2
•limits.storagequantityRarely used; most drivers ignore it.

4 · Deep dive — values compared

What

resources.requests.storage is the minimum capacity the claim needs. Raising it later expands the volume if the class allows it.

Why

Size drives cost and, on gp2/io2, performance. Databases grow; you need to expand without migration.

◆ Goals & Principles
Goals
  • Get at least the requested capacity
  • Grow online without downtime
  • Keep cost proportional to real need
Principles
  1. Start right-sized; expand when usage passes ~70%.
  2. Only increases are allowed — never shrink.
  3. EBS: one modification per volume every 6 h; plan big steps.
  4. Watch kubelet_volume_stats_used_bytes / available_bytes in Prometheus.
How

Edit the PVC → csi-resizer calls ControllerExpandVolume (EC2 ModifyVolume) → PVC condition FileSystemResizePending → kubelet calls NodeExpandVolume (resize2fs/xfs_growfs) on the mounted node. Newer releases also let you retry a failed expansion with a smaller target (feature RecoverVolumeExpansionFailure).

storage: 100Gi

Initial request. With static PVs, any PV ≥ 100Gi can match.

storage: 100Gi → 200Gi

Apply the change; no Pod restart for EBS + ext4/xfs.

expand.sh
kubectl patch pvc data-orders-db-0 -n jahez-prod \
  -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"200Gi"}}}}'
kubectl get pvc data-orders-db-0 -n jahez-prod -w
kubectl describe pvc data-orders-db-0 -n jahez-prod | grep -A3 Conditions
volumeClaimTemplates: storage: 100Gi

Changing the template does not resize existing PVCs (and older versions reject the edit). Patch each data-orders-db-N, then update the template (delete with --cascade=orphan and re-apply if required).

ActionAllowedDowntime
Increase✓ if allowVolumeExpansionnone (online)
Decrease✗—
Change on STS templateneeds per-PVC patchnone

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
volumeMode decides the shape of the storage the container sees: a formatted folder (almost always) or a raw block device.

See it happen — step through

▶ Filesystem vs Block
1 / 3
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Filesystem
The node formats the disk (ext4) and mounts it as a folder. The app works with files.
Step 2 · Block
The disk is passed to the container as a device file; no filesystem is created.
Step 3 · Choose
Almost everything uses Filesystem. Block is for engines that manage raw storage themselves.

3 · Every property

🌳 volumeMode
▸volumeModestringWHAT SHAPE the container gets.
Values
Filesystema formatted folder (volumeMounts)

Default: Filesystem
Deep dive: §6.3

4 · Deep dive — values compared

What

volumeMode is Filesystem (formatted and mounted as a directory) or Block (exposed as a raw device).

Why

Almost every app wants files. Some databases and storage engines manage raw devices themselves for performance.

◆ Goals & Principles
Goals
  • Default to the simple, portable filesystem mode
  • Allow raw device access when an engine needs it
Principles
  1. Leave the default unless the software documents raw-device support.
  2. Block volumes use volumeDevices (devicePath), not volumeMounts.
  3. PV and PVC volumeMode must match to bind.
How

For Block, the node plugin skips mkfs/mount and the runtime exposes the device node (e.g. /dev/xvda) inside the container.

volumeMode: Filesystem

Formatted (fsType) and mounted at mountPath.

volumeMode: Block

Raw device in the container.

snippet.yaml
containers:
- name: engine
  volumeDevices:
  - name: data
    devicePath: /dev/xvda

PVC storageClassName

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
storageClassName chooses where the PV comes from. A class name means "create one for me with these settings" (dynamic). An empty string means "only bind to a PV that already exists" (static). Omitting it means "use the default class".
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
New disk with known settings?
storageClassName: ebs-gp3
order from a menu
Existing PV only?
storageClassName: ""
pick from the shelf
Not written?
default class filled in
the house choice

2 · Full YAML

pvc-storageclass.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: cart-data
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What do I need?
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi
  # ② Where does it come from?
  storageClassName: ebs-gp3          # always write it explicitly in production

See it happen — step through

▶ Three ways to write storageClassName
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Named
storageClassName: ebs-gp3 → that class creates a new disk and PV.
Step 2 · Omitted
The API fills in the default class (marked ★). The result is the same as naming it — but you did not choose.
Step 3 · Empty string
"" means "no class": nothing is created; the claim can only bind a PV that already exists with no class.
Step 4 · Summary
The field decides whether a disk is built and with which recipe.

3 · Every property

🌳 storageClassName
▸storageClassNamestringWHERE FROM: which StorageClass creates or matches the PV.
Values
ebs-gp3 (a name)dynamic: that class creates a PV; static: only PVs with the same class match
omittedthe default class is filled in
"" (empty)no class: bind only to existing PVs with no class
Deep dive: §6.4

4 · Deep dive — values compared

What

storageClassName selects the StorageClass for dynamic provisioning, or the class label that static PVs must match.

Why

It is the one knob developers turn to pick performance/cost tiers without knowing cloud details.

◆ Goals & Principles
Goals
  • Choose a tier by name (gp3, io2, efs)
  • Keep manifests portable across clusters
  • Control whether dynamic provisioning happens at all
Principles
  1. Omit it to get the default class — but be explicit in production manifests.
  2. "" means "no class": only static PVs with no class can bind.
  3. Class names are a contract across environments: same name, different parameters per cluster.
  4. Classes are immutable; create a new one to change parameters.
How

The PV controller (admission plugin DefaultStorageClass) fills in the default when omitted; with a class set, external-provisioner handles claims whose class's provisioner matches its driver.

storageClassName: (omitted)

The default class (ebs-gp3) is filled in at creation.

storageClassName: ebs-gp3

Explicit: dynamic EBS gp3.

storageClassName: ""

Static only. Used with volumeName or a selector for imported disks.

ValueDynamic provisioningBinds to
omitted✓ default classnew PV of default class
name✓ that classPVs of that class
""✗PVs with no class

volumeName and selector narrow down which existing PV the claim may bind to. volumeName names one PV; selector filters a pool by labels. Both are for static PVs.

Fields

volumeName

pvc-volumename-selector.yaml

  name: orders-archive
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:

  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests:

---
apiVersion: v1

  name: finance-data
  namespace: jahez-prod

  # ① What do I need?

  selector:                          # any PV labelled team=finance
    matchLabels:

▶ Choosing an existing PV: name or labels
1 / 4

Step 1 · A pool of static PVs

Step 2 · volumeName

▸volumeNamestringWHERE FROM: pin to one existing PV by name (static). Also written by Kubernetes after binding.

Deep dive: §6.5
•matchLabelsmapLabels that must all be equal.
•matchExpressions[]listkey + operator (In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist) + values.

4 · Deep dive — values compared

What

volumeName pins a PVC to one named PV; selector restricts candidate PVs by labels.

Why

For static volumes you often need a specific disk — the one with last year's reports — not "any 300Gi disk".

◆ Goals & Principles
Goals
  • Bind to a known volume deterministically
  • Separate pools (prod/staging) of static PVs
Principles
  1. Use volumeName for imports and DR restores into a known PV.
  2. A claim with a selector is never dynamically provisioned.
  3. Reserve the PV for the claim with claimRef so nothing else grabs it first.
How

The binder only considers the named PV (still checking class, size and modes) or PVs whose labels match. See §4.3.

volumeName: legacy-reports

Only that PV is considered.

selector.matchLabels: tier: archive

Any matching PV; smallest that fits wins.

§ 6.6INTERACTIVE

PVC dataSource / dataSourceRef

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
dataSource makes the new disk start as a copy instead of empty: of a VolumeSnapshot (restore) or another PVC (clone). dataSourceRef is the newer general form that also accepts custom populators.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
Restore a snapshot?
kind: VolumeSnapshot
a backup
Copy a live claim?
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
a clone — driver must support it
Something else?
dataSourceRef
a populator

2 · Full YAML

pvc-datasource.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: orders-restore
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① What do I need?
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Gi                 # >= snapshot size
  # ② Where does it come from?
  storageClassName: ebs-gp3
  # ③ What does it start with?
  dataSource:
    apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io
    kind: VolumeSnapshot
    name: orders-db-2026-11-01

See it happen — step through

▶ Starting a disk as a copy of a snapshot
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · The original
orders-data holds live data on EBS in zone 1a.
Step 2 · Snapshot
A VolumeSnapshot asks the EBS driver for an AWS snapshot of the disk.
Step 3 · Restore claim
A new PVC with dataSource: VolumeSnapshot makes the driver create a NEW disk from that snapshot, plus a PV.
Step 4 · Use the copy
Another Pod mounts the restored disk. The original keeps running unchanged.

3 · Every property

🌳 dataSource · dataSourceRef
▸dataSourceobjectSTARTS WITH: create the new disk pre-filled from a snapshot or another PVC.
Deep dive: §6.6
•apiGroupstringsnapshot.storage.k8s.io for a snapshot; empty for a PVC.
•kindstringrequiredVolumeSnapshot or PersistentVolumeClaim.
•namestringrequiredObject name, same namespace.
▸dataSourceRefobjectSTARTS WITH: the newer, general form: any populator kind, optional namespace (cross-namespace needs a ReferenceGrant).
Deep dive: §6.6

4 · Deep dive — values compared

What

dataSource / dataSourceRef pre-populate a new volume from a VolumeSnapshot, another PersistentVolumeClaim (clone) or, with populators, a custom resource.

Why

Spinning up staging from yesterday's production snapshot, or restoring after a bad migration, should be one manifest.

◆ Goals & Principles
Goals
  • Create volumes that start with data
  • Make restore and staging refresh declarative
Principles
  1. The new size must be ≥ the source size.
  2. Clones require same namespace and class, and driver support.
  3. Snapshots can restore into any AZ of the region (EBS).
  4. Use dataSourceRef for cross-namespace sources (with ReferenceGrant) and volume populators.
How

external-provisioner passes the source to CreateVolume; for EBS that creates the volume from the snapshot ID (lazy-loaded from S3 — first reads are slower; consider Fast Snapshot Restore for latency-sensitive restores).

dataSource.kind: VolumeSnapshot
snippet.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: orders-db-staging
  namespace: jahez-staging
spec:
  storageClassName: ebs-gp3
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources: { requests: { storage: 100Gi } }
  dataSource:
    apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io
    kind: VolumeSnapshot
    name: orders-db-pre-migration
dataSource.kind: PersistentVolumeClaim

Clone of a live claim; source must be in the same namespace.

PVC status, annotations & finalizers

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
The rest of a PVC is written by Kubernetes: a protection finalizer, binding annotations, and status. Reading them tells you where the claim is in its life.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
Is it usable?
status.phase
Pending → Bound
What did I get?
status.capacity
the receipt
Why can't I delete it?
finalizers: pvc-protection
a Pod still uses it
Which node chose the zone?
annotation selected-node
WaitForFirstConsumer

2 · Full YAML

pvc-status-example.yaml
# kubectl get pvc data-orders-db-0 -n jahez-prod -o yaml   (output, trimmed)
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: data-orders-db-0
  namespace: jahez-prod
  annotations:                       # written by Kubernetes
    pv.kubernetes.io/bind-completed: "yes"
    pv.kubernetes.io/bound-by-controller: "yes"
    volume.beta.kubernetes.io/storage-provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
    volume.kubernetes.io/selected-node: worker-a
  finalizers:
  - kubernetes.io/pvc-protection
spec:
  # ① What do I need?
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOncePod]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Gi
  # ② Where does it come from?
  storageClassName: ebs-gp3
  volumeName: pvc-6f1c2a9e-0b7d-4e55-9a51-3c2b8d7e1f00   # written by Kubernetes on binding
# What did I get? (written by Kubernetes)
status:
  phase: Bound
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOncePod]
  capacity:
    storage: 100Gi

See it happen — step through

▶ Reading a claim's status and metadata
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Pending
Just created. With WaitForFirstConsumer nothing happens until a Pod needs the claim. The protection finalizer is already set.
Step 2 · selected-node
The scheduler placed the Pod on worker-a and wrote that into the claim's annotation, so the disk will be created in zone 1a.
Step 3 · Bound
Disk and PV created. volumeName and status.capacity are filled in.
Step 4 · Protected delete
Deleting the claim while the Pod uses it only marks it Terminating; the finalizer removes it after the Pod is gone.

3 · Every property

🌳 Kubernetes-written fields
▸status.phasestringWhere the claim is.
Values
Pendingno PV yet (waiting for a Pod with WaitForFirstConsumer, or no match)
Boundlinked to a PV — usable
Lostits PV was deleted — data gone or unreachable
•status.capacity.storagequantityActual size of the bound PV.
•status.conditions[]listResize progress: Resizing, FileSystemResizePending.
•metadata.finalizerslistkubernetes.io/pvc-protection holds deletion while any Pod uses the claim.
•annotationsmapselected-node (zone choice), storage-provisioner (which driver), bind-completed.
