PersistentVolume

§ 7.0INTERACTIVE

PV — The Logic, the Structure, the Full YAML

◆ The logic — read this first
A PV is the cluster's record of one real piece of storage — an EBS volume, an EFS access point, a local disk. It is written by an admin (static) or by a CSI provisioner (dynamic). Read every PV as four questions: what is the disk, where is it really, who may use it, and what happens at the end.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
① What is the disk?
capacity · accessModes · volumeMode · mountOptions
the label on the box
② Where is it really?
one source: csi · local · nfs · hostPath
the address
③ Who may use it?
nodeAffinity · storageClassName · claimRef
which nodes, which claim
④ What happens at the end?
persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy
keep or shred
Scope
cluster-wide
Written by
admin or provisioner
Binds to
exactly one PVC
Name (dynamic)
pvc-<claim uid>

Structure tree

🌳 PersistentVolume
▸metadataobjectIdentity. PVs are cluster-scoped (no namespace).
•namestringrequiredPV name. Dynamic PVs are named pvc-<uid of the claim>.
•labelsmapUsed by PVC selectors.
•annotationsmappv.kubernetes.io/provisioned-by marks dynamic PVs.
•finalizerslistkubernetes.io/pv-protection while bound; external-provisioner…/deletion-protection until the disk is deleted.
▸specobjectThe disk, in four groups.
▸① describe the diskgroupsize, sharing, shape, mount flags
•capacity.storagequantityrequiredHow big the disk is. Used for matching: a PVC binds only to a PV at least as big as it asks.
•accessModeslistrequiredWhat the backend supports (RWO, RWOP, ROX, RWX). The PVC's modes must be a subset.
▸volumeModestringFilesystem or Block — must equal the PVC.
Default: Filesystem
•mountOptionslistExtra options passed to mount(8), e.g. noatime, NFS nfsvers=4.1. Not validated — a wrong option fails the mount.
▸② where it really isgroupthe source
▸<one source key>objectWHERE the data really lives. Exactly one.
▸csiobjectAny CSI driver: EBS, EFS… — the modern choice.
Deep dive: §7.2
▸localobjectA disk or folder on one node.
Deep dive: §7.3
▸nfsobjectAn NFS export.
Deep dive: §7.4
▸hostPathobjectA node folder — single-node test clusters only.
Deep dive: §7.5
▸③ who may use itgroupplacement + binding
▸nodeAffinityobjectWHICH NODES can reach this disk. The scheduler only places the Pod there.

Zonal disks (EBS) → zone label. Local disks → node hostname. Dynamic PVs get it from the driver automatically.

Deep dive: §7.6
•required.nodeSelectorTerms[]listOR-ed terms; each term has matchExpressions[] (AND-ed): key, operator, values.
•storageClassNamestringMust equal the PVC's class for them to bind. "" = no class.
▸claimRefobjectWHICH CLAIM owns (or is reserved for) this PV. Written by Kubernetes on binding; write it yourself to reserve.
Deep dive: §7.7
•namespacestringClaim namespace.
•namestringClaim name.
•uidstringClaim UID — set by Kubernetes; delete it to let a new claim with the same name bind.
▸④ end of lifegroupafter the claim is gone
▸persistentVolumeReclaimPolicystringWHAT HAPPENS to the disk when its PVC is deleted.
Values
Retainkeep disk + PV (Released); an admin cleans up
Deletedelete the PV and the real disk
Recycledeprecated — do not use
Default: Delete for dynamic PVs (from the class) · Retain for manual PVs
Deep dive: §7.8
▸statusobjectWritten by Kubernetes.
Deep dive: §7.9
•phasestringAvailable → Bound → Released / Failed.

Full YAML — every PV field (static import of an EBS volume)

pv-every-field.yaml
# Static PV — import an existing EBS volume (historical reports, migrated)
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: legacy-reports
  labels:
    tier: archive
    team: finance
spec:
  # ① What is the disk?
  capacity:
    storage: 500Gi                         # what this PV offers for matching
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]             # what the backend supports
  volumeMode: Filesystem                   # Filesystem | Block
  mountOptions: [noatime]                  # passed to mount(8) by the driver
  # ② Where is it really?
  csi:
    driver: ebs.csi.aws.com
    volumeHandle: vol-0aa13c5e8f2b47d10    # the real EBS volume ID
    fsType: ext4
  # ③ Who may use it?
  nodeAffinity:                            # which nodes — REQUIRED for zonal disks
    required:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: topology.ebs.csi.aws.com/zone
          operator: In
          values: [me-central-1a]
  storageClassName: manual                 # which claims — "" or a name; must match the PVC
  claimRef:                                # which claim — optional reservation
    namespace: jahez-prod
    name: reports-archive
  # ④ What happens at the end?
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain    # Retain | Delete  (Recycle deprecated)

See it happen — step through

▶ One PV, four questions
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · ① The disk described
Size, access modes, shape and mount options — used for matching claims.
Step 2 · ② Where it is
The csi source points at the real EBS volume by ID.
Step 3 · ③ Who may use it
nodeAffinity allows only zone 1a nodes; claimRef links it to one claim.
Step 4 · ④ The end
reclaimPolicy decides the disk's fate when the claim is deleted.

See it happen — step through

▶ How a claim matches a PV
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · The request
A static claim for 300Gi, RWO, Filesystem, no class.
Step 2 · Too small
pv-200 is rejected: capacity must be at least the request.
Step 3 · Wrong shape
pv-blk is Block; the claim wants Filesystem. Then pv-gp3 has a different class.
Step 4 · Match
pv-ok passes every check. The claim binds and gets all 500Gi, more than it asked.

§ 7.2INTERACTIVE

PV source: csi

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
csi is the modern source: the PV just names a driver and the driver's ID for the disk. EBS, EFS and most cloud storage are CSI.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
Which driver?
driver
the plug-in
Which disk?
volumeHandle
the disk's ID in AWS
Format?
fsType
ext4 / xfs
Extra / secrets?
volumeAttributes · *SecretRef
driver settings

2 · Full YAML

pv-csi-ebs-and-efs.yaml
# EBS (block, one zone)
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: legacy-orders
spec:
  # ① What is the disk?
  capacity:
    storage: 500Gi
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  # ② Where is it really?
  csi:
    driver: ebs.csi.aws.com                  # which driver?
    volumeHandle: vol-0aa13c5e8f2b47d10      # which disk? (EBS volume ID)
    fsType: ext4                             # format?
    readOnly: false
  # ③ Who may use it?
  nodeAffinity:
    required:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: topology.ebs.csi.aws.com/zone
          operator: In
          values: [me-central-1a]
  storageClassName: ""
  # ④ What happens at the end?
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
---
# EFS (file, whole region — no nodeAffinity needed)
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: shared-media
spec:
  # ① What is the disk?
  capacity:
    storage: 100Gi                            # EFS ignores size; required by the API
  accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]
  # ② Where is it really?
  csi:
    driver: efs.csi.aws.com
    volumeHandle: fs-0c1d2e3f4a5b6c7d8::fsap-0123456789abcdef0   # file system :: access point
  # ③ Who may use it?
  storageClassName: ""                        # no nodeAffinity: every node can reach EFS
  # ④ What happens at the end?
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain

See it happen — step through

▶ csi source: EBS vs EFS
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · EBS PV
The PV names the EBS driver and the disk ID. The disk exists in one Availability Zone.
Step 2 · Attached to one node
A Pod on worker-a gets the disk attached through the AWS API. A node in another zone cannot use it.
Step 3 · EFS PV
The PV names the EFS driver and a file system / access point. EFS has mount targets in every zone.
Step 4 · Mounted everywhere
Pods on all three nodes mount the same files over NFS.

3 · Every property

🌳 spec.csi
•driverstringrequiredCSI driver name, e.g. ebs.csi.aws.com, efs.csi.aws.com.
•volumeHandlestringrequiredThe driver's ID for the disk: EBS vol-…, EFS fs-… or fs-…::fsap-….
▸fsTypestringFilesystem to create / expect on a block disk.
Default: ext4 (driver default)
▸readOnlyboolPublish read-only to all Pods.
Default: false
•volumeAttributesmapDriver-specific attributes (set by the provisioner for dynamic PVs).
•nodeStageSecretRef · nodePublishSecretRef · controllerPublishSecretRef · controllerExpandSecretRefobjectSecrets the driver needs at each stage (name + namespace). Not needed for EBS / EFS with IRSA.

PV source: local

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
local is a disk attached to one specific node (e.g. instance-store NVMe). Very fast, but the Pod can only run on that node, and the data dies with the node. nodeAffinity is mandatory.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
Which path on the node?
local.path
mounted disk or folder
Which node?
nodeAffinity (hostname)
required
Class?
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
so the scheduler can choose

2 · Full YAML

pv-local.yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: local-nvme
# ① Who builds the disk?
provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner    # nobody — static only
# ③ When and where?
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer      # let the scheduler pick the node first
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: nvme-worker-a
spec:
  # ① What is the disk?
  capacity:
    storage: 900Gi
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  volumeMode: Filesystem
  # ② Where is it really?
  local:
    path: /mnt/nvme0                          # already formatted + mounted on the node
    fsType: ext4
  # ③ Who may use it?
  storageClassName: local-nvme
  nodeAffinity:                               # REQUIRED for local
    required:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: kubernetes.io/hostname
          operator: In
          values: [worker-a]
  # ④ What happens at the end?
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain

See it happen — step through

▶ local PV: a disk inside one node
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · The disk
worker-c has a fast NVMe drive that belongs to the instance itself.
Step 2 · The PV
An admin writes a local PV with the path and a nodeAffinity for worker-c.
Step 3 · Pinned scheduling
The Pod can only run on worker-c. Fast, but tied to one machine.
Step 4 · Node lost
If worker-c dies, the Pod stays Pending and the data is lost with the instance. Use only for data you can rebuild.

•fsTypestringOnly for Block → formatted use.

See it happen — step through

▶ nodeAffinity: which nodes can reach the disk
1 / 3
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · The rule
The disk lives in zone 1b, so the PV allows only nodes labelled with that zone.
Step 2 · Scheduling
The scheduler filters out worker-c and worker-a; the Pod runs on worker-b.
Step 3 · No eligible node
If no 1b node is available the Pod stays Pending with a volume node affinity conflict. Keep nodes in every zone your disks use.

3 · Every property

🌳 spec.nodeAffinity
▸nodeAffinityobjectWHICH NODES can reach this disk. The scheduler only places the Pod there.

Zonal disks (EBS) → zone label. Local disks → node hostname. Dynamic PVs get it from the driver automatically.

Deep dive: §7.6
•required.nodeSelectorTerms[]listOR-ed terms; each term has matchExpressions[] (AND-ed): key, operator, values.

4 · Deep dive — values compared

What

spec.nodeAffinity on a PV lists which nodes can access the volume. Dynamic EBS PVs get a zone constraint automatically; local PVs get a hostname.

Why

The scheduler must not place a Pod where its disk cannot be attached.

◆ Goals & Principles
Goals
  • Keep Pods and their volumes co-located
  • Make topology explicit and visible
Principles
  1. Static zonal PVs must declare it — otherwise Pods can land in the wrong AZ and hang.
  2. Have node capacity in every zone that hosts stateful volumes.
  3. Local PVs pin a Pod to one node forever.
How

The VolumeBinding scheduler plugin filters nodes against the PV's nodeAffinity (and the class's allowedTopologies for unbound claims).

nodeAffinity: zone In [me-central-1a]
snippet.yaml
nodeAffinity:
  required:
    nodeSelectorTerms:
    - matchExpressions:
      - key: topology.ebs.csi.aws.com/zone
        operator: In
        values: [me-central-1a]
nodeAffinity: kubernetes.io/hostname In [worker-a]

For instance-store NVMe local PVs — the fastest, and the least durable.

ConstraintPod can move toUse
zoneany node in that AZEBS
hostnamethat node onlylocal NVMe
noneanywhereEFS / NFS

PV storageClassName & claimRef

1 · The logic

◆ The logic — read this first
storageClassName and claimRef decide which claim may bind. The class must match the PVC. claimRef is the PV's side of the link: Kubernetes fills it on binding, or you write it first to reserve the PV.
Question it answers
Fields
Think of it as
Which claims can match?

apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: reserved-orders
spec:

  # ③ Who may use it?

    namespace: jahez-prod

See it happen — step through

1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Two claims
One PV with Delete, one with Retain, both bound.
Step 2 · Claims deleted
Both PVCs are removed.
Step 3 · Different fates
Delete: the PV is removed and the driver deletes the EBS disk. Retain: the PV becomes Released and the disk stays in AWS.
Step 4 · Choose per data
Keep business data with Retain.

3 · Every property

🌳 persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy
▸persistentVolumeReclaimPolicystringWHAT HAPPENS to the disk when its PVC is deleted.
Values
Retainkeep disk + PV (Released); an admin cleans up
Deletedelete the PV and the real disk
Recycledeprecated — do not use
Default: Delete for dynamic PVs (from the class) · Retain for manual PVs
Deep dive: §7.8

4 · Deep dive — values compared

What

persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy (on the PV; inherited from the class's reclaimPolicy) decides what happens to the disk when its PVC is deleted.

Why

A single mistyped kubectl delete pvc with Delete destroys a production database disk.

◆ Goals & Principles
Goals
  • Make data loss require a deliberate admin action
  • Avoid orphaned disks for truly disposable data
Principles
  1. Retain for anything you cannot rebuild (DBs, uploads).
  2. Delete for caches and CI scratch.
  3. You can patch a live PV's policy at any time.
  4. Retained disks cost money — track Released PVs.
How

See the lifecycle diagram in §4.6.

persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain

PV goes Released; disk untouched.

persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Delete

Provisioner deletes the EBS volume.

RetainDelete
After PVC deletePV Released, data keptPV + disk deleted
Reusemanual (clear claimRef)—
Useprod datadisposable data

Full YAML — the Jahez classes

storageclasses.yaml
# StorageClasses for jahez-prod-eks (me-central-1)
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: ebs-gp3
  annotations:
    # ⑤ Default class?
    storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"
# ① Who builds the disk?
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
# ② What kind of disk?
parameters:
  type: gp3
  iops: "3000"
  throughput: "125"                        # MiB/s
  encrypted: "true"
  kmsKeyId: arn:aws:kms:me-central-1:111122223333:key/7a1e-jahez-ebs
  csi.storage.k8s.io/fstype: ext4
# ③ When and where?
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer    # create the disk in the Pod's zone
allowedTopologies:                         # optional: restrict zones
- matchLabelExpressions:
  - key: topology.ebs.csi.aws.com/zone
    values: [me-central-1a, me-central-1b, me-central-1c]
# ④ Life rules?
allowVolumeExpansion: true
reclaimPolicy: Retain                      # production: never auto-delete DB disks
---
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: ebs-io2-db
# ① Who builds the disk?
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
# ② What kind of disk?
parameters:
  type: io2
  iopsPerGB: "50"
  encrypted: "true"
# ③ When and where?
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
# ④ Life rules?
allowVolumeExpansion: true
reclaimPolicy: Retain
---
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: efs-shared
# ① Who builds the disk?
provisioner: efs.csi.aws.com
# ② What kind of disk?
parameters:
  provisioningMode: efs-ap                 # one access point per PVC
  fileSystemId: fs-0c1d2e3f4a5b6c7d8
  directoryPerms: "750"
  gidRangeStart: "50000"
  gidRangeEnd: "60000"
  basePath: /jahez-prod
# ③ When and where?
volumeBindingMode: Immediate               # EFS is regional: zone does not matter
# ④ Life rules?
reclaimPolicy: Retain
---
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshotClass
metadata:
  name: ebs-snapclass
# Who takes snapshots?
driver: ebs.csi.aws.com
# Keep the cloud snapshot when the object is deleted?
deletionPolicy: Retain

4 · Deep dive — values compared

What

provisioner names the CSI driver that creates volumes for the class; parameters are opaque, driver-specific settings.

Why

This is where cloud specifics live, so app manifests don't have to.

◆ Goals & Principles
Goals
  • Encode performance and encryption once, centrally
  • Let developers choose by name
Principles
  1. Encrypt by default (encrypted: "true" + a CMK).
  2. gp3 decouples IOPS/throughput from size — set them explicitly.
  3. Parameter typos are only caught at provisioning time — test new classes.
  4. Classes are immutable: version names (ebs-gp3-v2) to change parameters.
How

external-provisioner passes parameters to CreateVolume; keys prefixed csi.storage.k8s.io/ are consumed by the sidecar (fstype, secrets).

parameters.type: gp3

Baseline 3,000 IOPS / 125 MiB/s, raisable independently of size. Default for Jahez.

parameters.type: io2

Provisioned IOPS (up to very high levels), higher durability. For the hottest OLTP volume only.

provisioningMode: efs-ap

EFS: each PVC becomes an access point under basePath with its own uid/gid.

ClassProvisionerModeUse
ebs-gp3ebs.csi.aws.comRWOdefault
ebs-io2-dbebs.csi.aws.comRWOhot DB
efs-sharedefs.csi.aws.comRWXshared files

See it happen — step through

▶ Immediate vs WaitForFirstConsumer
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Immediate
The disk is created as soon as the claim exists — in a zone chosen without knowing where the Pod will run.
Step 2 · Conflict
The Pod must run on worker-a (zone 1a), but the disk is in 1b. The Pod stays Pending.
Step 3 · Wait for the Pod
With WaitForFirstConsumer the claim waits. The scheduler places the Pod first.
Step 4 · Right zone
The disk is built in the Pod's zone, attached, and the Pod runs.

3 · Every property

🌳 volumeBindingMode
▸volumeBindingModestringWHEN the disk is created.
Values
Immediateas soon as the PVC exists (zone picked blindly)
WaitForFirstConsumerafter a Pod is scheduled — in that Pod's zone
Default: Immediate
Deep dive: §8.2

4 · Deep dive — values compared

What

volumeBindingMode decides when binding and provisioning happen: Immediate (at PVC creation) or WaitForFirstConsumer (when a Pod using it is scheduled).

Why

Zonal disks created before scheduling can strand Pods in zones without capacity. See the diagram in §4.4.

◆ Goals & Principles
Goals
  • Create disks where the Pod can actually run
  • Respect all scheduling constraints, not just storage
Principles
  1. WaitForFirstConsumer for every zonal backend (EBS, local).
  2. Immediate is fine for regional backends (EFS).
  3. Pending PVCs with WFFC are normal until a Pod exists.
  4. Don't set nodeName on Pods with WFFC claims — it bypasses the scheduler.
How

With WFFC the scheduler's VolumeBinding plugin chooses the node, annotates the PVC with selected-node, and external-provisioner provisions with that node's topology.

volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer

Recommended for EBS.

volumeBindingMode: Immediate

For EFS and other regional storage.

ImmediateWaitForFirstConsumer
Provision timePVC createPod schedule
Zone chosen bydriverscheduler
Riskunschedulable PodsPVC Pending until used

🌳 allowVolumeExpansion
▸allowVolumeExpansionboolMAY claims grow later.

Deep dive: §8.3

4 · Deep dive — values compared

What

allowVolumeExpansion: true on a class lets claims of that class be resized by editing their request.

Why

Without it, growing a database means snapshot + restore into a bigger volume.

◆ Goals & Principles
Goals
  • Enable self-service, online growth
Principles
  1. Turn it on for every class whose driver supports expansion.
  2. It only allows growth; it never shrinks.
  3. Monitor and alert on capacity before it is urgent.
How

The admission plugin rejects size increases for claims whose class does not allow expansion. Flow described in §6.2.

allowVolumeExpansion: true

Edit the PVC; done.

allowVolumeExpansion: false

Edits to storage are rejected.

truefalse
Resizepatch the PVCsnapshot → restore → cut over
Downtimenoneyes

Full YAML — production Postgres

orders-db-statefulset.yaml
# orders-db — Postgres StatefulSet with one EBS volume per replica
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-db-hl
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  clusterIP: None                          # headless: orders-db-0.orders-db-hl...
  selector: { app: orders-db }
  ports: [{ name: pg, port: 5432 }]
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: orders-db
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  maxUnavailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: orders-db }
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: orders-db
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  serviceName: orders-db-hl
  replicas: 3
  podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: orders-db }
  # ── Delete the disks when? ──
  persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
    whenDeleted: Retain                    # kubectl delete sts → keep PVCs
    whenScaled: Retain                     # scale 3 → 1 → keep data-orders-db-1/2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: orders-db }
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120   # let Postgres checkpoint on SIGTERM
      # ── Who owns the files? ──
      securityContext:
        fsGroup: 999
        fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch
      topologySpreadConstraints:
      - maxSkew: 1
        topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels: { app: orders-db }
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:16.4
        env:
        - name: PGDATA
          value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata   # sub-dir: avoids lost+found clash
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef: { name: db-orders, key: password }
        ports: [{ name: pg, containerPort: 5432 }]
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: "1", memory: 4Gi }
          limits:   { memory: 4Gi }
        # ── Where does the container see the storage? ──
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data                       # from volumeClaimTemplates
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
        - name: shm
          mountPath: /dev/shm
        startupProbe:
          exec: { command: ["pg_isready", "-U", "postgres"] }
          periodSeconds: 5
          failureThreshold: 60             # up to 5 min for attach + WAL replay
        readinessProbe:
          exec: { command: ["pg_isready", "-U", "postgres"] }
          periodSeconds: 10
      # ── Shared, non-templated volumes ──
      volumes:
      - name: shm
        emptyDir:
          medium: Memory
          sizeLimit: 1Gi                   # Postgres shared memory
  # ── Which disk per replica? ──
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: data                           # → data-orders-db-0, -1, -2
      labels: { app: orders-db }
    spec:
      # ① What does it need?
      accessModes: [ReadWriteOncePod]      # one writer, guaranteed
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 100Gi
      # ② Where does it come from?
      storageClassName: ebs-gp3

See it happen — step through

▶ How claim templates are stamped
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · The template
One claim template named data.
Step 2 · Stamped names
The controller creates data-orders-db-0/1/2 — template name, StatefulSet name, ordinal.
Step 3 · Scale up
Scaling to 4 creates data-orders-db-3 and a new disk for it.
Step 4 · Rules
Each claim is created once and reused. Template edits affect only new claims.

3 · Every property

🌳 volumeClaimTemplates
▸volumeClaimTemplates[]listA PVC template stamped once per replica: <template>-<sts>-<ordinal>.
Deep dive: §9.1
•metadata.namestringrequiredTemplate name = the volume name containers mount.
•specPVC specrequiredaccessModes, storageClassName, resources… exactly as §6.

4 · Deep dive — values compared

What

volumeClaimTemplates in a StatefulSet is a PVC template; the controller creates <template>-<sts>-<ordinal> for each replica.

Why

Each replica of a clustered database needs its own disk and must get the same one back after every restart.

◆ Goals & Principles
Goals
  • One durable volume per replica
  • Stable Pod ↔ volume identity across reschedules and rollouts
Principles
  1. Name the template after the data (data), not the app.
  2. Templates are (mostly) immutable — plan size and class up front.
  3. Use RWOP for single-writer engines.
  4. Spread replicas across zones with topologySpreadConstraints.
How

The StatefulSet controller creates missing PVCs before creating each Pod and wires the Pod's volume of the same name to its claim. See §3.4.

volumeClaimTemplates[].metadata.name: data

Produces data-orders-db-0, -1, -2. Containers mount name: data.

volumeClaimTemplatessingle PVC in Pod template
PVCsone per replicashared
Scale-out✓✗ (RWO)

See it happen — step through

▶ Keeping or deleting the replica disks
1 / 4
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Scale down
With whenScaled: Retain the claims of removed replicas stay, and their disks keep costing money.
Step 2 · Scale back up
The returning replicas re-attach their old disks with the old data.
Step 3 · Delete, Retain
Deleting the StatefulSet keeps all claims by default.
Step 4 · Delete, Delete
With whenDeleted: Delete the claims are removed; with a Delete reclaim policy the disks go too.

3 · Every property

🌳 persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy
▸persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicyobjectKeep or delete the stamped PVCs.
Deep dive: §9.2
▸whenDeletedstringStatefulSet deleted.
Values
Retainkeep PVCs (default)
Deletedelete PVCs
Default: Retain
▸whenScaledstringReplicas reduced.
Values
Retainkeep PVCs of removed ordinals (default)
Deletedelete them
Default: Retain

4 · Deep dive — values compared

What

persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy (stable in recent releases; beta and on by default since 1.27) controls whether a StatefulSet's PVCs are deleted whenDeleted (the StatefulSet is deleted) and whenScaled (replicas reduced).

Why

By default PVCs outlive the StatefulSet — safe, but leaves paid-for disks behind for ephemeral environments.

◆ Goals & Principles
Goals
  • Safe defaults for production data
  • Automatic cleanup for preview/test environments
Principles
  1. Keep Retain/Retain (default) for production.
  2. Use Delete in ephemeral namespaces (PR previews).
  3. A deleted PVC still obeys the PV reclaim policy — two layers of protection.
How

The StatefulSet controller sets owner references on PVCs (to the StatefulSet or the Pod) so garbage collection deletes them per the policy.

▶ PVC retention when scaling down or deleting a StatefulSet
1 / 5
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Three replicas
Each replica owns data-orders-db-N.
Step 2 · Scale 3 → 1, whenScaled: Retain
Pods 1 and 2 are removed; their claims stay. Scaling back up reattaches the same data.
Step 3 · Scale 3 → 1, whenScaled: Delete
Claims of removed ordinals are deleted (then the PV reclaim policy applies).
Step 4 · Delete STS, whenDeleted: Retain
All claims remain; recreating the StatefulSet picks them up.
Step 5 · Delete STS, whenDeleted: Delete
All claims are deleted with the StatefulSet.
whenDeleted / whenScaled: Retain / Retain

Default. Production.

whenDeleted / whenScaled: Delete / Delete

Preview environments.

persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
  whenDeleted: Delete
  whenScaled: Delete

Operations

§ 10.1

StorageClass per Cloud

The class name is the portable contract; the parameters are per cloud. Jahez runs on EKS in me-central-1; the other tabs are for reference.

sc-aws-ebs.yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: ebs-gp3
  annotations:
    storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
allowVolumeExpansion: true
reclaimPolicy: Retain
parameters:
  type: gp3
  iops: "3000"
  throughput: "125"
  encrypted: "true"
  kmsKeyId: arn:aws:kms:me-central-1:111122223333:key/7a1e-jahez-ebs
sc-aws-efs.yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: efs-shared
provisioner: efs.csi.aws.com
reclaimPolicy: Retain
parameters:
  provisioningMode: efs-ap
  fileSystemId: fs-0c1d2e3f4a5b6c7d8
  directoryPerms: "750"
  basePath: /jahez-prod
sc-gcp.yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: gcp-pd-ssd
provisioner: pd.csi.storage.gke.io
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
allowVolumeExpansion: true
parameters:
  type: pd-ssd
  replication-type: regional-pd    # synchronous replication across 2 zones
sc-azure.yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: azure-premium
provisioner: disk.csi.azure.com
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
allowVolumeExpansion: true
parameters:
  skuName: Premium_LRS             # Standard_LRS | Premium_LRS | PremiumV2_LRS | UltraSSD_LRS
  cachingMode: ReadOnly
sc-local.yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: local-nvme
provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner   # static PVs only
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer     # REQUIRED for local volumes
reclaimPolicy: Retain
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: local-pv-worker-a
spec:
  capacity: { storage: 1700Gi }
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: local-nvme
  local:
    path: /mnt/nvme0
  nodeAffinity:
    required:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: kubernetes.io/hostname
          operator: In
          values: [worker-a]
sc-longhorn.yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: longhorn-replicated
provisioner: driver.longhorn.io
allowVolumeExpansion: true
reclaimPolicy: Delete
parameters:
  numberOfReplicas: "3"
  staleReplicaTimeout: "2880"
  fsType: ext4
§ 10.2

CSI Drivers

Definition · CSI driver
A plugin, shipped and upgraded separately from Kubernetes, that connects Kubernetes to one storage system. It runs as a controller Deployment (create, attach, resize, snapshot) and a node DaemonSet (format and mount on each node).
ℹ
In-tree pluginsThe old built-in cloud plugins (awsElasticBlockStore, gcePersistentDisk, azureDisk…) were migrated to CSI and their in-tree code removed over several releases (about 1.25–1.31). Use CSI drivers. emptyDir, configMap, secret, projected, downwardAPI, hostPath, local and nfs remain built in.
DriverProvisionerModesFeaturesPlatform
AWS EBS CSIebs.csi.aws.comRWO RWOPgp3/io2, snapshots, online resize, encryption, modifyEKS add-on
AWS EFS CSIefs.csi.aws.comRWXaccess points, TLS, elasticEKS add-on
Secrets Store CSIsecrets-store.csi.k8s.ioinlineSecrets Manager / Vault / Key Vault, rotationany
GCE PD CSIpd.csi.storage.gke.ioRWO ROXregional PD, snapshotsGKE
Azure Disk CSIdisk.csi.azure.comRWOPremium/Ultra, snapshotsAKS
Azure Files CSIfile.csi.azure.comRWXSMB / NFSAKS
Longhorndriver.longhorn.ioRWO RWXreplication, backups, UIon-prem
Rook-Cephrook-ceph.rbd.csi.ceph.comRWO RWXblock, file, objecton-prem

kubectl get csidrivers
kubectl get csinodes worker-a -o yaml          # drivers on the node + allocatable volume count
kubectl -n kube-system get deploy,ds | grep -E "ebs|efs|secrets-store"
kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/ebs-csi-controller -c csi-provisioner --tail=50
kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/ebs-csi-controller -c csi-attacher --tail=50
kubectl -n kube-system logs ds/ebs-csi-node -c ebs-plugin --tail=50
§ 10.3INTERACTIVE

Real Jahez Projects

Project A — menu-media pipeline (EFS, RWX, emptyDir, configMap)

▶ menu-media data flow across the cluster
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Upload
A restaurant uploads a dish photo; menu-uploader on worker-a writes /media/originals/1043.jpg to EFS.
Step 2 · Resize
menu-resizer on worker-b sees the file immediately, renders thumbnails in a tmpfs work dir and writes them to /media/thumbs.
Step 3 · Serve
media-cdn-origin nginx on worker-c serves /thumbs/… read-only to CloudFront.
Step 4 · Storage path
Each Pod's volume directory on its node is an NFS mount of the EFS access point, through the mount target in that AZ. One claim, many Pods.
menu-media.yaml
# Project A — menu-media: restaurants upload photos, a resizer makes thumbnails,
# nginx serves them. One RWX EFS claim shared by three Deployments on any node.
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: menu-media
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteMany]
  storageClassName: efs-shared
  resources: { requests: { storage: 200Gi } }
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-uploader
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: menu-uploader } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: menu-uploader } }
    spec:
      securityContext: { runAsUser: 10001, fsGroup: 10001 }
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-uploader:3.2.0
        env:
        - { name: MEDIA_ROOT, value: /media/originals }
        volumeMounts:
        - { name: media, mountPath: /media }
        - { name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp }
      volumes:
      - name: media
        persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: menu-media }
      - name: tmp
        emptyDir: { sizeLimit: 512Mi }
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: menu-resizer
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: menu-resizer } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: menu-resizer } }
    spec:
      securityContext: { runAsUser: 10001, fsGroup: 10001 }
      containers:
      - name: resizer
        image: ghcr.io/jahez/menu-resizer:1.9.4
        args: ["--in=/media/originals", "--out=/media/thumbs", "--sizes=160,480,960"]
        resources:
          limits: { memory: 1Gi }
        volumeMounts:
        - { name: media, mountPath: /media }
        - { name: work, mountPath: /work }
      volumes:
      - name: media
        persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: menu-media }
      - name: work
        emptyDir: { medium: Memory, sizeLimit: 256Mi }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: media-nginx
  namespace: jahez-prod
data:
  default.conf: |
    server {
      listen 8080;
      location /thumbs/ { root /media; expires 7d; }
    }
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: media-cdn-origin
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: media-cdn-origin } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: media-cdn-origin } }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.27
        ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
        volumeMounts:
        - { name: media, mountPath: /media, readOnly: true }
        - { name: conf, mountPath: /etc/nginx/conf.d, readOnly: true }   # dir mount → hot-reload capable
      volumes:
      - name: media
        persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: menu-media, readOnly: true }
      - name: conf
        configMap: { name: media-nginx }

Project B — nightly orders-db snapshots (CronJob + VolumeSnapshot)

Uses the ebs-snapclass from §8.0 and the StatefulSet from §9.0. Ties this guide to the Jobs and CronJobs guides.

orders-db-snapshot-cronjob.yaml
# Project B — nightly VolumeSnapshot of every orders-db replica, keep 7 days.
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: db-snapshotter
  namespace: jahez-prod
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: db-snapshotter
  namespace: jahez-prod
rules:
- apiGroups: ["snapshot.storage.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["volumesnapshots"]
  verbs: ["create", "get", "list", "delete"]
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["persistentvolumeclaims"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: db-snapshotter
  namespace: jahez-prod
subjects:
- { kind: ServiceAccount, name: db-snapshotter, namespace: jahez-prod }
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: db-snapshotter
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: orders-db-snapshot
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  schedule: "30 0 * * *"
  timeZone: Asia/Riyadh
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2
      ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 86400
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: db-snapshotter
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
          - name: snap
            image: bitnami/kubectl:1.30
            command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
            args:
            - |
              set -eu
              D=$(date +%Y%m%d)
              for PVC in $(kubectl get pvc -l app=orders-db -o name | cut -d/ -f2); do
                cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
              apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
              kind: VolumeSnapshot
              metadata:
                name: ${PVC}-${D}
                labels: { app: orders-db, backup: nightly }
              spec:
                volumeSnapshotClassName: ebs-snapclass
                source: { persistentVolumeClaimName: ${PVC} }
              EOF
              done
              # prune snapshots older than 7 days (keeps EBS snapshots: deletionPolicy Retain)
              CUT=$(date -d "-7 days" +%Y%m%d 2>/dev/null || date -v-7d +%Y%m%d)
              kubectl get volumesnapshot -l backup=nightly -o name | while read S; do
                N=${S##*-}; [ "$N" -lt "$CUT" ] && kubectl delete "$S" || true
              done
⚠
Crash-consistent vs app-consistentAn EBS snapshot of a running Postgres is crash-consistent — Postgres recovers it like after a power cut. For PITR-grade backups, also ship WAL (pgBackRest / WAL-G to S3).
§ 10.4INTERACTIVE

Debugging Storage Problems

▶ Storage triage — six symptoms, their causes and fixes
1 / 6
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · PVC Pending
kubectl describe pvc events tell you which: WaitForFirstConsumer (fine), no persistent volumes available (static mismatch), or failed to provision (driver/IAM/quota).
Step 2 · Pod Pending
0/3 nodes are available: 3 node(s) had volume node affinity conflict → the PV's zone has no free node. Scale the node group in that AZ.
Step 3 · ContainerCreating
Multi-Attach error → the volume is still attached elsewhere (node died or old Pod not gone). Check kubectl get volumeattachment; wait for the 6-min force detach or taint the dead node out-of-service.
Step 4 · PVC Terminating
pvc-protection waits for Pods using it. Find them with the command below and delete them; the PVC then goes away.
Step 5 · Permission denied
The volume root is owned by root; the app runs as 10001. Set fsGroup (and fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch to avoid slow recursive chown on big volumes).
Step 6 · Disk full / Evicted
Read the eviction message; it names the emptyDir or the container. Fix sizeLimit, ephemeral-storage limits, or expand the PVC.
storage-debug.sh
kubectl describe pvc data-orders-db-0 -n jahez-prod            # Events section first
kubectl get events -n jahez-prod --field-selector involvedObject.name=data-orders-db-0
kubectl get pv $(kubectl get pvc data-orders-db-0 -n jahez-prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumeName}') -o yaml | grep -A6 nodeAffinity
kubectl get volumeattachment -o wide | grep pvc-
kubectl get pods -n jahez-prod -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.volumes[]?.persistentVolumeClaim.claimName=="data-orders-db-0") | .metadata.name'
kubectl taint node worker-a node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service=nodeshutdown:NoExecute   # dead node only!
kubectl get csinode worker-b -o jsonpath='{.spec.drivers[?(@.name=="ebs.csi.aws.com")].allocatable.count}'
kubectl exec -n jahez-prod orders-db-0 -- df -h /var/lib/postgresql/data
§ 10.5

Best Practices & Command Reference

⚡

Dynamic + WaitForFirstConsumer

Every zonal class uses WFFC; one class is the default.

🛡

Retain for production data

Class or PV policy Retain for DBs and uploads; Delete only for disposable data.

📏

Always set sizeLimit

Plus ephemeral-storage requests/limits so one Pod cannot fill a node.

🔐

Secrets: encrypt, scope, externalise

KMS envelope encryption, tight RBAC, Secrets Store CSI for payment keys.

📸

Snapshot before change

VolumeSnapshot before migrations and upgrades; nightly CronJob (§10.3).

🧭

Capacity per zone

Stateful volumes pin Pods to AZs: keep nodes in each AZ and spread replicas.

🚫

No hostPath for apps

PSA baseline/restricted on jahez-prod; hostPath only for system DaemonSets.

📈

Monitor volumes

Alert on kubelet_volume_stats_available_bytes < 20% and on Pending PVCs.

Command reference

kubectl-storage.sh
kubectl get sc
kubectl get pv
kubectl get pvc -A
kubectl get pvc -n jahez-prod -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,STATUS:.status.phase,VOL:.spec.volumeName,SIZE:.status.capacity.storage,CLASS:.spec.storageClassName
kubectl describe pvc <name> -n jahez-prod
kubectl get volumeattachment
kubectl get volumesnapshot,volumesnapshotcontent -A
kubectl patch pvc <name> -n jahez-prod -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"200Gi"}}}}'
kubectl patch pv <pv> -p '{"spec":{"persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy":"Retain"}}'
kubectl patch pv <pv> --type json -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/claimRef"}]'   # Released → Available
kubectl exec -n jahez-prod <pod> -- df -h
kubectl exec -n jahez-prod <pod> -- mount | grep -E "nvme|nfs|tmpfs"
kubectl debug node/worker-a -it --image=busybox -- chroot /host ls /var/lib/kubelet/pods

emptyDir medium"" (disk) Memory (tmpfs)

Q1 · Share a Volume Between Two Containers

ns: venus⏱ 6 minApplication Design & Buildeasy
In namespace venus create a Pod named log-share with two containers that share one volume.
  1. Container writer, image busybox:1.36, command: while true; do date >> /var/log/app/app.log; sleep 5; done
  2. Container reader, image busybox:1.36, command: tail -f /logs/app.log
  3. A volume named logs of type emptyDir with a size limit of 100Mi
  4. Mount it at /var/log/app in writer and at /logs (read-only) in reader
  5. Confirm the reader prints the writer's lines
📖 Docs to open in the exam: Volumes
Show solution · commands · YAML · diagram · verification

1 · Fastest path

commands.sh
kubectl create ns venus 2>/dev/null
kubectl run log-share -n venus --image=busybox:1.36 --dry-run=client -o yaml \
  --command -- sh -c 'while true; do date >> /var/log/app/app.log; sleep 5; done' > q1.yaml
# edit q1.yaml: rename container to writer, add reader + volume (see full YAML)
kubectl apply -f q1.yaml

2 · Full YAML

q1-log-share.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: log-share
  namespace: venus
spec:
  containers:
  - name: writer
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do date >> /var/log/app/app.log; sleep 5; done"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: logs
      mountPath: /var/log/app
  - name: reader
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "tail -f /logs/app.log"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: logs
      mountPath: /logs
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: logs
    emptyDir:
      sizeLimit: 100Mi

3 · What happens on the cluster

▶ Q1 on the lab cluster
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Object created
One Pod object is stored in etcd. Nothing exists on the workers yet.
Step 2 · Scheduled + folder created
The scheduler picks node01 (controlplane is tainted). The kubelet creates pods/<uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/logs/ before starting the containers.
Step 3 · Two mounts, one folder
writer sees it at /var/log/app, reader at /logs (read-only).
Step 4 · Verified
The reader's log stream shows the timestamps the writer appends.

4 · Verify

verify.sh
kubectl get pod log-share -n venus
kubectl logs log-share -n venus -c reader --tail=3
kubectl exec log-share -n venus -c reader -- touch /logs/x   # must fail (read-only)
expected-output.txt
NAME        READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
log-share   2/2     Running   0          40s
Sat Oct 31 13:01:05 UTC 2026
Sat Oct 31 13:01:10 UTC 2026
Sat Oct 31 13:01:15 UTC 2026
touch: /logs/x: Read-only file system

5 · Exam traps

  • The reader may log tail: can't open '/logs/app.log' for the first seconds — the writer has not created it yet. Use tail -F or wait; it is not a wrong answer.
  • kubectl run only creates one container — generate YAML with --dry-run=client -o yaml and add the second one by hand.
  • readOnly: true goes on the volumeMount, not on the volume.
  • Always pass -c <container> to kubectl logs/exec for multi-container Pods.
§ Q2INTERACTIVE

Q2 · A RAM-backed Scratch Volume

ns: mars⏱ 5 minApplication Design & Buildeasy
In namespace mars create a Pod cache-pod, image nginx:1.27, with a memory-backed scratch volume.
  1. Volume cache: emptyDir stored in memory, size limit 64Mi
  2. Mount it at /cache
  3. Container resources: requests memory 128Mi, limits memory 256Mi
  4. Prove the volume is a tmpfs
📖 Docs to open in the exam: Volumes
Show solution · commands · YAML · diagram · verification

1 · Fastest path

commands.sh
kubectl create ns mars 2>/dev/null
kubectl run cache-pod -n mars --image=nginx:1.27 --dry-run=client -o yaml > q2.yaml
# add resources, volumeMounts and volumes (see full YAML)
kubectl apply -f q2.yaml

2 · Full YAML

q2-cache-pod.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: cache-pod
  namespace: mars
spec:
  containers:
  - name: cache-pod
    image: nginx:1.27
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: 128Mi
      limits:
        memory: 256Mi
    volumeMounts:
    - name: cache
      mountPath: /cache
  volumes:
  - name: cache
    emptyDir:
      medium: Memory
      sizeLimit: 64Mi

3 · What happens on the cluster

▶ Q2 on the lab cluster
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Object created
Pod spec with a Memory emptyDir.
Step 2 · tmpfs mounted on node02
The kubelet creates the empty folder on disk and mounts a tmpfs of 64M on it. All bytes written there live in RAM.
Step 3 · Container view
/cache looks like a normal directory; df reveals tmpfs.
Step 4 · Memory accounting
Every byte in /cache is charged to the container's memory cgroup. Heap + cache > 256Mi → OOMKilled.

4 · Verify

verify.sh
kubectl exec -n mars cache-pod -- df -h /cache
kubectl exec -n mars cache-pod -- mount | grep /cache
expected-output.txt
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
tmpfs            64M     0   64M   0% /cache
tmpfs on /cache type tmpfs (rw,relatime,size=65536k)

5 · Exam traps

  • The value is Memory with a capital M. memory is rejected.
  • Without sizeLimit the tmpfs can grow up to the node's memory — always set it.
  • df shows the tmpfs size; it is not reserved RAM until files are written.

Q3 · Mount a ConfigMap and Update It Live

ns: jupiter⏱ 7 minApp Environment, Config & Securityeasy
In namespace jupiter:
  1. Create ConfigMap app-config with keys mode=production and level=info
  2. Create Pod config-reader, image busybox:1.36, command sleep 3600
  3. Mount the whole ConfigMap read-only at /etc/app-config
  4. Change level to debug and show that the file inside the running Pod changes without a restart
📖 Docs to open in the exam: Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap
Show solution · commands · YAML · diagram · verification

1 · Fastest path

commands.sh
kubectl create ns jupiter 2>/dev/null
kubectl create configmap app-config -n jupiter --from-literal=mode=production --from-literal=level=info
kubectl run config-reader -n jupiter --image=busybox:1.36 --dry-run=client -o yaml --command -- sleep 3600 > q3.yaml
# add volume + volumeMount, then:
kubectl apply -f q3.yaml
kubectl patch configmap app-config -n jupiter -p '{"data":{"level":"debug"}}'

2 · Full YAML

q3-config-reader.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
  namespace: jupiter
data:
  mode: production
  level: info
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: config-reader
  namespace: jupiter
spec:
  containers:
  - name: config-reader
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: config
      mountPath: /etc/app-config
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: config
    configMap:
      name: app-config

3 · What happens on the cluster

▶ Q3 on the lab cluster
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · ConfigMap created
Two keys stored in etcd.
Step 2 · Files written on node01
The kubelet fetches app-config and writes each key into a timestamped folder; ..data and key symlinks point to it.
Step 3 · Mounted
The container reads /etc/app-config/mode → production.
Step 4 · Live update
After the patch, the kubelet writes a new folder and swaps ..data. cat level returns debug without restarting the Pod.

4 · Verify

verify.sh
kubectl exec -n jupiter config-reader -- cat /etc/app-config/mode
kubectl exec -n jupiter config-reader -- ls -la /etc/app-config
# after the patch (wait up to ~60-90s):
kubectl exec -n jupiter config-reader -- cat /etc/app-config/level
expected-output.txt
production
lrwxrwxrwx  ..data -> ..2026_10_31_13_02_11.001
lrwxrwxrwx  level -> ..data/level
lrwxrwxrwx  mode -> ..data/mode
debug

5 · Exam traps

  • The update is not instant — up to about a minute. Re-check instead of restarting the Pod.
  • Environment variables from a ConfigMap never update; only volume files do.
  • --from-literal = one key per flag. --from-file=app.properties = one key named after the file.
§ Q4INTERACTIVE

Q4 · Replace One File Inside an Image Directory

ns: saturn⏱ 8 minApp Environment, Config & Securitymedium
In namespace saturn nginx must listen on port 8080 using a custom default.conf, without hiding the other files in /etc/nginx.
  1. Create ConfigMap nginx-conf with key default.conf containing a server block listening on 8080
  2. Create Deployment web, image nginx:1.27, 2 replicas, containerPort 8080
  3. Mount only the key default.conf at /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
  4. Expose it with a ClusterIP Service web on port 8080 and test it
📖 Docs to open in the exam: Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap
Show solution · commands · YAML · diagram · verification

1 · Fastest path

commands.sh
kubectl create ns saturn 2>/dev/null
cat > default.conf <<'EOF'
server {
  listen 8080;
  location / { return 200 "saturn ok\n"; }
}
EOF
kubectl create configmap nginx-conf -n saturn --from-file=default.conf
kubectl create deployment web -n saturn --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=2 --port=8080 --dry-run=client -o yaml > q4.yaml
# add volume + subPath mount (see full YAML), then:
kubectl apply -f q4.yaml
kubectl expose deployment web -n saturn --port=8080

2 · Full YAML

q4-web.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: nginx-conf
  namespace: saturn
data:
  default.conf: |
    server {
      listen 8080;
      location / { return 200 "saturn ok\n"; }
    }
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: saturn
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: web }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: web }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.27
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        volumeMounts:
        - name: conf
          mountPath: /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
          subPath: default.conf           # one file, rest of the dir stays
          readOnly: true
      volumes:
      - name: conf
        configMap:
          name: nginx-conf
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: saturn
spec:
  selector: { app: web }
  ports:
  - port: 8080
    targetPort: 8080

3 · What happens on the cluster

▶ Q4 on the lab cluster
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Objects
ConfigMap + Deployment (2 replicas).
Step 2 · Per-node copies
Each replica's node gets the ConfigMap folder and a volume-subpaths bind of the single file.
Step 3 · One file replaced
Inside the container only conf.d/default.conf comes from the ConfigMap; the rest of /etc/nginx is from the image.
Step 4 · Service + caveat
The Service reaches both replicas on 8080. Because of subPath, later ConfigMap edits require kubectl rollout restart.

4 · Verify

verify.sh
kubectl get pods -n saturn -l app=web -o wide
kubectl exec -n saturn deploy/web -- ls /etc/nginx
kubectl run tmp -n saturn --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- web:8080
expected-output.txt
web-6c9…-a1   1/1   Running   node01
web-6c9…-b2   1/1   Running   node02
conf.d  fastcgi_params  mime.types  modules  nginx.conf  scgi_params  uwsgi_params
saturn ok

5 · Exam traps

  • Mounting at /etc/nginx/conf.d without subPath also works here, but at /etc/nginx it would hide nginx.conf and nginx would fail.
  • With subPath, mountPath is the full file path, and subPath is the key name.
  • subPath mounts never receive ConfigMap updates — restart the rollout after changes.

Q5 · Consume a Secret as Files and as an Env Var

ns: neptune⏱ 7 minApp Environment, Config & Securityeasy
In namespace neptune:
  1. Create Secret db-cred with username=admin and password=S3cr3t!
  2. Create Pod db-client, image busybox:1.36, command sleep 3600
  3. Mount the Secret read-only at /etc/db-cred with file mode 0400
  4. Also expose username as env var DB_USER
📖 Docs to open in the exam: Secrets
Show solution · commands · YAML · diagram · verification

1 · Fastest path

commands.sh
kubectl create ns neptune 2>/dev/null
kubectl create secret generic db-cred -n neptune --from-literal=username=admin --from-literal='password=S3cr3t!'
kubectl run db-client -n neptune --image=busybox:1.36 --dry-run=client -o yaml --command -- sleep 3600 > q5.yaml
# add env + volume (see full YAML), then:
kubectl apply -f q5.yaml

2 · Full YAML

q5-db-client.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-cred
  namespace: neptune
type: Opaque
stringData:
  username: admin
  password: "S3cr3t!"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: db-client
  namespace: neptune
spec:
  containers:
  - name: db-client
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
    env:
    - name: DB_USER
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: db-cred
          key: username
    volumeMounts:
    - name: cred
      mountPath: /etc/db-cred
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: cred
    secret:
      secretName: db-cred
      defaultMode: 0400

3 · What happens on the cluster

▶ Q5 on the lab cluster
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Secret stored
kubectl create secret generic base64-encodes the values into etcd.
Step 2 · RAM on node02 only
The kubelet on node02 mounts a tmpfs and writes decoded files there. node01 never sees the Secret.
Step 3 · Files
/etc/db-cred/username and password, mode 0400, read-only.
Step 4 · Env var
DB_USER=admin is set when the container starts and never changes.

4 · Verify

verify.sh
kubectl exec -n neptune db-client -- cat /etc/db-cred/password; echo
kubectl exec -n neptune db-client -- ls -lL /etc/db-cred
kubectl exec -n neptune db-client -- printenv DB_USER
kubectl exec -n neptune db-client -- df -h /etc/db-cred
expected-output.txt
S3cr3t!
-r--------    1 root     root     5 username
-r--------    1 root     root     7 password
admin
tmpfs   …   /etc/db-cred

5 · Exam traps

  • ls -l shows the symlinks (lrwxrwxrwx). Use ls -lL to see the real file mode 0400.
  • In YAML, 0400 is octal; in JSON you must write decimal 256.
  • Quote values with ! or $ in the shell: --from-literal='password=S3cr3t!'.
  • The volume field is secretName, not name (configMap uses name).
§ Q6INTERACTIVE

Q6 · Create a PersistentVolume, a Claim and a Pod

ns: pluto⏱ 9 minApplication Design & Buildmedium
Create persistent storage for an nginx log directory.
  1. PersistentVolume pv-log: capacity 100Mi, access mode ReadWriteOnce, hostPath /pv/log, storageClassName manual, reclaim policy Retain
  2. In namespace pluto, PersistentVolumeClaim pvc-log requesting 50Mi, ReadWriteOnce, class manual
  3. Pod logger, image nginx:1.27, mounting the claim at /var/log/nginx
  4. Make sure the PVC is Bound and the Pod is Running
📖 Docs to open in the exam: Configure a Pod to Use a PersistentVolume
Show solution · commands · YAML · diagram · verification

1 · Fastest path

commands.sh
kubectl create ns pluto 2>/dev/null
# no imperative command for PV/PVC → copy from the docs page, then:
kubectl apply -f q6.yaml
kubectl get pv pv-log; kubectl get pvc -n pluto

2 · Full YAML

q6-pv-pvc-pod.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: pv-log
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 100Mi
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: manual
  hostPath:
    path: /pv/log
    type: DirectoryOrCreate
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: pvc-log
  namespace: pluto
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: manual
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50Mi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: logger
  namespace: pluto
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:1.27
    volumeMounts:
    - name: logs
      mountPath: /var/log/nginx
  volumes:
  - name: logs
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: pvc-log

3 · What happens on the cluster

▶ Q6 on the lab cluster
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · PV
Cluster-scoped PV with no namespace. Status Available.
Step 2 · PVC binds
Same class, compatible mode, 50Mi ≤ 100Mi → Bound. The whole 100Mi PV is now reserved for this claim.
Step 3 · Pod running
On node01 the kubelet bind-mounts node01's /pv/log into nginx. Log files appear on the node.
Step 4 · The hostPath trap
A Pod recreated on node02 sees node02's /pv/log. Fine for single-node exam clusters; on real clusters add nodeAffinity to the PV or use a real storage backend.

4 · Verify

verify.sh
kubectl get pv pv-log
kubectl get pvc pvc-log -n pluto
kubectl get pod logger -n pluto -o wide
kubectl exec -n pluto logger -- ls /var/log/nginx
expected-output.txt
NAME     CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS   CLAIM            STORAGECLASS
pv-log   100Mi      RWO            Retain           Bound    pluto/pvc-log    manual
NAME      STATUS   VOLUME   CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS
pvc-log   Bound    pv-log   100Mi      RWO            manual
logger    1/1      Running  …  node01
access.log  error.log

5 · Exam traps

  • PVs are not namespaced — never put namespace: on a PV.
  • PVC CAPACITY shows 100Mi (the PV size), not the 50Mi you asked for. That is correct.
  • If the class names differ (or one side omits it and a default class exists), the claim stays Pending — check storageClassName on both.
  • Pod volume uses persistentVolumeClaim.claimName; the PV name never appears in the Pod.

ns: mercury⏱ 8 minApplication Design & Buildmedium
The cluster has a StorageClass local-path. In namespace mercury:
  1. Create PVC data-pvc, 200Mi, ReadWriteOnce, class local-path
  2. Create Pod writer, image busybox:1.36, that runs echo hello > /data/hello.txt; sleep 3600 with the claim mounted at /data
  3. Delete the Pod, create it again, and prove /data/hello.txt still exists
📖 Docs to open in the exam: Persistent Volumes
Show solution · commands · YAML · diagram · verification

1 · Fastest path

commands.sh
kubectl get sc                                   # confirm the class name + binding mode
kubectl create ns mercury 2>/dev/null
kubectl apply -f q7.yaml
kubectl get pvc -n mercury -w                     # Pending → Bound once the Pod is scheduled
kubectl delete pod writer -n mercury --now
kubectl apply -f q7.yaml                          # PVC unchanged, Pod recreated

2 · Full YAML

q7-dynamic.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: data-pvc
  namespace: mercury
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: local-path
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 200Mi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: writer
  namespace: mercury
spec:
  containers:
  - name: writer
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "[ -f /data/hello.txt ] || echo hello > /data/hello.txt; sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: data
      mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: data
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: data-pvc

in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)

Step 1 · Pending is expected
With WaitForFirstConsumer nothing is provisioned until a Pod uses the claim.
Step 2 · Pod scheduled
The scheduler picks node02 and records it on the PVC.
Step 3 · Provisioned on node02
The local-path provisioner creates /opt/local-path-provisioner/pvc-…_mercury_data-pvc on node02 and a PV pinned to node02. The Pod writes hello.txt.
Step 4 · Data survives
The recreated Pod must run on node02 (PV nodeAffinity) and mounts the same folder.

4 · Verify

verify.sh
kubectl get pvc data-pvc -n mercury
kubectl get pv
kubectl exec -n mercury writer -- cat /data/hello.txt
expected-output.txt
NAME       STATUS   VOLUME          CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS
data-pvc   Bound    pvc-7f2c…      200Mi      RWO            local-path
NAME         CAPACITY  RECLAIM POLICY  STATUS  CLAIM             STORAGECLASS
pvc-7f2c…    200Mi     Delete          Bound   mercury/data-pvc  local-path
hello

5 · Exam traps

  • Do not "fix" a Pending PVC with WaitForFirstConsumer — create the Pod first.
  • Never set nodeName on the Pod: it skips the scheduler and the claim stays Pending.
  • Dynamic PVs default to Delete: deleting the PVC deletes the data.
  • Use the exact class name from kubectl get sc; a typo leaves the claim Pending forever.

Q8 · Fix a PVC That Stays Pending

ns: earth⏱ 8 minObservability & Maintenancemedium
In namespace earth, Pod earth-app is Pending because its claim earth-pvc never binds. PV earth-pv exists and must be used.
  1. Find why earth-pvc does not bind to earth-pv
  2. Fix the claim (keep the name earth-pvc) so it binds to earth-pv
  3. Make sure earth-app is Running. Do not modify the PV
📖 Docs to open in the exam: Persistent Volumes
Show solution · commands · YAML · diagram · verification

1 · Fastest path

commands.sh
kubectl describe pvc earth-pvc -n earth | tail -5
kubectl get pv earth-pv -o custom-columns=CAP:.spec.capacity.storage,MODES:.spec.accessModes,CLASS:.spec.storageClassName
kubectl get pvc earth-pvc -n earth -o yaml > q8.yaml
# edit q8.yaml: accessModes [ReadWriteOnce], storage 1Gi, storageClassName manual
#               remove status:, metadata.uid, resourceVersion, creationTimestamp, annotations
kubectl replace --force -f q8.yaml               # delete + recreate (spec is immutable)
kubectl delete pod earth-app -n earth --now && kubectl apply -f earth-app.yaml   # only if it doesn't recover

2 · Full YAML

q8-earth-pvc-fixed.yaml
# given (do not change)
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: earth-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 1Gi
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: manual
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/earth
---
# fixed claim
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: earth-pvc
  namespace: earth
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]       # was ReadWriteMany
  storageClassName: manual           # was standard
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi                   # was 2Gi

3 · What happens on the cluster

▶ Q8 on the lab cluster
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Symptom
Pod Pending, PVC Pending.
Step 2 · Diagnose
Compare PVC vs PV: access modes, size and class all mismatch. describe pvc shows storageclass "standard" not found or no persistent volumes available.
Step 3 · Fix
Most PVC spec fields are immutable (only the size can be increased), so recreate it with replace --force.
Step 4 · Running
The claim binds and the Pod starts.

4 · Verify

verify.sh
kubectl get pvc earth-pvc -n earth
kubectl get pod earth-app -n earth
expected-output.txt
NAME        STATUS   VOLUME     CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS
earth-pvc   Bound    earth-pv   1Gi        RWO            manual
NAME        READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
earth-app   1/1     Running   0          20s

5 · Exam traps

  • kubectl edit pvc on accessModes or storageClassName is rejected: spec is immutable after creation except resources.requests. Use replace --force.
  • A PVC in use can only be deleted once the Pod is gone (pvc-protection). replace --force may hang until you delete the Pod.
  • Strip status, uid and resourceVersion from exported YAML before replacing.
  • Requesting less than the PV size is fine; more is not.

  • Mounting the emptyDir over /usr/share/nginx/html hides the default page; that is intended here.

Q10 · Expose Pod Metadata and Limits as Files

ns: sun⏱ 7 minApp Environment, Config & Securitymedium
In namespace sun create Pod info-pod, image busybox:1.36, command sleep 3600, labels app=info, tier=backend, limits cpu 200m / memory 128Mi.
  1. Mount a downwardAPI volume at /etc/podinfo with files:
  2. labels → all Pod labels · name → Pod name
  3. cpu_limit → CPU limit in millicores (value 200) · mem_limit → memory limit in MiB (value 128)
📖 Docs to open in the exam: Downward API volume
Show solution · commands · YAML · diagram · verification

1 · Fastest path

commands.sh
kubectl create ns sun 2>/dev/null
kubectl run info-pod -n sun --image=busybox:1.36 --labels=app=info,tier=backend \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml --command -- sleep 3600 > q10.yaml
# add resources + downwardAPI volume (see full YAML)
kubectl apply -f q10.yaml

2 · Full YAML

q10-info-pod.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: info-pod
  namespace: sun
  labels:
    app: info
    tier: backend
spec:
  containers:
  - name: info-pod
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: 200m
        memory: 128Mi
    volumeMounts:
    - name: podinfo
      mountPath: /etc/podinfo
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: podinfo
    downwardAPI:
      items:
      - path: labels
        fieldRef:
          fieldPath: metadata.labels
      - path: name
        fieldRef:
          fieldPath: metadata.name
      - path: cpu_limit
        resourceFieldRef:
          containerName: info-pod
          resource: limits.cpu
          divisor: 1m
      - path: mem_limit
        resourceFieldRef:
          containerName: info-pod
          resource: limits.memory
          divisor: 1Mi

3 · What happens on the cluster

▶ Q10 on the lab cluster

in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)

Step 1 · Pod spec
Labels, limits and a downwardAPI volume with four items.
Step 2 · Written from the Pod itself
The kubelet reads its own Pod object and writes the files on node02's disk.
Step 3 · Values with divisors
cpu_limit=200 (divisor 1m), mem_limit=128 (divisor 1Mi).
Step 4 · Labels update
kubectl label pod info-pod release=v2 -n sun → the labels file changes.

4 · Verify

verify.sh
kubectl exec -n sun info-pod -- sh -c 'for f in labels name cpu_limit mem_limit; do echo "$f: $(cat /etc/podinfo/$f)"; done'
expected-output.txt
labels: app="info"
tier="backend"
name: info-pod
cpu_limit: 200
mem_limit: 128

5 · Exam traps

  • resourceFieldRef needs containerName in a volume (optional only for env vars).
  • Without divisor, CPU is rounded up to whole cores → 1, and memory is in bytes.
  • Use metadata.labels / metadata.annotations in volumes; as env vars only single keys like metadata.labels['app'] work.

Q11 · Combine Several Sources into One Mount

ns: titan⏱ 9 minApp Environment, Config & Securityhard
In namespace titan, Secret api-key (key token), ConfigMap api-config (key endpoint) and ServiceAccount titan-sa exist. Create Pod combined, image busybox:1.36, command sleep 3600, running as titan-sa.
  1. One volume mounted read-only at /etc/combined containing:
  2. api-token ← Secret key token · endpoint ← ConfigMap key endpoint
  3. sa-token ← a service-account token with audience vault, valid 3600 seconds
  4. namespace ← the Pod's namespace (downward API)
📖 Docs to open in the exam: Projected Volumes
Show solution · commands · YAML · diagram · verification

1 · Fastest path

commands.sh
kubectl create ns titan 2>/dev/null
kubectl create secret generic api-key -n titan --from-literal=token=abc123        # given in the exam
kubectl create configmap api-config -n titan --from-literal=endpoint=https://api.titan.local
kubectl create sa titan-sa -n titan
kubectl apply -f q11.yaml

2 · Full YAML

q11-combined.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: combined
  namespace: titan
spec:
  serviceAccountName: titan-sa
  containers:
  - name: combined
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: combined
      mountPath: /etc/combined
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: combined
    projected:
      sources:
      - secret:
          name: api-key
          items:
          - key: token
            path: api-token
      - configMap:
          name: api-config
          items:
          - key: endpoint
            path: endpoint
      - serviceAccountToken:
          audience: vault
          expirationSeconds: 3600
          path: sa-token
      - downwardAPI:
          items:
          - path: namespace
            fieldRef:
              fieldPath: metadata.namespace

Secret, ConfigMap and ServiceAccount already exist in titan.
Step 2 · One RAM folder
Projected volumes are tmpfs: the kubelet writes every source, plus a freshly requested token, into one folder.
Step 3 · One mount
/etc/combined contains four files from four sources.

The kubelet replaces sa-token before it expires.

https://api.titan.local
{"aud":["vault"],"exp":1793448000,"iat":1793444400,"iss":"https://kubernetes.default.svc…

5 · Exam traps

  • The field is projected.sources (a list); each item is secret, configMap, serviceAccountToken or downwardAPI.
  • Inside projected sources, a Secret is referenced with name, not secretName.
  • expirationSeconds minimum is 600.
  • All sources must be in the Pod's namespace.

ns: io⏱ 10 minApplication Design & Buildmedium
In namespace io:

  3. Each replica gets its own 100Mi ReadWriteOnce claim from class local-path, named via template data, mounted at /usr/share/nginx/html
  4. Write each Pod's hostname to index.html, delete db-0, and prove it comes back with its own data

Show solution · commands · YAML · diagram · verification

1 · Fastest path

commands.sh
kubectl create ns io 2>/dev/null
kubectl apply -f q12.yaml
kubectl rollout status sts/db -n io

2 · Full YAML

q12-statefulset.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: db
  namespace: io
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: db
  ports:
  - port: 80
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: db
  namespace: io
spec:
  serviceName: db
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: db
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.27
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: data
    spec:
      accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
      storageClassName: local-path
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 100Mi

Q13 · Keep Data When a Claim Is Deleted

ns: europa⏱ 9 minObservability & Maintenancehard
PV europa-pv (hostPath /mnt/europa, class manual, reclaim policy Delete) is bound to claim europa-pvc in namespace europa. The claim must be removed but the data kept.
  1. Change the PV so its data is kept when the claim is deleted
  2. Delete Pod old-app and claim europa-pvc
  3. Create claim europa-pvc-2 (1Gi, RWO, class manual) bound to europa-pv
  4. Create Pod reader (busybox, sleep 3600) mounting it at /data and show the old file
📖 Docs to open in the exam: Persistent Volumes
Show solution · commands · YAML · diagram · verification

1 · Fastest path

commands.sh
kubectl patch pv europa-pv -p '{"spec":{"persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy":"Retain"}}'
kubectl delete pod old-app -n europa --now
kubectl delete pvc europa-pvc -n europa
kubectl get pv europa-pv                                   # STATUS Released
kubectl patch pv europa-pv --type json -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/claimRef"}]'
kubectl get pv europa-pv                                   # STATUS Available
kubectl apply -f q13.yaml

2 · Full YAML

q13-rebind.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: europa-pvc-2
  namespace: europa
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: manual
  volumeName: europa-pv              # pin to this PV
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: reader
  namespace: europa
spec:
  containers:
  - name: reader
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: data
      mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: data
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: europa-pvc-2

3 · What happens on the cluster

▶ Q13 on the lab cluster
1 / 5
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Retain first
Patch the PV's reclaim policy while it is still bound.
Step 2 · Delete the claim
Pod first (pvc-protection), then the PVC. The files in /mnt/europa stay.
Step 3 · Released
The PV keeps the old claimRef and refuses new claims.
Step 4 · Available again
Removing claimRef makes it Available; volumeName binds the new claim to exactly this PV.
Step 5 · Old data visible
The new Pod reads the old file.

4 · Verify

verify.sh
kubectl get pv europa-pv
kubectl get pvc europa-pvc-2 -n europa
kubectl exec -n europa reader -- ls /data
expected-output.txt
NAME        CAPACITY  RECLAIM POLICY  STATUS  CLAIM                 STORAGECLASS
europa-pv   1Gi       Retain          Bound   europa/europa-pvc-2   manual
europa-pvc-2   Bound   europa-pv   1Gi   RWO   manual
report-2026.csv

5 · Exam traps

  • Patch the policy before deleting the claim — with Delete the volume is reclaimed immediately.
  • A Released PV never binds again on its own; removing claimRef is required.
  • Deleting a PVC used by a Pod hangs in Terminating until the Pod is deleted.

  4. Prove the root filesystem is read-only

Show solution · commands · YAML · diagram · verification

1 · Fastest path

commands.sh
kubectl create ns ganymede 2>/dev/null
kubectl run secure-web -n ganymede --image=nginx:1.27 --dry-run=client -o yaml > q14.yaml
# add securityContext + 3 emptyDirs (see full YAML)
kubectl apply -f q14.yaml
kubectl logs secure-web -n ganymede      # if it crashes, the log names the path it could not write

2 · Full YAML

q14-secure-web.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secure-web
  namespace: ganymede
spec:
  containers:
  - name: secure-web
    image: nginx:1.27
    securityContext:
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
    volumeMounts:
    - name: cache
      mountPath: /var/cache/nginx
    - name: run
      mountPath: /var/run
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp
  volumes:
  - name: cache
    emptyDir: {}
  - name: run
    emptyDir: {}
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}

3 · What happens on the cluster

▶ Q14 on the lab cluster
1 / 4
in container — the mountPath the app seeson node — the real host path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/volumes/kubernetes.io~<type>/<volume-name> (shown as pods/<uid>/volumes/…)arrow — bind mount (node dir → container path)
↔ swipe the diagram to pan · tap Next to advance
Step 1 · Requirement
The image filesystem must be read-only.
Step 2 · Without volumes
nginx fails at start: mkdir() "/var/cache/nginx/client_temp" failed (30: Read-only file system).
Step 3 · Writable holes
Three emptyDirs are mounted exactly where nginx writes. Mounts are not part of the read-only root.
Step 4 · Verified
Writing under /etc fails; nginx is Running and serves pages.

4 · Verify

verify.sh
kubectl get pod secure-web -n ganymede
kubectl exec -n ganymede secure-web -- touch /etc/test
kubectl exec -n ganymede secure-web -- touch /tmp/test && echo tmp-writable
expected-output.txt
NAME         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
secure-web   1/1     Running   0          12s
touch: cannot touch '/etc/test': Read-only file system
tmp-writable

5 · Exam traps

  • readOnlyRootFilesystem is a container securityContext field, not a Pod-level one.
  • Read the crash log: it tells you exactly which path needs a volume.
  • Mounting one emptyDir at /var would also work but hides files from the image — mount the narrowest paths.
